docs.title: 2.17 — IAsyncEnumerable and await foreach
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.16 Async exceptions · Next: 2.18 Thread safety

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• IAsyncEnumerable<T> is IEnumerable<T> where getting the next item is itself awaitable.
  • It solves a real gap: Task<List<T>> gives you everything at once, and IEnumerable<T> cannot await. Async streams give you items one at a time, as they arrive.
  • Consume it with await foreach. Pass cancellation with [EnumeratorCancellation].

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Before C# 8 there were two options for returning a sequence from an async method, and both had a flaw:

Task<List<Order>> GetOrdersAsync();   // must build the WHOLE list before returning
IEnumerable<Order> GetOrders();       // streams one at a time, but cannot await

The first loses streaming — a million rows means a million objects in memory before the caller sees one. The second cannot do async I/O, so it blocks a thread on every read.

IAsyncEnumerable<T> gives you both: stream one item at a time, and await between items.

A picture: a conveyor belt from a warehouse rather than a delivery van. The van (Task<List<T>>) turns up once with everything, and you wait for the whole load. The belt delivers items as they are picked, you start working on the first one immediately, and you can stop the belt whenever you have enough.

docs.title: Producing one
docs.text:
Same as a normal iterator (2.4), but async with IAsyncEnumerable<T>:

public async IAsyncEnumerable<Order> StreamOrdersAsync(
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    await using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
    await connection.OpenAsync(ct);

    await using var command = new SqlCommand("SELECT * FROM Orders", connection);
    await using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);

    while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))          // await INSIDE the iterator
    {
        yield return new Order
        {
            Id    = reader.GetGuid(0),
            Total = reader.GetDecimal(1)
        };
    }
}

Note there is no return type of Task — it is async IAsyncEnumerable<T>, and you still use yield return. The compiler builds an async state machine that also implements IAsyncEnumerator<T>.

docs.title: Consuming one
docs.text:
await foreach (var order in StreamOrdersAsync(ct))
{
    Console.WriteLine(order.Total);
}

await foreach calls MoveNextAsync() — which returns a ValueTask<bool> — and awaits it before each item.

docs.title: [EnumeratorCancellation] — the bit people get wrong
docs.text:
Look again at that parameter attribute. Without it, cancellation silently does nothing.

The problem: await foreach can supply its own token via WithCancellation(...), and the method also has a ct parameter. Which one wins?

// The consumer supplies a token here
await foreach (var o in StreamOrdersAsync().WithCancellation(ct))

[EnumeratorCancellation] tells the compiler "wire the token from WithCancellation into this parameter". Without the attribute, ct stays at its default value of None and cancellation is ignored entirely — with no warning.

So the two ways to cancel are:

// Pass it directly as an argument
await foreach (var o in StreamOrdersAsync(ct)) { }

// Or via WithCancellation — needs [EnumeratorCancellation] to work
await foreach (var o in StreamOrdersAsync().WithCancellation(ct)) { }

Always add the attribute. It costs nothing and makes both forms work.

docs.title: LINQ over async streams
docs.text:
The standard LINQ operators do not work on IAsyncEnumerable<T> — they are built for IEnumerable<T>. You need the System.Linq.Async NuGet package:

var expensive = await StreamOrdersAsync(ct)
    .Where(o => o.Total > 1000)
    .Take(10)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

.NET 10 began bringing some of these into the base library, but for now the package is the usual answer.

docs.title: Where it earns its place in ASP.NET Core
Streaming a large API response
docs.text:
[HttpGet("orders/stream")]
public async IAsyncEnumerable<OrderDto> Stream(
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (var order in _repo.StreamAllAsync(ct))
        yield return _mapper.ToDto(order);
}

ASP.NET Core understands IAsyncEnumerable<T> return types natively. It serialises items to the response as they are produced, so:

  • Memory stays flat regardless of how many rows there are.
  • The client starts receiving data almost immediately rather than after the full query.
  • If the client disconnects, ct fires and the query stops.

Compare with returning Task<List<OrderDto>> for a million rows: a million DTOs in memory, one enormous JSON string built in memory, and nothing sent until it is all ready.

docs.title: EF Core
docs.text:
AsAsyncEnumerable() streams rows instead of buffering them:

await foreach (var order in _db.Orders.AsAsyncEnumerable().WithCancellation(ct))
{
    await ProcessAsync(order, ct);
}

⚠️ The database connection stays open for the whole loop. If processing each item is slow, you are holding a connection from the pool for a long time. For heavy per-item work, read in batches instead:

const int BatchSize = 500;
var skip = 0;

while (true)
{
    var batch = await _db.Orders.OrderBy(o => o.Id)
        .Skip(skip).Take(BatchSize).ToListAsync(ct);

    if (batch.Count == 0) break;

    foreach (var order in batch)
        await ProcessAsync(order, ct);      // connection already released

    skip += BatchSize;
}

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Reading a huge file line by line without loading it, and without blocking:

public async IAsyncEnumerable<LogEntry> ParseLogAsync(
    string path,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(path);

    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync(ct) is { } line)     // pattern match: not null
    {
        if (TryParse(line, out var entry))
            yield return entry;
    }
}

Used with early exit:

await foreach (var entry in ParseLogAsync("huge.log", ct))
{
    if (entry.Level == LogLevel.Error)
    {
        _logger.LogWarning("First error at {Time}", entry.Timestamp);
        break;               // stops reading — the file reader is disposed properly
    }
}

A 10 GB file where the first error is on line 40 reads 40 lines. Memory stays at one line. And because break disposes the enumerator, the using inside the iterator runs and the file handle closes.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is IAsyncEnumerable<T> and what problem does it solve?

It is a sequence where fetching each item is itself asynchronous. Before it existed you had to choose between Task<List<T>>, which forces you to build the entire collection before returning anything, and IEnumerable<T>, which streams but cannot await — so any I/O inside it blocks a thread. Async streams give you both: items are produced one at a time as they become available, and the producer can await between them. You consume it with await foreach.

Q: What does [EnumeratorCancellation] do?

It connects the token supplied by the consumer through WithCancellation to the CancellationToken parameter of your iterator method. Without the attribute, that parameter just keeps its default value of CancellationToken.None, so cancellation silently does nothing — the compiler has no way to know which parameter should receive the consumer's token. It is easy to miss because there is no error, just cancellation that quietly fails to work.

Q: When would you use it in ASP.NET Core?

Mainly for streaming large responses. ASP.NET Core supports returning IAsyncEnumerable<T> directly from an action and serialises items as they are produced, so memory stays flat and the client starts receiving data immediately rather than after the whole result set is built. For a query returning hundreds of thousands of rows that is the difference between a predictable memory profile and an out-of-memory exception. It is also useful for background processing pipelines where you want to start work on early items while later ones are still being fetched.

Q: What is the catch with AsAsyncEnumerable in EF Core?

The database connection stays open for the entire duration of the loop, because rows are being streamed as you consume them. If the work you do per item is slow, you are holding a pooled connection for a long time, and under load that can exhaust the pool. For lightweight per-item work it is fine; for anything heavy I would read in batches with Skip and Take instead, so the connection is released between batches.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] means cancellation silently does nothing.
  • Standard LINQ does not work on IAsyncEnumerable<T>. You need the System.Linq.Async package.
  • AsAsyncEnumerable holds a database connection for the whole loop. Batch instead if per-item work is slow.
  • You cannot use await foreach in a non-async method. The whole call chain must be async.
  • Enumerating twice runs the source twice, exactly as with IEnumerable. See 2.6.
  • Returning IAsyncEnumerable<T> from a controller means you cannot easily set a status code partway through — the response has already started once the first item is written.
  • Exceptions thrown mid-stream in a controller action arrive after headers are sent, so the client gets a truncated response rather than a clean error.

docs.title: 2.18 — Thread Safety: lock, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked, volatile
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.17 IAsyncEnumerable · Next: 2.19 Parallel programming

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Thread safety means your code still gives the right answer when several threads run it at the same time. Nothing in C# is thread-safe automatically — you have to make it so.

  • lock is the default tool. Simple, fast, covers most cases — but you cannot await inside it.
  • SemaphoreSlim is the async-friendly alternative, because it has WaitAsync.
  • Interlocked updates a single number atomically with no lock at all — much faster when it fits.
  • The real answer in ASP.NET Core is usually do not share mutable state at all.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Every term this note uses, and — importantly — what kind of C# thing each one actually is.

Term What it is in C# What it means Thread safe a property of your code Several threads can run it at once and the result is still correct. Race condition a bug, not an API The result depends on which thread happens to win. Works in testing, fails under load. Atomic a property of an operation It cannot be interrupted halfway. Other threads see it as either not started or completely done — never partly done. Critical section a block of code Code that only one thread may be inside at a time. Mutual exclusion a guarantee The rule that enforces a critical section: one in, everyone else waits. lock a C# keyword Marks a critical section. lock (x) { ... } compiles into Monitor.Enter(x) and Monitor.Exit(x) wrapped in a try/finally. Monitor a static class in System.Threading What lock actually calls underneath. You rarely write it by hand. SemaphoreSlim a class you create with new Holds a count of permits. Lets N threads through and makes the rest wait. Uniquely, it has an async wait (WaitAsync). Interlocked a static class in System.Threading Methods that read-modify-write a number as one single CPU instruction, so no lock is needed. volatile a field modifier, like readonly Tells the compiler and CPU never to cache this field in a register. Every read goes to real memory. Thread affinity a property of a lock The lock must be released by the same thread that took it. This is exactly why await inside lock is banned. Deadlock a bug Two threads each holding a lock the other one needs. Neither can ever continue.

The three you will actually type are lock, SemaphoreSlim and Interlocked. volatile is included because it gets asked about, not because you should use it.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
count++ looks like one instruction. It is three:

  1. Read the current value from memory
  2. Add one to it
  3. Write the result back

Two threads running that at the same time can interleave:

Thread A Thread B count 1 reads 5 5 2 reads 5 5 3 computes 6 5 4 computes 6 5 5 writes 6 6 6 writes 6 6

Two increments, one result. That is a race condition — the outcome depends on timing, so it works in testing and fails occasionally under load.

The picture: two people updating the same paper tally. Both read "5", both cross it out and write "6". One increment is silently lost. The fix is that only one person may hold the pen at a time.

docs.title: lock — one thread at a time
docs.text:
private readonly object _gate = new();
private int _count;

public void Increment()
{
    lock (_gate)          // only one thread inside this block at any moment
    {
        _count++;
    }
}

Rules that matter:

lock (this)              // ✗ BAD — external code can lock on your instance too
lock (typeof(MyClass))   // ✗ BAD — shared across the whole app domain
lock ("some string")     // ✗ BAD — string literals are interned and shared
lock (_gate)             // ✓ a private readonly object, used only for this

Always lock on a private readonly object that exists only to be a lock. Locking on anything publicly reachable means unrelated code can deadlock you.

.NET 9 added a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type which is faster and clearer:

private readonly Lock _gate = new();     // .NET 9+

docs.title: ⚠️ You cannot await inside a lock
docs.text:
lock (_gate)
{
    await SaveAsync();      // COMPILE ERROR
}

The compiler blocks it, and rightly so. A lock is tied to a specific thread — it must be released by the same thread that took it. After an await, your code may resume on a different thread, which could not release the lock. Deadlock.

docs.title: SemaphoreSlim — the async-safe lock
docs.text:
private readonly SemaphoreSlim _gate = new(1, 1);   // 1 = acts like a lock

public async Task UpdateAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await _gate.WaitAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        await _db.SaveAsync(order, ct);      // await IS allowed here
    }
    finally
    {
        _gate.Release();                     // MUST be in finally
    }
}

The (1, 1) means "initially 1 slot free, maximum 1 slot" — so it behaves like a mutex. Larger numbers make it a throttle:

private readonly SemaphoreSlim _throttle = new(10, 10);   // max 10 at once

The finally is not optional. If an exception escapes without releasing, that slot is gone forever and every future caller blocks. That is a total, permanent hang — a genuinely nasty production bug.

docs.title: Interlocked — atomic without locking
docs.text:
For simple numeric updates, the CPU can do it in one instruction:

private int _count;

Interlocked.Increment(ref _count);          // ++ atomically
Interlocked.Decrement(ref _count);
Interlocked.Add(ref _count, 5);
Interlocked.Exchange(ref _count, 0);        // set, returning the old value

// Set only if it currently equals the expected value
Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _count, newValue, expectedValue);

Much faster than a lock — no blocking, no context switches. Use it whenever your shared state is a single number or reference. It cannot help with anything more complex.

docs.title: volatile — usually not what you want
docs.text:
volatile prevents the compiler and CPU from caching or reordering reads of a field:

private volatile bool _stopping;

// Thread A
_stopping = true;

// Thread B
while (!_stopping) { DoWork(); }    // without volatile, may never see the change

Without volatile, the JIT may hoist _stopping into a register and loop forever on a stale value.

But volatile does not make operations atomic. _count++ on a volatile field is still three steps and still races.

In practice you rarely want it. For a stop flag, use CancellationToken (2.14). For counters, use Interlocked. volatile is for lock-free algorithms, which almost nobody should be writing.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: Situation Use Simple counter or flag swap Interlocked Short synchronous critical section lock Critical section containing await SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync Limiting concurrency to N SemaphoreSlim(n, n) Shared collection A concurrent collection (2.3) Anything else Restructure so nothing is shared

docs.title: The best answer: do not share
docs.text:
In ASP.NET Core, most thread-safety problems come from state that should never have been shared. The framework already gives you the tools to avoid it:

// PROBLEM — a singleton holding mutable state needs locking everywhere
public class OrderService
{
    private List<Order> _pending = new();     // shared across ALL requests
}

// SOLUTION — scoped lifetime means one instance per request.
// No sharing, so no locking needed at all.
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();

Scoped services are the answer to most of this. Each request gets its own instance, so there is nothing to race over. Reserve singletons for things that are genuinely stateless or genuinely designed for concurrency. See 6.3.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A rate limiter using SemaphoreSlim as a throttle:

public class ApiClient(HttpClient http) : IDisposable
{
    // Allow at most 5 concurrent outbound calls
    private readonly SemaphoreSlim _throttle = new(5, 5);

    public async Task<T?> GetAsync<T>(string url, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await _throttle.WaitAsync(ct);
        try
        {
            return await http.GetFromJsonAsync<T>(url, ct);
        }
        finally
        {
            _throttle.Release();      // ALWAYS, even on exception or cancellation
        }
    }

    public void Dispose() => _throttle.Dispose();
}

And the Interlocked version of a metrics counter, which needs no lock at all:

public class RequestCounter
{
    private long _total;
    private long _failed;

    public void RecordSuccess() => Interlocked.Increment(ref _total);

    public void RecordFailure()
    {
        Interlocked.Increment(ref _total);
        Interlocked.Increment(ref _failed);
    }

    // Reading a long is NOT atomic on 32-bit systems, so read it properly
    public (long Total, long Failed) Snapshot() =>
        (Interlocked.Read(ref _total), Interlocked.Read(ref _failed));
}

⚠️ Note that the two increments in RecordFailure are individually atomic but not atomic together — a reader could see _total updated and _failed not yet. For metrics that is acceptable. If it were not, you would need a lock.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is count++ not thread-safe?

Because it is three separate operations: read the value, add one, write it back. Two threads can both read the same starting value before either writes, so both compute the same result and one increment is lost. The failure depends entirely on timing, which is why it passes tests and fails intermittently under production load. Interlocked.Increment fixes it by doing the whole read-modify-write as a single atomic CPU instruction.

Q: Why can't you await inside a lock?

Because a lock has thread affinity — it must be released by the same thread that acquired it. After an await, the continuation can resume on a completely different thread, which would then try to release a lock it does not own. The compiler rejects it outright rather than letting you create that deadlock. When you need mutual exclusion around async work you use SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync, because a semaphore is not tied to a thread.

Q: What should you lock on?

A private readonly object that exists solely as a lock. Locking on this, on a type, or on a string literal is dangerous because those are all reachable from outside your class — other code can take the same lock and deadlock you in ways that are extremely hard to trace. String literals are especially bad because they are interned, so two unrelated classes locking on the same literal share a lock. In .NET 9 there is a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type which is both clearer and faster.

Q: What is the best way to handle shared state in ASP.NET Core?

Usually to not have any. Most thread-safety problems there come from putting mutable state in a singleton, which is then shared across every concurrent request. Registering the service as scoped gives each request its own instance and the problem disappears entirely — no locks, no races, nothing to reason about. I would only reach for synchronisation primitives when state genuinely must be shared, like a cache or a counter, and even then a ConcurrentDictionary or Interlocked usually beats a hand-written lock.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Locking on this, a type, or a string literal. All publicly reachable, all can deadlock you from outside.
  • Forgetting Release() in a finally. One leaked semaphore slot hangs every future caller permanently.
  • volatile does not make operations atomic. It only prevents caching and reordering.
  • Two atomic operations are not atomic together. A reader can see a half-updated pair.
  • Holding a lock while doing I/O serialises your whole application on that call.
  • Nested locks in different orders deadlock. Always take locks in a consistent order.
  • lock in an async method is a compile error — but Monitor.Enter around an await is not, and it is a real deadlock. Do not work around the compiler.
  • long reads and writes are not atomic on 32-bit platforms. Use Interlocked.Read.

docs.title: 2.19 — Parallel.For, PLINQ, and When Not to Use Them
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 2. Collections, LINQ and Async Prev: 2.18 Thread safety · Next: 3.1 .NET history

Markers: ⭐ ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Parallel ≠ async. Parallel means "use many CPU cores on one job". Async means "do not block a thread while waiting".
  • Parallel.For and PLINQ are for CPU-bound work over lots of items. They are almost always wrong for I/O.
  • In ASP.NET Core they are usually a mistake, because the server is already busy running other requests in parallel.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
These two words get confused constantly, and the distinction is the point of this note.

Async is about waiting efficiently. Your code asks the network for something and gets on with other work instead of standing idle. It does not make anything faster — it stops threads being wasted.

Parallel is about working faster. You split a computation across CPU cores so it finishes sooner. It genuinely reduces wall-clock time, but only for work that actually uses the CPU.

A picture: one cook waiting for a pot to boil versus four cooks chopping vegetables.

The waiting cook should go and do something else meanwhile — that is async. It does not matter how many cooks you have; the pot boils at its own pace. But chopping a mountain of vegetables genuinely goes four times faster with four cooks — that is parallelism.

Using parallelism for waiting is like hiring four cooks to stand and watch the same pot.

docs.title: Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach
docs.text:
// Sequential — one core
foreach (var image in images)
    Resize(image);

// Parallel — all available cores
Parallel.ForEach(images, image => Resize(image));

The runtime splits the collection across threads and manages the work. For genuinely CPU-heavy work over many items, this scales close to linearly with core count.

Controlling how many run at once:

Parallel.ForEach(
    images,
    new ParallelOptions
    {
        MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4,
        CancellationToken = ct
    },
    image => Resize(image));

docs.title: Parallel.ForEachAsync (.NET 6+)
docs.text:
This one is genuinely useful, and it is the exception to "parallel is not for I/O". It runs async operations with a concurrency limit:

await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    urls,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 10, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (url, token) =>
    {
        var data = await http.GetStringAsync(url, token);
        await SaveAsync(data, token);
    });

This is the clean solution to the throttling problem from 2.12 — instead of SemaphoreSlim wrapped around a WhenAll, you get a built-in concurrency cap. Prefer this for "call a service for each of these 1,000 items, but not all at once".

docs.title: PLINQ — AsParallel()
docs.text:
// Sequential
var results = numbers.Where(IsPrime).ToList();

// Parallel — one word added
var results = numbers.AsParallel().Where(IsPrime).ToList();

Options:

numbers.AsParallel()
    .WithDegreeOfParallelism(4)
    .WithCancellation(ct)
    .AsOrdered()                    // preserve input order (costs performance)
    .Where(IsPrime)
    .ToList();

⚠️ PLINQ does not preserve order by default. Results come back in whatever order the threads finish. If order matters you need AsOrdered(), which adds buffering and sorting overhead and eats into the benefit.

docs.title: When parallelism actually pays
docs.text:
There is a fixed cost: partitioning the work, spinning up threads, coordinating, and merging results. That cost has to be smaller than what you save.

// ✓ WORTH IT — expensive work, many items
Parallel.ForEach(images, img => ApplyComplexFilter(img));

// ✗ NOT WORTH IT — trivial work, overhead dominates
Parallel.ForEach(numbers, n => n * 2);       // SLOWER than a plain loop

The rough rule: the per-item work needs to be meaningfully more expensive than the coordination overhead, and there need to be enough items to spread across cores. A hundred items of trivial work will be slower in parallel. A hundred thousand items of real computation will be much faster.

Always measure. BenchmarkDotNet exists for exactly this — 19.14.

docs.title: ⚠️ Why this is usually wrong in ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
This is the part interviewers care about.

A web server is already parallel. It is handling many requests at once, spread across all your cores. Those cores are not sitting idle waiting for you to use them.

When one request calls Parallel.ForEach, it grabs threads from the same shared pool that serves every other request. So:

  • One request gets faster.
  • Every other request gets slower, because the pool is now busier.
  • Under load, requests queue and overall throughput drops.

You have optimised one request at the expense of total capacity. On a server, throughput usually matters more than the latency of any single request.

// In a controller — usually the wrong instinct
[HttpPost("process")]
public IActionResult Process(List<Item> items)
{
    Parallel.ForEach(items, ProcessItem);   // steals threads from other requests
    return Ok();
}

When it is defensible: the work is genuinely CPU-heavy, takes seconds, and the endpoint is low-traffic — a nightly report, an admin-only bulk operation. Even then, MaxDegreeOfParallelism should be capped so it cannot consume every core.

The better answer for heavy work is usually to push it out of the request entirely — onto a background service or a queue — so the request returns immediately and the work happens where it cannot hurt request throughput. See 21.1.

docs.title: Never use Parallel.ForEach with async lambdas
docs.text:
// BROKEN — this is async void
Parallel.ForEach(urls, async url => await http.GetStringAsync(url));

Parallel.ForEach takes an Action<T>, so an async lambda becomes async void (2.15). The loop returns immediately with all the work still running, unobserved, and any exception crashes the process.

Use Parallel.ForEachAsync or Task.WhenAll instead.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The three ways to handle a batch, and when each is right:

// 1. I/O-bound, all at once — fine for a handful of items
var results = await Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(id => FetchAsync(id, ct)));

// 2. I/O-bound, throttled — the right answer for hundreds or thousands
var results = new ConcurrentBag<Result>();
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    ids,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 10, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (id, token) => results.Add(await FetchAsync(id, token)));

// 3. CPU-bound — genuine parallelism across cores
var results = items
    .AsParallel()
    .WithCancellation(ct)
    .Select(ExpensiveTransform)
    .ToList();

Note the ConcurrentBag in the second example. Writing to a plain List<T> from a parallel loop will corrupt it — see 2.3. This is one of the most common bugs in parallel code:

var results = new List<Result>();
Parallel.ForEach(items, item =>
{
    results.Add(Process(item));      // ✗ RACE — List is not thread-safe
});

The failure is nasty because it is intermittent: sometimes you lose items, sometimes you get a corrupted internal array, sometimes it throws IndexOutOfRangeException from inside Add.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between parallel and asynchronous?

Async is about not blocking a thread while waiting for something external — a network call or a disk read. It does not make the operation faster; it frees the thread to do other work during the wait. Parallel is about using multiple CPU cores to complete a computation sooner. So async is the answer for I/O-bound work and parallelism is the answer for CPU-bound work. Using parallelism for I/O just occupies several threads all doing nothing, which is strictly worse than one async call.

Q: Why is Parallel.ForEach usually wrong in ASP.NET Core?

Because the server is already parallel — it is handling many requests concurrently across all the cores. Threads come from a shared pool, so when one request parallelises, it takes capacity away from every other request. That makes one request faster and everything else slower, and under load overall throughput drops. On a server, total throughput normally matters more than the latency of an individual request. If the work is genuinely heavy, the better answer is to move it out of the request onto a background service or queue.

Q: When does parallelism actually help?

When the work is CPU-bound, there are enough items to spread across cores, and the per-item cost is significantly larger than the coordination overhead. Partitioning, thread management and merging results all cost something, so parallelising trivial work over a small collection is slower than a plain loop. It also has to be work that can be done independently — if every iteration needs a lock on shared state, you have serialised it again and paid the overhead for nothing. And I would always measure rather than assume.

Q: What is Parallel.ForEachAsync for?

It runs asynchronous operations over a collection with a configurable concurrency limit, which is the missing piece between Task.WhenAll and manual throttling. WhenAll over a thousand items starts a thousand operations at once, which exhausts connections and gets you rate-limited. Before .NET 6 you would wrap a SemaphoreSlim around it; now Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism does it cleanly. Despite the name it is about controlled concurrency for I/O, not CPU parallelism.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Writing to a List<T> from a parallel loop corrupts it. Use a concurrent collection or collect per-thread results.
  • Parallel.ForEach with an async lambda is async void. Use Parallel.ForEachAsync.
  • PLINQ does not preserve order unless you add AsOrdered(), which costs performance.
  • Parallelism on small or cheap work is slower than sequential, because of coordination overhead.
  • In ASP.NET Core it steals threads from other requests and reduces overall throughput.
  • Exceptions come back wrapped in AggregateException. See 2.16.
  • A lock inside a parallel loop serialises it, so you pay all the overhead and get none of the benefit.
  • Never nest parallel loops. The thread explosion makes it far slower than a single level.

docs.title: 3.1 — .NET Framework vs .NET Core vs .NET 5+
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 2.19 Parallel programming · Next: 3.2 CLR and compilation

Markers: 🔥 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
There have been three generations of .NET: Framework (2002, Windows only), Core (2016, the cross-platform rewrite), and .NET 5+ (2020, where the names merged back into one).

  • .NET Framework 4.8 is the final version, forever. Security fixes only. No new features.
  • Today there is just one .NET. ".NET 8" or ".NET 10" always means the modern one.
  • .NET 4.8 and .NET 8 are unrelated products. The similar numbers are an accident of history.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Runtime a program The engine that executes your compiled code. Also called the CLR — see 3.2. SDK a toolkit you install What you need to build code: compiler, dotnet CLI, build system. Includes a runtime. Class library a set of built-in types The types you use every day — List<T>, String, HttpClient. .NET Framework the original product (2002) Windows only. Installed into Windows, so one shared copy per machine. Ended at 4.8. .NET Core the rewrite (2016) Cross-platform, open source, much faster. Ships with your app. Ended at 3.1. .NET 5+ the unified product (2020) .NET Core, renamed. The current one. Versions 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. TFM a short code in your .csproj Target Framework Moniker. Says which .NET you build against — net10.0, net48. Side-by-side an installation model Several runtime versions installed at once, each app using its own. Impossible with Framework. Self-contained a publish mode Your app ships with its runtime, so the target machine needs nothing installed. LTS / STS support lengths Long-Term Support (3 years, even numbers) vs Standard-Term Support (18 months, odd). See 3.10. ASP.NET Core the web framework Confusingly kept the word "Core" after the rename. ASP.NET Core 10 runs on .NET 10.

docs.title: First, what does ".NET" actually mean?
docs.text:
Before comparing versions it helps to know what the word covers. It is three things bundled together:

  1. A runtime — the program that runs your compiled code.
  2. A class library — thousands of ready-made types.
  3. Tools — the compiler, the dotnet command, the build system.

When someone asks "which .NET are you on?", they mean which version of that bundle.

docs.title: Why there are three generations
docs.text:
The story explains almost everything else, so it is worth knowing.

2002 — .NET Framework. Microsoft built .NET for Windows. It was tied deeply into Windows and installed into the operating system rather than shipped with your app.

That worked for years. Then two problems grew.

Problem one: it only ran on Windows. The industry moved to Linux servers, containers and cloud hosting. .NET could not follow.

Problem two: only one version could exist per machine. Because it lived inside Windows, every application on that machine shared it. Upgrading it for one app risked breaking all the others. Teams became afraid to upgrade, so servers sat on ancient versions for years.

2016 — .NET Core. Rather than patch the old one, Microsoft rewrote it from scratch. The result was cross-platform, much faster, open source, and — crucially — shipped with your application rather than installed into the OS.

The cost was that it started empty. Not everything from Framework came across.

2020 — .NET 5. By then Core had caught up. Having two products both called ".NET" was confusing, so the names merged. .NET Core 3.1 was followed by .NET 5, and it has been a single product ever since.

docs.title: ⚠️ The naming trap
docs.text:
There is no .NET Core 4 and no .NET 5 Framework. Microsoft deliberately skipped 4.

Why? Because .NET Framework 4.x already existed. A ".NET 4" would have been endlessly confused with it. Jumping to 5 made it unmistakable.

If you see It means .NET Framework 1.0 → 4.8 The old Windows-only one .NET Core 1.0 → 3.1 The rewrite, before the rename .NET 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 The modern one (Core, renamed)

docs.title: The simple version — what actually differs
docs.text: .NET Framework .NET (modern) Runs on Windows only Windows, Linux, macOS Where it lives Installed into Windows Ships with your app Versions per machine One, shared by everything As many as you like Open source No Yes Still developed? No — security fixes only Yes, yearly releases Speed Slower Much faster Containers Poor fit Designed for it

docs.title: How it actually works — the side-by-side point
docs.text:
This is the difference that mattered most in practice.

With .NET Framework, a server has one copy of .NET inside Windows. Every application uses it. Upgrade it because App A needs a new feature, and Apps B and C are suddenly running on a version nobody tested them against.

With modern .NET, each app either carries its own runtime or picks from several installed side by side. App A on .NET 8 and App B on .NET 10 coexist on one machine and never interact. You upgrade one without telling the other team.

This is also why .NET works properly in containers. A container image holds one app and its exact runtime. Nothing is shared, so nothing conflicts.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what got left behind
docs.text:
The rewrite dropped some Windows-specific pieces permanently:

  • Web Forms (.aspx) — replaced by Razor Pages and Blazor
  • WCF server-side — replaced by gRPC (21.6); the community CoreWCF project covers some client cases
  • .NET Remoting — replaced by HTTP and gRPC
  • App domains — partly replaced by AssemblyLoadContext (3.6)

If a legacy app depends on any of these, migrating means rewriting that part rather than upgrading. That is the honest answer to "why is that old app still on Framework?" — usually one of these four, or a third-party library that was never ported.

WPF and WinForms did make the jump and run on modern .NET. They are desktop UI frameworks, so naturally they remain Windows-only.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The version a project targets is one line in the .csproj:

<!-- Modern .NET -->
<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>

<!-- Old .NET Framework -->
<TargetFramework>net48</TargetFramework>

Checking what a machine has installed:

dotnet --version          # the SDK version currently in use
dotnet --list-runtimes    # every runtime installed side by side
dotnet --list-sdks        # every SDK installed

A typical --list-runtimes output shows the side-by-side idea directly:

Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 8.0.11
Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.0
Microsoft.NETCore.App 8.0.11
Microsoft.NETCore.App 10.0.0

Two versions, both present, neither interfering. That was impossible with .NET Framework.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between .NET Framework and .NET Core?

.NET Framework is the original from 2002. It runs only on Windows and is installed into the operating system, so every app on a machine shares one copy. .NET Core was a complete rewrite released in 2016 — cross-platform, open source, considerably faster, and shipped with your application rather than installed into the OS, which means different apps on one server can safely use different versions. .NET Core was renamed to just .NET at version 5, so the modern product is the continuation of Core, not of Framework.

Q: Why did Microsoft skip .NET 4?

Because .NET Framework 4.x already existed and had done for over a decade. Calling the new one .NET 4 would have been constantly confused with .NET Framework 4.8, which is a completely different product. Jumping from .NET Core 3.1 straight to .NET 5 made it unambiguous that this was the unified successor rather than a Framework update.

Q: Should a new project use .NET Framework?

No. .NET Framework 4.8 is the final version — it receives security patches but no new features and never will. Anything new should target the current .NET, preferably an LTS release. The only reason to touch Framework today is maintaining an existing app that depends on something never ported, such as Web Forms or server-side WCF.

Q: What was dropped in the move to .NET Core?

The pieces tied fundamentally to Windows or to old architecture: Web Forms, server-side WCF, .NET Remoting, and app domains. They were replaced rather than ported — Razor Pages and Blazor for Web Forms, gRPC for WCF and Remoting, AssemblyLoadContext for app domains. WPF and WinForms did come across and run on modern .NET, though naturally still only on Windows. In practice, when an app is stuck on Framework it is usually one of those four or a third-party dependency that was never updated.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• .NET 4.8 and .NET 8 are not related. One is the final old version; the other is a modern release. The close numbers are historical accident.
  • "Core" was dropped from the runtime name but kept by ASP.NET Core. ASP.NET Core 10 runs on .NET 10. This confuses everybody.
  • .NET Framework is not deprecated, it is finished. Still supported and patched — but no new features, ever.
  • Not everything ported. Web Forms, server-side WCF and Remoting are gone permanently.
  • Saying "dotnet core" today sounds dated. The product has been called .NET since 2020.

docs.title: 3.2 — CLR, CTS, CLS, IL, JIT, AOT, ReadyToRun
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.1 .NET history · Next: 3.3 Managed vs unmanaged

Markers: ⭐ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
C# is compiled in two stages. First your source becomes IL, a CPU-independent middle language — that is what goes in the .dll. Then, while the app runs, the CLR turns that IL into real machine code for the actual processor.

  • The second stage happens one method at a time, as each is first called. That is JIT.
  • AOT and ReadyToRun move that second stage to build time, trading flexibility for startup speed.
  • CTS and CLS are the rules that let C#, VB.NET and F# share compiled code.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Roslyn the C# compiler What runs when you press Build. Turns .cs files into IL. IL a language Intermediate Language. A simple instruction set not tied to any CPU. Your .dll contains this, not machine code. Assembly a file The .dll or .exe Roslyn produces. Holds IL plus metadata describing every type inside. Metadata data inside the assembly A description of every type, method and field. Reflection reads this. CLR the runtime engine Common Language Runtime. Runs your code — JIT compilation, memory, garbage collection, exceptions. JIT a compilation step Just-In-Time. The CLR turning IL into machine code the moment a method is first called, then caching it. Tiered compilation a JIT strategy Compile fast first for quick startup, then recompile hot methods with full optimisation. Managed code code the CLR runs Your C#. The CLR handles its memory and safety. CTS a specification Common Type System. The shared rules for what a type is across all .NET languages. CLS a specification Common Language Specification. A subset of CTS containing only what every .NET language supports. AOT a compilation step Ahead-Of-Time. Compiling straight to native machine code at build time, leaving no IL and no JIT. ReadyToRun (R2R) a compilation step A middle ground. Pre-compiles to machine code but keeps the IL as a fallback. Trimming a build step Removing unused code to shrink output. Used with AOT, and the reason reflection breaks there.

docs.title: The one story that explains all seven acronyms
docs.text:
A CPU only understands machine code, and machine code differs by processor. An Intel laptop and an ARM phone speak different languages.

Most older languages compile straight to machine code. That works, but it means one build per CPU type, decided when you build.

.NET does something different. It compiles in two stages:

flowchart LR
    A["Your C# code<br/>Program.cs"] -->|"Roslyn compiler<br/>at BUILD time"| B["IL<br/>MyApp.dll"]
    B -->|"JIT compiler<br/>at RUN time"| C["Machine code<br/>for THIS computer"]

Stage one, when you build. Roslyn turns your C# into IL — a simple, CPU-independent instruction set. Your .dll contains IL, not machine code.

Stage two, when you run. The CLR reads that IL and converts it to machine code for whatever CPU it finds. It does this just in time, hence JIT.

Every acronym in this note is a piece of that story.

docs.title: Why bother with two stages?
docs.text:
Three real benefits:

  1. One build runs anywhere. The same .dll works on Windows, Linux, x64 and ARM, because the machine-specific step waits until the machine is known.
  2. The JIT knows things the build machine could not. It sees the actual CPU and can use instructions specific to it.
  3. It improves while running. The runtime notices which methods are hot and recompiles them with heavier optimisation. This is why a .NET service often gets faster in its first minute of traffic.

The cost is startup time. The first call to every method pays for its compilation.

docs.title: The simple version — what IL looks like
docs.text:
This C#:

public int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;

becomes roughly this IL:

ldarg.1        // load the first argument
ldarg.2        // load the second argument
add            // add them
ret            // return the result

Simple, readable, tied to no CPU. Tools like ILSpy or sharplab.io let you inspect this for any code you write — genuinely useful for seeing what the compiler does with async, yield and records.

This is also why decompilers exist. A .dll full of IL plus metadata can be turned back into readable C#, which is why commercial software often ships obfuscated.

docs.title: CTS and CLS — the two people mix up
docs.text:
These exist because .NET was designed for several languages. VB.NET and F# compile to the same IL and can use each other's libraries. For that, they must agree on some things.

CTS — Common Type System defines what a type is. Every type derives from object, there are value types and reference types, interfaces work a certain way. It is the shared model.

CLS — Common Language Specification is a subset of CTS: the features every .NET language is guaranteed to support.

Why a subset? Because languages differ. C# is case-sensitive, so this is legal:

public void Process() { }
public void process() { }     // legal C#, but NOT CLS-compliant

VB.NET is case-insensitive. It cannot tell those apart, so it could never use your library properly.

If you publish a library other .NET languages might consume, ask the compiler to check:

[assembly: CLSCompliant(true)]     // warns about anything outside the safe subset

If your library is only ever used from C#, you can ignore CLS entirely.

The memory aid: CTS is the full rulebook. CLS is the part every language agreed to follow.

docs.title: How it actually works — JIT and tiered compilation
docs.text:
The JIT does not compile your program at startup. It compiles one method, the first time that method is called, then caches the result. A method you never call is never compiled.

Modern .NET adds tiered compilation:

  • Tier 0 — first run: compile quickly with few optimisations. Startup stays fast.
  • Tier 1 — if a method is called many times, recompile it in the background with full optimisation and swap it in.

So the app starts fast and gets faster as the hot paths reveal themselves.

This matters practically: benchmarks must warm up first. Measuring the first few calls measures Tier 0 code plus the compilation itself, not your real throughput. BenchmarkDotNet handles that automatically, which is one reason to use it over a stopwatch — see 19.14.

docs.title: The deeper detail — AOT and ReadyToRun
docs.text:
JIT costs startup time. For a serverless function that runs for 200 milliseconds, a large fraction of its life is compilation.

Two options move that work earlier.

ReadyToRun (R2R) pre-compiles IL to machine code at publish time but keeps the IL too. If the pre-compiled version cannot be used, the JIT compiles normally. Faster startup, bigger file, everything still works everywhere.

<PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>

Native AOT goes all the way — a real native executable, with no IL and no JIT at all.

<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>

The gains are dramatic: startup in single-digit milliseconds, much lower memory, a self-contained binary needing no installed runtime. What you give up:

  • Reflection over types the compiler could not see. Trimming removes unused code, and anything reached only by reflection looks unused. See 1.23.
  • Runtime code generation. Expression.Compile() and Reflection.Emit do not work, ruling out some ORMs and serializers.
  • One build per platform. A Linux x64 build runs only on Linux x64.

This is a large part of why source generators became popular — they do at build time what reflection used to do at runtime, which keeps AOT working. See 21.10.

JIT ReadyToRun Native AOT Startup Slowest Faster Fastest Peak speed Best Best Slightly lower File size Smallest Larger Largest Reflection Full Full Limited Build per platform No Partly Yes

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Publishing with each strategy:

# Normal — IL only, JIT at runtime. Needs .NET installed on the target.
dotnet publish -c Release

# ReadyToRun — pre-compiled, IL kept as a fallback
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishReadyToRun=true

# Native AOT — a real native binary, no runtime needed
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true

Turning off tiered compilation, which you would only do while measuring:

<TieredCompilation>false</TieredCompilation>

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens when you compile and run a C# program?

Two stages. At build time the C# compiler turns your source into IL, an intermediate language not tied to any CPU, and that is what goes into the .dll. At run time the CLR compiles that IL into machine code for the actual processor, one method at a time as each is first called — JIT compilation. The benefit is that a single build runs on any platform and the JIT can optimise for the specific CPU. The cost is that the first call to each method pays for its compilation, which is why startup is slower than a natively compiled language.

Q: What is the difference between CTS and CLS?

CTS, the Common Type System, is the shared model of what a type is across all .NET languages — value types versus reference types, everything deriving from object, how interfaces work. CLS, the Common Language Specification, is a subset of that: the features every .NET language is guaranteed to support. The subset exists because languages differ — C# is case-sensitive and permits two methods differing only by case, but VB.NET is case-insensitive and could never call them. So CTS is the full rulebook and CLS is the part everyone agreed to follow. It only matters if you publish a library for other .NET languages.

Q: What is tiered compilation?

The JIT compiles a method twice with different priorities. The first time it runs, the method is compiled quickly with minimal optimisation, keeping startup fast. If the runtime then sees that method called frequently, it recompiles it in the background with full optimisation and swaps it in. So the app starts quickly and gets faster as the hot paths emerge. It matters practically when benchmarking, because measuring the first calls measures unoptimised code plus the compilation cost rather than real steady-state performance.

Q: What is Native AOT, and what does it cost?

Native AOT compiles all the way to a native executable at build time, with no IL and no JIT. Startup drops to a few milliseconds, memory falls, and you get a self-contained binary needing no installed runtime — very attractive for serverless and short-lived containers. The trade-off is that dynamic behaviour breaks: reflection over types the compiler could not see, Expression.Compile, and Reflection.Emit. That rules out some serializers and ORMs. You also build separately per platform. It is a large part of why .NET has moved towards source generators.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "C# compiles to machine code." It compiles to IL. Machine code comes later, from the JIT.
  • The .dll contains IL, not machine code. That is why decompilers work and obfuscators exist.
  • Confusing CTS and CLS. CTS is the whole type system; CLS is the smaller safe subset.
  • Benchmarking without warm-up measures Tier 0 code, not real performance.
  • Native AOT silently breaks reflection. It compiles fine, then fails at runtime with a missing type — often not until production.
  • ReadyToRun does not remove the JIT, it just gives it less to do. AOT removes it entirely.
  • AOT builds are platform-specific, unlike normal .NET output.

docs.title: 3.3 — Managed vs Unmanaged Code, unsafe, P/Invoke
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.2 CLR and compilation · Next: 3.4 Garbage collection

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Managed code is code the CLR runs and looks after — it handles the memory, checks the types, and catches mistakes like reading past the end of an array. Unmanaged code is everything else: C, C++, operating system calls. Nobody is watching it for you.

  • Almost all C# you write is managed. You only meet unmanaged code when calling something outside .NET.
  • P/Invoke is how you call an unmanaged function from C#.
  • unsafe lets you use raw pointers in C#. You will rarely need it.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is in .NET What it means Managed code code the CLR executes Your C#. The CLR handles memory, garbage collection, type safety and bounds checking. Unmanaged code code outside the CLR Compiled C or C++, Windows API functions, native libraries. No GC, no safety checks. Managed resource an object on the .NET heap Cleaned up automatically by the garbage collector. Unmanaged resource something the OS gave you A file handle, socket, or window handle. The GC knows nothing about it — you must release it. P/Invoke a mechanism Platform Invoke. Calling a function in a native .dll or .so from C#. DllImport an attribute Marks a C# method as actually living in a native library. The classic P/Invoke syntax. LibraryImport an attribute (.NET 7+) The modern replacement. A source generator writes the interop code at build time, so it works with AOT. Marshalling a conversion step Translating data between .NET's layout and the native layout — for example a C# string to a C char*. unsafe a C# keyword Allows pointer syntax (*, &) inside a block or method. Must be enabled in the .csproj. fixed a C# statement Pins an object so the GC cannot move it while you hold a pointer to it. Pinning what fixed does Telling the GC "do not relocate this object during compaction". IntPtr / nint a struct A raw pointer-sized integer. How native handles are represented in C#. SafeHandle an abstract class A wrapper around a native handle that releases it reliably. The correct way to hold one.

docs.title: What "managed" actually buys you
docs.text:
When the CLR runs your code, it does a lot of work in the background that you never see:

  • Memory is allocated and freed for you by the garbage collector.
  • Array bounds are checked. Reading array[10] on a 5-element array throws an exception rather than silently reading whatever memory happens to be next.
  • Types are verified. You cannot treat a string as an int by lying about it.
  • Pointers are not exposed, so you cannot accidentally read freed memory.

That collection of guarantees is what "managed" means. It removes an entire category of bug — buffer overruns, use-after-free, memory corruption — that has caused a large share of the security vulnerabilities in software history.

Unmanaged code has none of that. C and C++ let you write past the end of a buffer, use a pointer after freeing it, or interpret one type as another. Faster and more flexible, and far easier to get catastrophically wrong.

A picture: managed code is driving a car with seatbelts, airbags and lane assist. Unmanaged code is a racing car with none of it. The racing car can be faster, and a small mistake is much more expensive.

docs.title: Why you would ever leave the safety
docs.text:
Three reasons, and only three:

  1. The functionality only exists natively. Windows API calls, hardware drivers, a C library like SQLite or FFmpeg with no .NET equivalent.
  2. Extreme performance in a very narrow spot, where even the small cost of bounds checking matters. This is rare and should always be measured first.
  3. You are given a handle by the operating system — a file, socket or window — and must release it yourself.

Number three is the one that touches ordinary application code, and it is why IDisposable exists at all.

docs.title: The simple version — managed vs unmanaged resources
docs.text:
This distinction matters far more day to day than pointers do.

public class Example
{
    private byte[] _buffer = new byte[1024];   // MANAGED — the GC frees this
    private FileStream _file;                  // holds an UNMANAGED file handle inside
}

The byte[] is a normal .NET object. When nothing references it, the garbage collector reclaims it and you do nothing.

The FileStream is also a .NET object, but inside it is a file handle given out by the operating system. The GC knows how to free the FileStream object's own memory. It has no idea what a file handle is or how to close one.

So the handle stays open — and the file stays locked — until something calls Dispose. That is the entire reason for IDisposable and using:

using var file = File.OpenRead(path);   // Dispose closes the OS handle

Covered fully in 1.21.

docs.title: How it actually works — P/Invoke
docs.text:
To call a native function you declare it in C# and tell the runtime where it lives.

The classic form uses DllImport:

using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

public static class Native
{
    [DllImport("user32.dll", CharSet = CharSet.Unicode)]
    public static extern int MessageBox(IntPtr hWnd, string text, string caption, uint type);
}

Native.MessageBox(IntPtr.Zero, "Hello", "Title", 0);

Note extern and no body. You are describing a function that lives elsewhere; the runtime finds it and wires up the call.

Modern .NET prefers LibraryImport (.NET 7+), which uses a source generator to write the interop code at build time:

public static partial class Native
{
    [LibraryImport("user32.dll", StringMarshalling = StringMarshalling.Utf16)]
    public static partial int MessageBox(IntPtr hWnd, string text, string caption, uint type);
}

Two differences worth knowing: the class and method must be partial so the generator can fill them in, and because the code is generated at build time it works with Native AOT, whereas DllImport relies on runtime generation that AOT removes. See 3.2.

Marshalling is the conversion in between. A C# string is UTF-16 and length-prefixed; a C char* is a pointer to null-terminated bytes. The runtime converts, and telling it exactly how is most of the work in real interop.

docs.title: The deeper detail — unsafe, pointers and pinning
docs.text:
unsafe lets you use C-style pointers in C#. You must opt in per project:

<AllowUnsafeBlocks>true</AllowUnsafeBlocks>

unsafe
{
    int value = 42;
    int* pointer = &value;      // address of value
    Console.WriteLine(*pointer); // 42 — read through the pointer
}

Now the important part, and it connects directly to garbage collection.

The GC moves objects. During the compact phase it slides survivors together to remove gaps (3.4). So an object's address is not stable.

That is fine normally, because the CLR updates every reference when it moves something. But it cannot update a raw pointer — it does not know the pointer exists.

unsafe
{
    byte[] data = new byte[1024];

    fixed (byte* p = data)          // PIN it — the GC may not move it
    {
        NativeFunction(p, data.Length);
    }
    // unpinned here — the GC may move it again
}

fixed pins the object for the duration of the block. Without it, a collection mid-call could relocate the array and leave your native function writing to memory that no longer holds it — which corrupts the heap in ways that surface much later and are extremely hard to diagnose.

⚠️ Keep fixed blocks short. A pinned object cannot be moved, so it creates a hole in the heap that compaction has to work around. Long-lived pins cause fragmentation.

docs.title: The right way to hold a native handle
docs.text:
Do not store raw IntPtr handles. Use SafeHandle:

public sealed class MyFileHandle : SafeHandleZeroOrMinusOneIsInvalid
{
    public MyFileHandle() : base(ownsHandle: true) { }

    protected override bool ReleaseHandle() => CloseHandle(handle);

    [LibraryImport("kernel32.dll")]
    [return: MarshalAs(UnmanagedType.Bool)]
    private static partial bool CloseHandle(IntPtr handle);
}

SafeHandle gives you three things a raw IntPtr does not: guaranteed release even if the process is being torn down, protection against the handle being recycled while in use, and correct behaviour with the finalizer pattern. This is the reason you almost never need to write the full dispose pattern by hand — see 1.21.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The realistic version of this in ASP.NET Core: you will almost never write any of it.

What you actually do is release unmanaged resources properly:

public class ReportService
{
    public async Task<byte[]> GenerateAsync(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // Every one of these holds an unmanaged resource internally:
        //   FileStream  → an OS file handle
        //   SqlConnection → a network socket
        // 'await using' releases them even if something throws.

        await using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
        await connection.OpenAsync(ct);

        await using var output = File.Create(_tempPath);

        // ... work ...

        return await File.ReadAllBytesAsync(_tempPath, ct);
    }
}

The takeaway: managed versus unmanaged mostly reaches you as "which things do I have to dispose?" The answer is anything wrapping an OS resource — files, sockets, database connections, HTTP handlers, cryptography objects.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between managed and unmanaged code?

Managed code runs under the CLR, which handles memory allocation and garbage collection, verifies types, and checks array bounds — so a whole class of bugs like buffer overruns and use-after-free simply cannot happen. Unmanaged code is compiled native code such as C or C++, or operating system functions, running outside the CLR with none of those guarantees. Almost all C# is managed; you meet unmanaged code when calling into the OS or a native library, or when holding a resource the OS gave you.

Q: What is the difference between a managed and an unmanaged resource?

A managed resource is an ordinary .NET object on the heap — the garbage collector reclaims it automatically. An unmanaged resource is something the operating system handed you, like a file handle, socket or window handle. The GC can free the .NET object that wraps it, but it has no idea what the handle is or how to close it. So the file stays locked until something calls Dispose. That gap is exactly why IDisposable and using exist.

Q: What is P/Invoke?

Platform Invoke — the mechanism for calling a function in a native library from C#. You declare a method with no body marked extern, and attribute it with DllImport or, in .NET 7 and later, LibraryImport. The runtime locates the function and handles marshalling, which is converting data between .NET's representation and the native one. LibraryImport is preferred now because it uses a source generator to produce the interop code at build time, which means it works under Native AOT, whereas DllImport relies on runtime generation that AOT strips out.

Q: Why do you need the fixed statement?

Because the garbage collector moves objects. During the compaction phase it slides surviving objects together to remove gaps, and it updates every managed reference to match. It cannot update a raw pointer, because it has no idea the pointer exists. So if you take a pointer to a managed array and a collection happens mid-call, your pointer now refers to memory that no longer holds that array. fixed pins the object so the GC will not relocate it for the duration of the block. Pins should be short, because a pinned object blocks compaction and causes fragmentation.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Forgetting that a managed object can hold an unmanaged resource. FileStream is a .NET object, but the file handle inside it needs disposing.
  • Taking a pointer without fixed. The GC can move the object underneath you and corrupt memory in a way that surfaces much later.
  • Long-lived fixed blocks fragment the heap, because pinned objects cannot be moved during compaction.
  • DllImport breaks under Native AOT. Use LibraryImport for anything new.
  • Marshalling mistakes are silent. Getting a struct layout or string encoding wrong reads garbage rather than throwing.
  • Raw IntPtr handles can leak or be recycled. Use SafeHandle.
  • unsafe needs enabling in the .csproj. It is off by default on purpose.
