docs.title: 3.4 — Garbage Collection
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.3 Managed vs unmanaged · Next: 3.5 Memory leaks

Markers: 🔥 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Garbage collection is .NET automatically finding objects that nothing is using any more and freeing the memory they occupied. You never write "delete this object" in C#.

  • It works out what is still in use by starting from known roots and following every reference. Anything it cannot reach is garbage.
  • It sorts objects into three generations by age, and mostly only cleans the youngest — because most objects die young.
  • It manages memory only. Files, sockets and database connections still need IDisposable.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is in .NET What it means Heap a region of memory Where all reference-type objects live. Managed by the GC. Stack a region of memory Where local variables live. Cleared automatically when a method returns — the GC is not involved. Garbage collector (GC) part of the CLR The component that finds and frees unreachable objects. Root a starting point for the search Somewhere the GC knows is definitely live: local variables of running methods, static fields, CPU registers. Reachable a property of an object The GC can get to it by following references from a root. Reachable = keep. Garbage a property of an object Not reachable from any root. Nothing can ever use it again, so its memory is freed. Mark / Sweep / Compact the three phases of a collection Mark what is reachable → free what is not → slide survivors together to close the gaps. Generation an age bucket on the heap Gen 0 (new), Gen 1 (survived once), Gen 2 (survived twice or more). Promotion what happens to a survivor An object that survives a collection moves up to the next generation. Collection one run of the GC A "Gen 0 collection" checks only Gen 0. A "Gen 2 collection" checks everything and is the expensive one. LOH a separate heap Large Object Heap. Anything 85,000 bytes or larger goes here. Not compacted by default. Fragmentation a memory problem Free space exists but is split into scattered gaps, so a large request still fails. GC.Collect() a static method Forces a collection immediately. Almost always the wrong thing to call. Finalizer a method, written ~ClassName() Runs before an object's memory is reclaimed. Makes the object survive an extra collection, so avoid it. Server GC / Workstation GC two configuration modes Server GC uses one heap per CPU core for speed. Workstation GC uses one heap, for lower memory.

docs.title: Start here: what problem does this solve?
docs.text:
In older languages like C, you asked for memory and had to give it back yourself:

char* buffer = malloc(1024);   // ask for memory
free(buffer);                  // you MUST return it

Two things go wrong constantly. Forget to free and the memory is lost forever — a leak. Free it twice, or use it after freeing, and the program corrupts itself or crashes. Whole categories of security vulnerability come from exactly this.

.NET removes the problem by tracking it for you. You create objects and stop using them. The garbage collector notices and reclaims the memory.

var buffer = new byte[1024];   // ask for memory
// ...and that is it. Nothing to free.

docs.title: The key question: how does it know what is garbage?
docs.text:
This is the part worth understanding properly, because everything else follows from it.

The GC does not count how many things point at an object. It does something simpler and more reliable.

It starts from places it knows are definitely live — the roots:

  • Local variables in methods currently running
  • Static fields
  • CPU registers

Then it follows every reference from those roots, and from whatever they point to, and so on. Everything it can reach is in use. Everything it cannot reach is garbage.

A picture: a room full of objects, with strings tying some of them to hooks on the wall. The hooks are the roots. Anything you can trace back to a hook by following strings is kept. Anything with no path back to a hook — even if it is tied to other objects — is rubbish and gets swept away.

That last part matters. Two objects pointing at each other with no path from a root are both garbage. This is why .NET has no problem with circular references, whereas reference-counting systems do.

flowchart LR
    R1["ROOT<br/>local variable"] --> A["Order"]
    A --> B["Customer"]
    A --> C["List of lines"]
    R2["ROOT<br/>static field"] --> D["Cache"]

    E["Old Order"] <--> F["Old Customer"]

    style E fill:#f99,stroke:#900
    style F fill:#f99,stroke:#900

The two red objects point at each other, but nothing reaches them from a root. Both are collected.

docs.title: The simple version — the three phases
docs.text:
When a collection runs, the GC does three things:

  1. Mark. Start at the roots, follow every reference, mark everything reachable.
  2. Sweep. Everything unmarked is garbage. Its memory is now free.
  3. Compact. Slide the survivors together so free space is one continuous block rather than scattered gaps.

That third phase has a consequence worth knowing: objects move, so an object's address is not stable. That is fine in normal C#, and it is exactly why you need fixed and pinning when handing a pointer to native code — see 3.3.

Compaction also makes allocation extremely fast. Because free memory is one continuous block, allocating is just moving a pointer forward. It is close to free.

docs.title: How it actually works — generations
docs.text:
Everything is built on one observation:

Most objects die very young. A string built inside a method, a DTO created for one request, the result of a LINQ query — the vast majority become garbage almost immediately. A small minority live for the whole application.

Scanning every object every time would be wasteful, since most old ones are still alive. So the GC splits the heap into three generations by age:

Generation Holds Collected Gen 0 Brand new objects Very often, very fast Gen 1 Objects that survived one collection Less often Gen 2 Objects that survived twice or more Rarely, and it is expensive

The rules are simple:

  • Every new object starts in Gen 0.
  • Survive a collection and you are promoted to the next generation.
  • A Gen 0 collection looks only at Gen 0. Often under a millisecond.
  • A Gen 2 collection examines everything, including Gen 0 and Gen 1. This is a full collection and it is the expensive one.
flowchart LR
    N["new object"] --> G0["Gen 0<br/>collected often<br/>very fast"]
    G0 -->|"survived"| G1["Gen 1<br/>collected sometimes"]
    G1 -->|"survived again"| G2["Gen 2<br/>collected rarely<br/>expensive"]
    G0 -.->|"most objects<br/>die here"| X["freed"]

So the design makes the common case — short-lived objects — almost free, and accepts that the rare case is slow.

Why this matters for your code: an object that survives into Gen 2 is expensive to clean up later. Caching things "just in case" pushes objects into Gen 2 and makes your full collections slower and more frequent.

docs.title: The Large Object Heap
docs.text:
Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go somewhere separate: the Large Object Heap, or LOH. Usually big arrays, large strings, or buffers.

The LOH has two special properties:

  • It is collected only during a Gen 2 collection, so large objects hang around longer.
  • It is not compacted by default, because moving an 800 KB object is expensive.

Not compacting causes fragmentation. Imagine allocating and freeing many differently-sized large arrays. You end up with free gaps scattered between live objects. Ask for a 500 KB array and, even with 2 MB free in total, there may be no single 500 KB gap — so the process asks the OS for more memory.

The result is an application whose memory keeps climbing even though nothing is really leaking. Repeatedly resizing large buffers is a classic cause.

The fix is not to force compaction — that exists but is very expensive:

// A last resort. Causes a long pause. Not for normal code.
GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = GCLargeObjectHeapCompactionMode.CompactOnce;
GC.Collect();

The real fix is to stop churning large objects. Reuse buffers with ArrayPool<T>, or avoid allocating them at all with Span<T> — see 1.25 and 19.13.

docs.title: The deeper detail — GC modes
docs.text:
Two settings matter in production, and interviewers do ask.

Workstation vs Server GC

Workstation Server Heaps One One per CPU core GC threads One One per core, in parallel Optimised for Low latency, low memory Maximum throughput Default for Desktop apps ASP.NET Core

Server GC gives each core its own heap and collection thread, so collections finish much faster on multi-core hardware. The cost is higher memory use, since there are several heaps.

<ServerGarbageCollection>true</ServerGarbageCollection>

⚠️ This is a real container gotcha. Server GC assumes it owns the machine. In a container limited to one core with a tight memory cap, several heaps waste memory and can push you past the limit — which the orchestrator handles by killing the container. If you run small containers, test with Workstation GC:

<ServerGarbageCollection>false</ServerGarbageCollection>

Modern .NET reads container limits much better than it used to, and .NET 9 enabled DATAS by default, which adapts the number of heaps to actual load. Still worth checking if containers are being killed for memory.

Concurrent / background GC lets most of a Gen 2 collection run on a background thread while your app keeps working, so the pause is much shorter. On by default; rarely changed.

docs.title: Do not call GC.Collect()
docs.text:
GC.Collect();                      // almost always wrong
GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();

The GC has far better information than you do about when collecting is worthwhile. Forcing it usually:

  • triggers a full Gen 2 collection, the most expensive kind
  • promotes objects that would otherwise have died cheaply in Gen 0
  • pauses all your threads for no benefit

The only defensible uses are in a benchmark harness, or immediately after deliberately dropping something very large. If you are reaching for it to fix a memory problem, the problem is a reference being held somewhere — see 3.5.

docs.title: What you should actually do
docs.text:
The GC handles memory. It does not handle file handles, sockets or database connections:

// The GC will eventually free this object's memory,
// but the file stays LOCKED until Dispose runs.
await using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);

That distinction is the practical takeaway — see 1.21.

Reducing GC pressure, in order of usefulness:

// 1. Do not allocate in a loop when you can build once
var sb = new StringBuilder();          // not string concatenation

// 2. Reuse large buffers instead of allocating new ones
var buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(4096);
try { /* use it */ }
finally { ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer); }

// 3. Avoid the allocation entirely when slicing
ReadOnlySpan<char> slice = text.AsSpan(0, 100);   // no new string

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does the garbage collector know an object can be freed?

It uses reachability, not reference counting. It starts from a set of roots — local variables in running methods, static fields and CPU registers — and follows every reference from there, marking everything it can reach. Anything unmarked is unreachable and therefore garbage. An important consequence is that circular references are not a problem: two objects pointing at each other with no path from a root are both collected, whereas a reference-counting system would leak them.

Q: What are generations and why do they exist?

The heap is divided into three generations by age. New objects go into Gen 0, and anything surviving a collection is promoted upward. The design rests on the observation that most objects die very young — temporary strings, DTOs, LINQ results. So collecting only Gen 0 catches the vast majority of garbage while examining a small fraction of the heap, which makes it very fast. Gen 2 collections examine everything and are expensive, so the GC does them rarely. The practical implication is that keeping objects alive longer than necessary pushes them into Gen 2 and makes your expensive collections more frequent.

Q: What is the Large Object Heap and why does it cause problems?

Objects of 85,000 bytes or more — usually large arrays or strings — go on a separate heap. It is collected only as part of a Gen 2 collection, so large objects survive longer, and it is not compacted by default because moving very large objects is costly. Not compacting means fragmentation: after allocating and releasing many differently-sized large objects you can have plenty of free memory in total but no single contiguous block big enough for the next request, so the process grows. The symptom is memory climbing steadily without an actual leak. The fix is to stop churning large objects — pool buffers with ArrayPool<T> rather than allocating fresh ones.

Q: What is the difference between Workstation and Server GC?

Workstation GC uses a single heap and a single collection thread, favouring low latency and low memory. Server GC creates one heap and one collection thread per CPU core, so collections run in parallel and finish much faster on multi-core hardware, at the cost of higher memory use. Server GC is the default for ASP.NET Core because throughput matters more there. The thing to watch is containers — Server GC assumes it owns the machine, so in a small container with a tight memory limit the multiple heaps can push you over and get the container killed. Modern .NET reads container limits much better, and .NET 9 turned on DATAS which adapts heap count dynamically, but it is still worth testing.

Q: Should you ever call GC.Collect()?

Almost never. The runtime has far better information about when collecting is worthwhile, and forcing it triggers a full Gen 2 collection — the most expensive kind — while also promoting objects that would otherwise have been collected cheaply in Gen 0. The only reasonable uses are benchmarking, where you want a known starting state, and immediately after deliberately dropping something very large. If someone is calling it to fix a memory problem, the real issue is something holding a reference, and forcing collections cannot help because the object is still reachable.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "The GC handles all cleanup." It handles memory only. Files, sockets and connections need IDisposable.
  • Calling GC.Collect() to fix memory usage. If an object is still referenced, no amount of collecting frees it.
  • Forcing collection promotes objects, making things worse rather than better.
  • Objects move during compaction. An object's address is not stable, which is why pinning exists for interop.
  • The LOH threshold is 85,000 bytes — smaller than people expect. An array of about 21,000 ints already qualifies.
  • Server GC in a small container can get you OOM-killed. More heaps means more memory.
  • A finalizer makes an object survive an extra collection. Never add one unless you truly need it — see 1.21.
  • "No memory leaks in .NET" is false. You cannot leak by forgetting to free, but you can very easily leak by holding a reference. See 3.5.

docs.title: 3.5 — Memory Leaks in Managed Code
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.4 Garbage collection · Next: 3.6 Assemblies and NuGet

Markers: 🔥 ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A memory leak in .NET is not forgetting to free memory — you cannot do that. It is accidentally keeping a reference to something you have finished with, so the garbage collector is not allowed to reclaim it.

  • The GC only frees what is unreachable. Anything still reachable from a root is kept, forever if necessary.
  • The big four causes: static collections, event handlers never unsubscribed, undisposed resources, and captured variables in long-lived closures.
  • The symptom is memory that climbs steadily and never comes back down, ending in an out-of-memory crash or a container restart.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Memory leak (managed) a bug Memory that is still reachable but will never be used again, so the GC cannot free it. Memory leak (unmanaged) a different bug An OS resource — file handle, socket — never released because nothing called Dispose. Reachable a property of an object The GC can get to it by following references from a root. Reachable objects are never freed. Root a starting point Static fields, local variables of running methods, CPU registers. See 3.4. Retention path a chain of references The route from a root to the leaked object. Finding this is how you fix a leak. WeakReference<T> a class Holds a reference that does not stop the GC collecting the target. Memory dump a file A snapshot of everything in the process's memory, for offline analysis. dotnet-counters a CLI tool Shows live metrics — heap size, GC counts, thread-pool queue. First thing to run. dotnet-dump a CLI tool Captures and analyses memory dumps. Finds what is holding an object alive. dotnet-gcdump a CLI tool Captures just the object graph. Much smaller than a full dump and usually enough.

docs.title: "You cannot leak memory in .NET" is wrong
docs.text:
People say this because the garbage collector frees things automatically. And it is true you cannot make the C-style mistake of forgetting to call free.

But the GC has one rule: free anything that is unreachable (3.4). It never asks "is this still needed?" — only "can this still be reached?"

So if you keep a reference to something you have finished with, the GC dutifully keeps it alive. Forever, if the reference lives in a static field.

That is a memory leak. The memory is not lost — it is being deliberately protected by your own code.

A picture: a warehouse where the rule is "throw away anything nobody has a claim ticket for". You cannot lose items. But if you keep handing out claim tickets and never collect them back, the warehouse fills up with things nobody actually wants — and the rule says every one of them must be kept.

docs.title: Why it matters more in a web app
docs.text:
A desktop app gets restarted regularly. A web server is meant to run for weeks.

A leak of a few kilobytes per request sounds trivial. At 100 requests per second it is 35 gigabytes a day. In practice what happens is:

  1. Memory climbs steadily over hours.
  2. Gen 2 collections become more frequent and take longer, because the heap is huge.
  3. Latency gets worse as those pauses grow.
  4. Eventually the process hits its memory limit and is killed, or throws OutOfMemoryException.
  5. In Kubernetes the container restarts, memory resets, and the cycle begins again.

The classic signature is a sawtooth graph — memory rising steadily, dropping vertically at each restart. If you see that, you have a leak, not a tuning problem.

docs.title: The simple version — the big four causes
docs.text:
1. Static collections that only grow ⚠️ the most common by far

public class OrderService
{
    // static = a GC root. Everything in here is reachable FOREVER.
    private static readonly List<Order> _processed = new();

    public void Process(Order order)
    {
        _processed.Add(order);      // nothing ever removes it
        // ...
    }
}

Every order ever processed stays in memory for the life of the process. And because Order holds a Customer, which holds an address, which holds..., you are retaining a whole object graph per order.

The fix is either to not keep it, or to use something with eviction:

// IMemoryCache has size limits and expiry. A raw dictionary does not.
_cache.Set(order.Id, order, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10));

See 19.2.

2. Event handlers never unsubscribed ⚠️

public class OrderPage
{
    public OrderPage(OrderService longLivedService)
    {
        longLivedService.OrderCompleted += OnCompleted;   // subscribe
    }

    private void OnCompleted(object? s, EventArgs e) { }
}

Subscribing means the publisher stores a reference to the subscriber. The long-lived service now holds the short-lived page alive. Create a thousand pages and all thousand stay in memory, still receiving events.

The fix is to unsubscribe in Dispose — covered fully in 1.12, including the trap that you cannot unsubscribe a lambda unless you stored it in a variable.

3. Undisposed resources

var stream = File.OpenRead(path);    // never disposed

This is an unmanaged leak. The GC eventually frees the FileStream object's memory, but the operating system's file handle stays open until Dispose runs. Handles are a limited resource — run out and every subsequent file operation fails.

The fix is using — see 1.21.

4. Captured variables in long-lived closures

public class Registry
{
    private static readonly List<Action> _callbacks = new();

    public void Register(HugeObject data)
    {
        // The lambda captures 'data', so the closure object holds it.
        // The static list holds the closure. So 'data' lives forever.
        _callbacks.Add(() => Console.WriteLine(data.Name));
    }
}

A closure is a hidden object holding every captured variable (1.13). Store the lambda somewhere long-lived and you have stored everything it captured.

Worse, capturing any field of this captures the entire containing object, not just that field.

docs.title: How it actually works — the ASP.NET Core specific ones
docs.text:
Injecting a scoped service into a singleton — the captive dependency problem:

public class CacheService                    // registered as a SINGLETON
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _db;       // SCOPED — meant to live one request

    public CacheService(AppDbContext db) => _db = db;
}

The singleton captures the first request's DbContext and holds it for the life of the application. That context's change tracker keeps every entity it has ever loaded, so it grows without limit. This is a leak and a correctness bug, since DbContext is not thread-safe. See 6.4.

Creating HttpClient per request:

using var client = new HttpClient();     // looks correct. Is not.

Disposing does not immediately release the underlying socket — it sits in TIME_WAIT for a couple of minutes. Under load you exhaust available ports. Use IHttpClientFactory — 19.10.

Long-lived DbContext in a background service:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var scope = _factory.CreateScope();          // ONE scope for the whole loop
    var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

    while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        var orders = await db.Orders.ToListAsync(ct);   // tracker grows every iteration
        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1), ct);
    }
}

The scope must be created inside the loop, not outside — see 21.2.

docs.title: The deeper detail — finding a leak in production
docs.text:
The method matters more than the tools, and this is a genuinely common interview scenario.

Step 1 — confirm it is actually a leak. Watch the heap size across several Gen 2 collections. A leak keeps climbing after a full collection. Normal load fluctuation drops back down.

dotnet-counters monitor --process-id <pid> --counters System.Runtime

Look at gen-2-gc-count and gc-heap-size. Rising heap with rising Gen 2 count means a leak.

Step 2 — capture the object graph.

dotnet-gcdump collect --process-id <pid>

Take two, several minutes apart. The difference between them is far more informative than either alone — it shows what is growing rather than what is merely large.

Step 3 — find the retention path. Open the dumps in Visual Studio or dotnet-dump, sort by object count, and find what grew. Then ask the crucial question: what is holding this alive? The chain from a root down to the leaked object is the retention path, and it points straight at the bug.

dotnet-dump analyze core_dump
> dumpheap -stat              # what is on the heap, by count and size
> gcroot <address>            # THE key command: what is keeping this alive

gcroot is the one to remember. It answers the only question that matters.

docs.title: WeakReference<T> — occasionally the right tool
docs.text:
A weak reference lets you point at an object without stopping the GC collecting it:

private readonly WeakReference<ExpensiveThing> _cached = new(thing);

if (_cached.TryGetTarget(out var thing))
    Use(thing);            // still alive
else
    thing = Rebuild();     // was collected, rebuild it

Genuinely useful for caches where losing an entry is acceptable. Not a general fix for leaks — if you need the object, a weak reference just moves the bug. Reach for IMemoryCache first; it has proper eviction policies.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The most common real leak, and its fix:

// LEAK — a singleton with an unbounded dictionary
public class PriceCache
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, decimal> _prices = new();

    public decimal Get(string sku)
    {
        if (!_prices.TryGetValue(sku, out var price))
        {
            price = LookUp(sku);
            _prices[sku] = price;      // never removed, never expires
        }
        return price;
    }
}

Three problems, and being able to name all three is a strong answer:

  1. It only grows. New SKUs are added forever. This is the leak.
  2. It is not thread-safe. A Dictionary written from concurrent requests can corrupt — see 2.3.
  3. It is per-instance. Scale to three servers and you have three inconsistent caches.
// FIXED — bounded, expiring, thread-safe
public class PriceCache(IMemoryCache cache, IPriceApi api)
{
    public async Task<decimal> GetAsync(string sku, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        return await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(sku, async entry =>
        {
            entry.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(15);
            entry.Size = 1;                       // counts against the cache size limit
            return await api.LookUpAsync(sku, ct);
        });
    }
}

Registered with a hard ceiling so it can never grow without limit:

builder.Services.AddMemoryCache(options => options.SizeLimit = 10_000);

That SizeLimit is the line that turns a potential leak into a bounded cache. Without it, IMemoryCache will also grow indefinitely — it only evicts on memory pressure, which may arrive too late.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Can you have a memory leak in .NET?

Yes, though not in the C sense of forgetting to free memory. The garbage collector frees anything unreachable, but it never asks whether an object is still needed — only whether it can still be reached. So if you hold a reference to something you have finished with, the GC is obliged to keep it. A static collection that only grows, an event subscription never removed, or a lambda stored somewhere long-lived that captured a large object — all of those keep memory alive indefinitely. There is also the separate case of unmanaged resources like file handles, which the GC cannot release at all without Dispose.

Q: What are the most common causes?

Four, in roughly that order of frequency. Static collections that only ever get added to. Event handlers where the subscriber never unsubscribes, so a long-lived publisher pins a short-lived object. Undisposed resources holding operating system handles. And closures capturing large objects that are then stored somewhere long-lived — worth remembering that capturing any field implicitly captures the whole containing object. In ASP.NET Core specifically, injecting a scoped service like DbContext into a singleton is a very common one, because the singleton pins that context for the life of the app and its change tracker grows forever.

Q: How would you find a memory leak in production?

First confirm it is a leak rather than normal load, by watching whether the heap keeps growing after full Gen 2 collections — dotnet-counters shows heap size and Gen 2 count live. Then capture two dotnet-gcdump snapshots several minutes apart, because the difference tells you what is growing rather than just what is big. Then find the retention path: open the dump, sort by object count, identify what grew, and use gcroot to ask what is keeping it alive. That chain from root to object points at the bug. The mistake is jumping straight to a dump without first confirming there is actually a leak.

Q: What is a WeakReference and when would you use it?

A reference that does not prevent the garbage collector from collecting its target — you ask for the object with TryGetTarget and it may tell you it has gone. It suits caches where losing an entry is acceptable and rebuilding is cheaper than the memory cost of guaranteed retention. It is not a general fix for leaks though. If your code genuinely needs the object, making the reference weak just relocates the bug. For caching in ASP.NET Core I would reach for IMemoryCache with an explicit size limit first, because it gives you real eviction policies rather than depending on GC timing.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "The GC means no leaks." The GC frees unreachable objects. Reachable-but-unwanted is the entire problem.
  • static is a GC root. Anything a static field points to lives for the whole process.
  • Capturing one field captures the whole object. A lambda using this.Name retains this.
  • Event subscribers are held by the publisher. Long-lived publisher plus short-lived subscriber equals a leak.
  • IMemoryCache without a SizeLimit can still grow indefinitely. It evicts on memory pressure, which may arrive too late.
  • Scoped services in singletons pin a request-lifetime object forever. See 6.4.
  • A DbContext held open accumulates every entity it has tracked. Use AsNoTracking for reads and short-lived contexts everywhere.
  • GC.Collect() will not fix a leak. The object is still reachable, which is exactly the problem.
  • One dump is much less useful than two. You need the delta to see what is growing.

docs.title: 3.6 — Assemblies, Load Contexts, NuGet Packaging
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.5 Memory leaks · Next: 3.7 csproj and target frameworks

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
An assembly is a single compiled .dll or .exe. It is the unit .NET actually loads, versions and ships — one project produces exactly one assembly.

  • A NuGet package is a zip file containing one or more assemblies plus metadata about its dependencies.
  • The runtime finds assemblies at startup using a generated file called deps.json, not by searching folders.
  • Two different versions of the same package in one app cause a diamond dependency conflict, which .NET resolves by picking the highest version.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Assembly a .dll or .exe file The compiled output of one project. Contains IL plus metadata. The unit of deployment and versioning. Metadata data inside the assembly A full description of every type, method and field. Reflection reads this. Manifest part of the metadata The assembly's own identity: name, version, culture, and what it depends on. NuGet package a .nupkg file A zip containing assemblies, a .nuspec describing them, and a list of dependencies. PackageReference an entry in your .csproj How you declare a NuGet dependency in modern .NET. deps.json a generated file Sits next to your app and lists every assembly it needs. The runtime reads this to find them. runtimeconfig.json a generated file Says which .NET version the app needs and carries runtime settings like GC mode. Strong name a signature An assembly signed with a key pair. Mostly a .NET Framework concern; largely irrelevant now. AssemblyLoadContext an abstract class An isolated container for loading assemblies. Lets you load two versions of the same library, or unload one. Diamond dependency a conflict Two of your dependencies each need a different version of the same third package. Transitive dependency an indirect dependency A package your package depends on. You get it without asking. InternalsVisibleTo an attribute Opens internal types to a named assembly, usually a test project.

docs.title: What an assembly actually is
docs.text:
When you build a project, you get one assembly — a .dll (a library) or .exe (a runnable app). It is not just compiled code. Inside are two things:

  1. IL — your compiled code (3.2).
  2. Metadata — a complete description of every type, method, property and field.

That metadata is why .NET can do things other platforms find hard. Reflection reads it. The debugger reads it. IntelliSense reads it when you reference a package. A decompiler reads it to reconstruct readable C#.

An assembly is also the unit of three things:

  • Deployment — you ship .dll files.
  • Versioning — each assembly has its own version number.
  • Access control — internal means "visible inside this assembly", so the boundary is real (1.4).

docs.title: The difference between an assembly and a package
docs.text:
People use these interchangeably and they are not the same.

An assembly is one file. Newtonsoft.Json.dll.

A NuGet package is a container. Newtonsoft.Json.13.0.3.nupkg — a zip file holding assemblies for several target frameworks, plus a description of what it depends on.

A picture: the assembly is the book; the package is the box it ships in. One box may hold several editions of the book — one for .NET 8, one for .NET Standard 2.0 — and a note saying which other boxes you also need.

docs.title: The simple version — referencing things
docs.text:
Modern .NET uses PackageReference directly in the .csproj:

<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="Serilog.AspNetCore" Version="8.0.0" />
  <ProjectReference Include="../MyApp.Core/MyApp.Core.csproj" />
</ItemGroup>

Two kinds of reference:

  • PackageReference — a NuGet package, downloaded from a feed.
  • ProjectReference — another project in your solution, built alongside yours.

Transitive dependencies come along automatically. Referencing Serilog.AspNetCore also gives you Serilog itself and several sinks, without you naming them. That is convenient and occasionally surprising — dotnet list package --include-transitive shows the full picture, and is worth running when you are auditing what your app actually pulls in.

docs.title: How it actually works — how assemblies get found at runtime
docs.text:
This surprises people who remember .NET Framework. The runtime does not search folders.

When you build, the SDK generates a deps.json next to your app listing every assembly it needs and where to find it:

{
  "targets": {
    ".NETCoreApp,Version=v10.0": {
      "MyApp/1.0.0": {
        "dependencies": { "Serilog": "4.0.0" },
        "runtime": { "MyApp.dll": {} }
      }
    }
  }
}

At startup the host reads that file and resolves everything from it. So:

  • Dropping a .dll into the output folder does nothing. If it is not in deps.json, the runtime will not load it.
  • A missing entry gives you FileNotFoundException at runtime, not at build.

Alongside it sits runtimeconfig.json, which says which .NET version to run on and carries runtime settings:

{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "tfm": "net10.0",
    "framework": { "name": "Microsoft.NETCore.App", "version": "10.0.0" },
    "configProperties": {
      "System.GC.Server": true
    }
  }
}

That System.GC.Server line is the Server GC setting from 3.4 — it ends up here.

docs.title: Version conflicts — the diamond problem
docs.text:
The most common real problem with packages:

Your app
├── PackageA  →  needs Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.0
└── PackageB  →  needs Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.0

Only one version can be loaded, because assembly identity includes the version. .NET resolves this by picking the highest — 13.0.0 — and hoping PackageA still works.

Usually it does, because most libraries are backwards compatible. When it does not, you get MethodNotFoundException or TypeLoadException at runtime, which is a confusing failure because the code compiled fine.

You can force a version explicitly:

<PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.0.3" />

And <CentralPackageManagement> lets you pin versions once for a whole solution, which is worth doing on anything larger than a couple of projects.

docs.title: The deeper detail — AssemblyLoadContext
docs.text:
Normally every assembly loads into one shared context and stays for the life of the process. That is fine for an application.

AssemblyLoadContext gives you an isolated container instead. It solves two problems:

Loading two versions of the same assembly. Impossible in the default context, since identity includes version. Separate contexts each get their own copy.

Unloading. A collectible context can be released, and its assemblies unloaded, which is how plugin systems avoid growing forever.

var context = new AssemblyLoadContext("PluginContext", isCollectible: true);

var assembly = context.LoadFromAssemblyPath(pluginPath);
var type = assembly.GetType("Plugin.Entry");
var plugin = (IPlugin)Activator.CreateInstance(type)!;

plugin.Run();

context.Unload();      // assemblies become eligible for collection

⚠️ Unloading only works if nothing outside the context still references anything inside it. One lingering reference — a cached type, an event subscription, a static field — and the whole context stays loaded. This is a memory leak that is genuinely hard to diagnose, and it is why plugin unloading has a reputation for being fiddly. See 3.5.

This replaced app domains, which .NET Framework used for isolation and which do not exist in modern .NET (3.1). App domains offered stronger isolation — including separate security boundaries — and AssemblyLoadContext deliberately does not. If you need real isolation now, the answer is a separate process or container.

docs.title: Strong naming
docs.text:
A strong name is a cryptographic signature giving an assembly a unique identity. In .NET Framework it was required for the shared Global Assembly Cache.

In modern .NET it is mostly irrelevant. There is no GAC, assemblies are app-local, and strong naming provides no security guarantee — the signature proves the key holder built it, not that the code is safe. You still see it on Microsoft's own libraries for compatibility. For your own code, ignore it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Producing a NuGet package from a project:

<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  <PackageId>MyCompany.OrderClient</PackageId>
  <Version>1.2.0</Version>
  <Authors>Your Name</Authors>
  <Description>Client library for the Orders API.</Description>
  <PackageLicenseExpression>MIT</PackageLicenseExpression>
  <RepositoryUrl>https://github.com/you/orderclient</RepositoryUrl>

  <!-- Ship the XML doc file so consumers get IntelliSense on your API -->
  <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
</PropertyGroup>

dotnet pack -c Release                      # produces bin/Release/*.nupkg
dotnet nuget push MyCompany.OrderClient.1.2.0.nupkg \
    --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json \
    --api-key $NUGET_KEY

Useful commands when a dependency is misbehaving:

dotnet list package --include-transitive     # everything you actually depend on
dotnet list package --outdated               # what has newer versions
dotnet list package --vulnerable             # known CVEs — run this in CI
dotnet nuget locals all --clear              # nuke the cache when it lies to you

--vulnerable is worth wiring into your build pipeline. It is the cheapest security check available in .NET and catches known vulnerabilities in transitive dependencies you never chose directly. See 17.7 and 24.7.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is an assembly?

It is the compiled output of a single project — a .dll or .exe. It contains the IL your code compiled to, plus metadata fully describing every type and member inside. That metadata is what reflection, the debugger and IntelliSense all read. The assembly is also the unit of deployment, of versioning, and of access control — internal means visible within one assembly, so the boundary is real rather than conventional.

Q: What is the difference between an assembly and a NuGet package?

An assembly is a single file. A NuGet package is a zip container that holds one or more assemblies — often several builds of the same library for different target frameworks — plus metadata describing what else it depends on. So one package can deliver several assemblies, and installing it also pulls in its transitive dependencies automatically.

Q: How does the runtime find assemblies at startup?

Through the deps.json file the SDK generates next to your application, which lists every assembly the app needs. The host reads that and resolves from it — it does not scan folders the way .NET Framework did. A practical consequence is that dropping a .dll into the output directory achieves nothing if it is not listed there, and a missing entry surfaces as a FileNotFoundException at runtime rather than a build error.

Q: What happens when two packages need different versions of the same dependency?

That is a diamond dependency. Only one version can load, because assembly identity includes the version number, so .NET picks the highest and assumes backwards compatibility. Usually that works. When it does not you get a MethodNotFoundException or TypeLoadException at runtime, which is confusing because everything compiled. You can force a specific version with an explicit PackageReference, and on a larger solution central package management lets you pin versions in one place.

Q: What is AssemblyLoadContext for?

It is an isolated container for loading assemblies, and it solves two problems the default context cannot. It lets you load two different versions of the same assembly side by side, which is otherwise impossible because identity includes version. And a collectible context can be unloaded, so plugin systems can release code rather than accumulating it. The catch is that unloading only succeeds if nothing outside the context still holds a reference to anything inside it — one cached type or lingering event subscription keeps the whole thing loaded, which is a hard leak to track down.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Copying a .dll into the output folder does nothing unless it is in deps.json.
  • Version conflicts fail at runtime, not build time. The code compiles, then throws MethodNotFoundException.
  • Transitive dependencies arrive without you asking. Run dotnet list package --include-transitive to see what you actually ship.
  • AssemblyLoadContext.Unload silently does nothing if any outside reference survives.
  • Strong naming provides no security. It proves who built it, not that it is safe.
  • App domains do not exist in modern .NET. Code expecting them will not port.
  • internal is per-assembly. Splitting one project into two changes what is visible.
  • Not running dotnet list package --vulnerable in CI means shipping known CVEs in packages you never chose.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The .csproj file is your project's build instructions. Modern .NET uses the SDK-style format, which is short because it assumes sensible defaults instead of listing every file.

  • <TargetFramework> says which .NET you build against. net10.0 is a TFM — Target Framework Moniker.
  • Files are included automatically by pattern. You do not list them.
  • Multi-targeting builds one project for several frameworks at once, which is how libraries support both old and new .NET.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means .csproj an XML file The build definition for one project: what to target, what to reference, how to package. SDK-style project the modern .csproj format Starts with <Project Sdk="...">. Short, because everything sensible is a default. MSBuild the build engine Reads the .csproj and runs the build. The dotnet build command drives it. TFM a short code string Target Framework Moniker. net10.0, net48, netstandard2.0. Says what you build against. <TargetFramework> a property, singular One TFM. The normal case. <TargetFrameworks> a property, plural Several TFMs, semicolon-separated. Triggers multi-targeting. Multi-targeting a build mode Building the same source once per TFM, producing several assemblies. RID a short code string Runtime Identifier. Names an OS and CPU: win-x64, linux-musl-arm64. <PropertyGroup> an XML element Holds settings — single values like the target framework or version. <ItemGroup> an XML element Holds lists — references, files, package dependencies. Implicit usings a build feature The SDK adds common using lines automatically based on project type. Directory.Build.props a shared file Settings applied to every project in a folder tree. Avoids repetition. Conditional compilation a compiler feature #if NET10_0_OR_GREATER — include code only for certain targets.

docs.title: Why the file got so much shorter
docs.text:
An old .NET Framework .csproj was hundreds of lines. It listed every single source file by name:

<!-- The OLD format — every file listed explicitly -->
<ItemGroup>
  <Compile Include="Program.cs" />
  <Compile Include="Models\Order.cs" />
  <Compile Include="Models\Customer.cs" />
  <Compile Include="Services\OrderService.cs" />
  <!-- ...and on, and on -->
</ItemGroup>

This caused constant pain. Adding a file meant editing the project. Two developers adding files at once caused a merge conflict in XML. Renaming a folder broke everything.

The SDK-style format replaced it. Here is a complete, working modern project file:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

That is the whole thing. Every .cs file in the folder and below is included automatically by a wildcard pattern the SDK supplies. You never list files again.

The Sdk attribute at the top says which set of defaults to use:

SDK For Microsoft.NET.Sdk Class libraries, console apps Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web ASP.NET Core apps Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Razor Razor class libraries Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Worker Background service apps

docs.title: What a TFM actually is
docs.text:
A Target Framework Moniker is just a short code saying which .NET you are building against. It determines which APIs the compiler will let you use.

TFM Means net10.0 .NET 10, cross-platform net8.0 .NET 8, cross-platform net48 .NET Framework 4.8, Windows only netstandard2.0 The old shared-API bridge (3.9) net10.0-windows .NET 10 plus Windows-only APIs — needed for WPF or WinForms

That last form is worth knowing. The suffix unlocks platform-specific APIs, and it means the resulting assembly only runs on that platform.

docs.title: The simple version — the properties you will actually set
docs.text:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>

    <!-- Turn on nullable reference type warnings — see 1.15 -->
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>

    <!-- Add common usings automatically, so files start at the namespace -->
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>

    <!-- Treat warnings as errors. Worth doing in CI. -->
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>

    <!-- Produce the XML docs file so consumers get IntelliSense -->
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>

    <!-- Required for pointers — see 3.3 -->
    <AllowUnsafeBlocks>false</AllowUnsafeBlocks>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Serilog.AspNetCore" Version="8.0.0" />
    <ProjectReference Include="../MyApp.Core/MyApp.Core.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

<PropertyGroup> holds single settings. <ItemGroup> holds lists. That is the only structural rule you need.

docs.title: Implicit usings — where did the using lines go?
docs.text:
With <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>, the SDK adds a standard set of using directives to every file, chosen by project type. A web project gets things like:

global using System;
global using System.Collections.Generic;
global using System.Linq;
global using System.Threading.Tasks;
global using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Builder;
// ...and more

This is why a modern file often starts straight at the namespace declaration with no using block. You can add your own project-wide ones:

<ItemGroup>
  <Using Include="MyApp.Common.Extensions" />
  <Using Include="System.Text.Json" Alias="Json" />
</ItemGroup>

⚠️ The downside is discoverability. When a type resolves and you cannot see why, the using is not in the file you are reading. That is worth knowing when someone new joins the project and cannot work out where something came from.

docs.title: How it actually works — multi-targeting
docs.text:
A library often needs to support several .NET versions. Multi-targeting builds it once per target:

<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFrameworks>net10.0;net8.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks>
</PropertyGroup>

Note the plural element name. That single change produces three separate assemblies, and dotnet pack puts all three in one NuGet package. Consumers automatically get the one matching their project.

Since each build sees a different set of APIs, you need conditional compilation where they differ:

public static string Describe(ReadOnlySpan<char> input)
{
#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
    // Available on modern .NET only
    return string.Concat("Value: ", input);
#else
    // netstandard2.0 fallback
    return "Value: " + input.ToString();
#endif
}

The SDK defines these symbols for you: NET10_0, NET8_0_OR_GREATER, NETSTANDARD2_0, NETFRAMEWORK and so on. Prefer the _OR_GREATER forms — #if NET8_0 is false when you later add net10.0, which produces a very confusing regression.

You can also vary references per target:

<ItemGroup Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'netstandard2.0'">
  <!-- Only the old target needs this polyfill package -->
  <PackageReference Include="System.Text.Json" Version="8.0.5" />
</ItemGroup>

Only multi-target when you actually need to. It multiplies build time and testing effort. An application should target exactly one framework — multi-targeting is for libraries with consumers you do not control.

docs.title: The deeper detail — sharing settings across a solution
docs.text:
Repeating the same properties in fifteen project files is a maintenance problem. Two files solve it.

Directory.Build.props at the solution root applies to every project beneath it:

<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

Individual projects then only carry what makes them different.

Directory.Packages.props centralises package versions so they cannot drift apart:

<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Serilog.AspNetCore" Version="8.0.0" />
    <PackageVersion Include="FluentValidation" Version="11.9.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

Projects then reference without a version:

<PackageReference Include="Serilog.AspNetCore" />

This directly prevents the diamond dependency problem from 3.6 within your own solution, and it is worth setting up on anything with more than about three projects.

docs.title: RIDs and publishing
docs.text:
A Runtime Identifier names a specific OS and CPU. You need one when publishing something self-contained:

dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained

Common values: win-x64, linux-x64, linux-musl-x64 (Alpine), osx-arm64.

⚠️ linux-musl-x64 is the Alpine one. Building linux-x64 and running it in an Alpine container fails at startup with a confusing missing-library error, because Alpine uses musl rather than glibc. This catches people out regularly — see 24.3.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic library that supports both modern .NET and .NET Framework consumers:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFrameworks>net10.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>

    <PackageId>MyCompany.Orders</PackageId>
    <Version>2.1.0</Version>
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
    <PackageLicenseExpression>MIT</PackageLicenseExpression>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <!-- netstandard2.0 predates nullable annotations, so it needs a shim -->
  <ItemGroup Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'netstandard2.0'">
    <PackageReference Include="Nullable" Version="1.3.1" PrivateAssets="all" />
    <PackageReference Include="System.Text.Json" Version="8.0.5" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

PrivateAssets="all" means that package is used to build this library but not passed on to whoever consumes it — right for build-time helpers and analysers.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between the old and SDK-style project formats?

The old format listed every source file explicitly, which made project files hundreds of lines long and caused merge conflicts whenever two people added files. SDK-style projects include files automatically by wildcard, so a complete modern project file can be six lines. The Sdk attribute at the top selects a set of defaults appropriate to the project type — web, library, worker. The practical difference day to day is that you almost never edit the project file except to add a package or change a property.

Q: What is a TFM?

A Target Framework Moniker — a short code in the project file saying which .NET version you build against, like net10.0 or net48. It controls which APIs the compiler allows. There is also a platform-suffixed form such as net10.0-windows, which unlocks Windows-only APIs for things like WinForms and means the output only runs on Windows.

Q: What is multi-targeting and when would you use it?

Building one project against several target frameworks at once, using the plural <TargetFrameworks> property. The compiler runs once per target, producing several assemblies that dotnet pack bundles into a single NuGet package, and consumers automatically get the one matching their project. You need it for libraries that must support both modern .NET and older consumers. Where the APIs differ you use conditional compilation with symbols like NET8_0_OR_GREATER. Applications should target exactly one framework — multi-targeting costs build time and testing effort, so it is only worth it when you do not control your consumers.

Q: How do you avoid repeating settings across many projects?

Directory.Build.props at the solution root, which MSBuild applies to every project beneath it — so target framework, nullable settings and language version live in one place. For package versions there is Directory.Packages.props with central package management, where projects reference a package without a version and the version is declared once. That also prevents the situation where two projects in the same solution drift onto different versions of the same dependency.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• <TargetFramework> versus <TargetFrameworks>. One letter changes single-target into multi-target, and the error if you get it wrong is unhelpful.
  • #if NET8_0 breaks when you add a newer target. Use NET8_0_OR_GREATER.
  • Implicit usings hide where types come from. The using is not in the file you are reading.
  • Multi-targeting multiplies your test matrix. Only do it for libraries that need it.
  • linux-x64 does not run on Alpine. Alpine needs linux-musl-x64.
  • Files are included by wildcard, so a stray .cs file anywhere under the project folder gets compiled — including in a backup folder someone left behind.
  • Forgetting PrivateAssets="all" on build-time packages leaks them to your consumers.
  • Changing the TFM can silently change behaviour, because the SDK applies different defaults per version.

docs.title: 3.8 — The .NET CLI
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.7 csproj and target frameworks · Next: 3.9 .NET Standard

Markers: ⭐ 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The .NET CLI is the dotnet command — a single tool that creates, builds, tests, runs and publishes .NET projects from a terminal, with no IDE involved.

  • It is what your CI pipeline actually runs. Visual Studio calls the same underlying build engine.
  • The commands you need daily: new, restore, build, run, test, publish.
  • build and publish are different. build compiles for development; publish produces the deployable output.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means CLI a command-line tool Command-Line Interface. The dotnet command. dotnet new a command Creates a project or file from a template. dotnet restore a command Downloads the NuGet packages a project needs. Usually implicit. dotnet build a command Compiles the project. Output goes to bin/. For development. dotnet run a command Builds and then runs the project. For development only. dotnet publish a command Produces the deployable output — trimmed, optimised, with deps.json. dotnet test a command Builds and runs the test projects. dotnet tool a command group Installs extra CLI tools, globally or per project. Configuration a build setting Debug (default, no optimisation, full symbols) or Release (optimised). Framework-dependent a publish mode Output needs .NET installed on the target machine. Small. Self-contained a publish mode Output includes the runtime. Needs nothing installed. Large. Global tool an installed CLI tool Available anywhere on the machine, like dotnet-ef or dotnet-counters. Local tool a project-scoped tool Pinned per repository in .config/dotnet-tools.json, so everyone gets the same version.

docs.title: Why learn the CLI when you have an IDE?
docs.text:
Three reasons, and the first is the one that matters in interviews.

1. CI/CD runs the CLI, not your IDE. Every GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps pipeline for .NET is a sequence of dotnet commands. If you cannot build from a terminal, you cannot debug a broken pipeline.

2. It is the same build. Visual Studio, Rider and dotnet build all drive MSBuild with the same project file. "It works in Visual Studio but not in CI" almost always means an environment difference — a missing package source, a different SDK version — not a genuinely different build.

3. It works everywhere. Linux containers have no IDE.

docs.title: The simple version — the daily commands
docs.text:
# Create things
dotnet new webapi -o MyApp.Api          # a Web API project
dotnet new classlib -o MyApp.Core       # a class library
dotnet new xunit -o MyApp.Tests         # a test project
dotnet new sln -n MyApp                 # a solution file
dotnet new gitignore                    # a .NET-aware .gitignore

# Wire them together
dotnet sln add MyApp.Api/MyApp.Api.csproj
dotnet add MyApp.Api reference MyApp.Core
dotnet add MyApp.Api package Serilog.AspNetCore

# Work
dotnet build                            # compile
dotnet run --project MyApp.Api          # build and run
dotnet watch --project MyApp.Api        # rerun automatically on file change
dotnet test                             # run all tests

# Ship
dotnet publish -c Release -o ./out

dotnet new list shows every available template, and templates can be installed from NuGet — Clean Architecture and other solution starters are distributed this way.

dotnet watch is the one people underuse. It rebuilds and restarts on every save, and for a web app it also refreshes the browser. It removes the stop-edit-start loop entirely.

docs.title: ⚠️ build versus publish
docs.text:
This distinction gets asked about, and it matters in practice.

dotnet build dotnet publish Purpose Development Deployment Output bin/Debug/net10.0/ bin/Release/net10.0/publish/ Includes dependencies? Only project ones All of them Includes deps.json, runtimeconfig.json? Partly Yes, complete Ready to copy to a server? No Yes

Never deploy the output of dotnet build. It is missing pieces the runtime needs to resolve assemblies (3.6), and it defaults to a Debug build with no optimisation. This is a genuinely common mistake — the app may even start, then fail on a code path that needs a package that was not copied.

docs.title: Framework-dependent versus self-contained
docs.text:
# Framework-dependent (default) — small, needs .NET installed on the target
dotnet publish -c Release
# → about 1 MB

# Self-contained — carries the runtime, needs nothing installed
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained
# → about 70 MB

# Self-contained + trimmed — unused framework code removed
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained -p:PublishTrimmed=true
# → about 30 MB

# Single file — everything in one executable
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained \
    -p:PublishSingleFile=true -p:PublishTrimmed=true

In Docker you normally want framework-dependent, because the base image already contains the runtime. Self-contained is for machines you do not control. See 24.1.

⚠️ PublishTrimmed removes code it believes is unused. Anything reached only through reflection looks unused and gets deleted, producing a runtime failure that never happened in development. Same underlying problem as Native AOT — see 3.2.

docs.title: How it actually works — tools
docs.text:
Global tools install once and work anywhere:

dotnet tool install -g dotnet-ef              # EF Core migrations
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-counters        # live performance metrics
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-dump            # memory dumps
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-trace           # performance traces
dotnet tool install -g dotnet-outdated-tool   # find outdated packages

Those middle three are the production diagnostics set from 3.5 and 18.9. Worth being able to name them.

Local tools are pinned per repository, so every developer and the CI agent use the same version:

dotnet new tool-manifest                      # creates .config/dotnet-tools.json
dotnet tool install dotnet-ef                 # no -g: local to this repo
dotnet tool restore                           # what CI runs
dotnet ef migrations add Initial              # runs the pinned version

Prefer local tools for anything a build depends on. A global dotnet-ef that is three versions ahead of the project's EF Core packages produces confusing failures.

docs.title: The deeper detail — commands worth knowing
docs.text:
# Diagnosing dependency problems
dotnet list package --include-transitive      # everything you actually depend on
dotnet list package --outdated                # newer versions available
dotnet list package --vulnerable              # known CVEs — put this in CI
dotnet nuget locals all --clear               # clear the package cache

# Build troubleshooting
dotnet build -v detailed                      # verbose MSBuild output
dotnet build --no-restore                     # skip restore when it is already done
dotnet clean                                  # delete bin and obj

# Testing
dotnet test --filter "Category=Integration"
dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"   # coverage via coverlet
dotnet test --logger "trx;LogFileName=results.trx"

# Info
dotnet --info                                 # SDKs, runtimes, OS, everything
dotnet --list-sdks
dotnet --list-runtimes

dotnet --info is the first thing to run when a build behaves differently on two machines. It shows the SDK version, the runtimes present, and the OS — which is usually where the difference is.

docs.title: Controlling the SDK version
docs.text:
A global.json pins which SDK a repository uses:

{
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.100",
    "rollForward": "latestFeature"
  }
}

Without this, whoever has the newest SDK installed builds with it, and subtle differences appear between machines. Worth adding to any repository with more than one developer.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic CI pipeline is just these commands in order:

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4

  - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
    with:
      dotnet-version: '10.0.x'

  - name: Restore
    run: dotnet restore

  - name: Build
    run: dotnet build --no-restore -c Release

  - name: Test
    run: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --logger trx

  - name: Check for vulnerable packages
    run: dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive

  - name: Publish
    run: dotnet publish -c Release -o ./out --no-build

Two details worth noticing:

  • --no-restore and --no-build stop each step redoing the previous one's work. On a large solution that saves minutes per run.
  • The steps mirror exactly what you would type locally, which is why being fluent in the CLI makes pipeline problems easy to reproduce on your own machine.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between dotnet build and dotnet publish?

build compiles the project for development — output goes to bin/Debug, and it does not gather everything needed to run elsewhere. publish produces the deployable output: all dependencies copied in, plus the deps.json and runtimeconfig.json the runtime needs to resolve assemblies at startup. Deploying the output of build is a common mistake — it may start and then fail on a code path needing a package that was never copied, and it defaults to an unoptimised Debug build.

Q: What is the difference between framework-dependent and self-contained publishing?

Framework-dependent output relies on .NET being installed on the target machine, so it is small — around a megabyte. Self-contained output includes the entire runtime, so it needs nothing installed but is much larger, around seventy megabytes before trimming. In Docker you normally want framework-dependent because the base image already has the runtime. Self-contained suits machines you do not control, or where you cannot guarantee a runtime version.

Q: What are local tools and why use them over global ones?

A global tool is installed once per machine and available anywhere. A local tool is pinned per repository in a manifest file, so dotnet tool restore gives every developer and the CI agent the exact same version. That matters for anything the build depends on — dotnet-ef is the usual example, because a globally installed version that is ahead of the project's EF Core packages produces confusing failures that only affect one machine.

Q: A colleague says the build works locally but fails in CI. Where do you start?

dotnet --info on both, because it shows the SDK version, installed runtimes and OS, and the difference is usually there. If the SDK versions differ, a global.json pinning the version fixes it permanently. After that I would check the package sources, since a private feed configured locally but not in CI produces restore failures, and confirm the CI is running the same commands rather than a different build path. The underlying point is that Visual Studio and dotnet build drive the same engine with the same project file, so a genuine difference in output almost always means an environment difference.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Deploying dotnet build output instead of dotnet publish. Missing dependencies and runtime config files.
  • Forgetting -c Release. Debug builds are unoptimised and much slower.
  • PublishTrimmed silently removes reflection-only code. Fails at runtime, not at build.
  • A global dotnet-ef mismatched with the project's EF Core version causes confusing errors. Use a local tool.
  • No global.json means whoever has the newest SDK builds differently.
  • dotnet run is not for production. It builds first and adds overhead — run the published DLL directly.
  • --no-build without a preceding build fails, unhelpfully.
  • linux-x64 is not Alpine. Alpine needs linux-musl-x64.

docs.title: 3.9 — .NET Standard
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.8 The .NET CLI · Next: 3.10 Release cadence

Markers: — · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
.NET Standard is a list of APIs that several different .NET platforms all promised to provide. A library targeting it could run on .NET Framework, .NET Core, Xamarin and Mono without being rebuilt for each.

  • It is not a runtime. Nothing "runs on .NET Standard" — it is a contract, not a platform.
  • It solved a real problem in the split years, and the unification in .NET 5 made it mostly obsolete.
  • Today you only target it if you must support .NET Framework consumers.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means .NET Standard a specification A list of APIs that multiple .NET platforms all agree to implement. Not a runtime. netstandard2.0 a TFM The most useful version. The last one .NET Framework supports. netstandard2.1 a TFM A later version .NET Framework never supported. Usually the wrong choice. Implementation an actual platform .NET Framework, .NET Core, Mono, Xamarin — the things that provide the APIs. Contract assembly a reference-only .dll Has the API shapes but no working code. What you compile against when targeting Standard. PlatformNotSupportedException an exception type Thrown when an API exists in the contract but is not implemented on the platform you are running on. Type forwarding a linking mechanism Lets a type declared in the contract resolve to the real one in the running platform.

docs.title: The problem it was invented to solve
docs.text:
Rewind to around 2016. There were several separate .NET platforms, and they were genuinely different products:

  • .NET Framework — Windows
  • .NET Core — cross-platform servers
  • Xamarin — iOS and Android
  • Mono — Linux and Unity
  • UWP — Windows Store apps

If you wrote a library, which one did you build for? Building for all of them meant five builds, five test runs and five sets of quirks.

.NET Standard was the answer: an agreed list of APIs that all of them promised to provide. Target the list rather than any one platform, and your single library works on all of them.

A picture: a plug standard rather than a specific socket. You do not build one kettle for UK sockets, one for EU, one for US. You agree a shape, everyone supports it, and one kettle works everywhere.

docs.title: Why it is mostly obsolete now
docs.text:
The reason is simple: the platforms merged.

.NET 5 unified .NET Core, Mono and Xamarin into one product (3.1). When there is only one platform, there is nothing to standardise between.

Microsoft's own guidance now is:

net10.0 for anything new. netstandard2.0 only if you must support .NET Framework.

.NET Standard is frozen at 2.1 and will never gain a new version. It exists purely for backwards compatibility.

docs.title: The simple version — which version to pick
docs.text:
Version Supported by Use it? netstandard2.0 .NET Framework 4.6.1+, .NET Core 2.0+, Mono, Xamarin ✅ The only one worth targeting, if you need Framework consumers netstandard2.1 .NET Core 3.0+, Mono, Xamarin — not .NET Framework ❌ Almost never. See below.

netstandard2.1 is the trap. It looks like the newer, better option. But .NET Framework never supported it, which removes the entire reason to target Standard in the first place. If your consumers are all on modern .NET, target net10.0 directly and get the full API surface. So netstandard2.1 occupies a niche that barely exists.

The decision comes down to one question:

Do I need .NET Framework consumers?
├── Yes → netstandard2.0
└── No  → net10.0 (or whichever current version)

docs.title: How it actually works — contracts and type forwarding
docs.text:
When you compile against netstandard2.0, you are not compiling against real code. You are compiling against a contract assembly — a .dll containing the API shapes with no implementations.

At runtime, on whichever platform you land, type forwarding redirects each type to the platform's real implementation. So System.String in the contract resolves to .NET Framework's String on Framework, and .NET 10's String on .NET 10.

That is why one build genuinely works everywhere: the contract is stable and each platform supplies the real thing.

docs.title: ⚠️ The compiles-but-throws problem
docs.text:
Because the contract lists APIs the majority of platforms support, some entries are not actually implemented everywhere. Those compile fine and throw at runtime:

// Compiles against netstandard2.0.
// Throws PlatformNotSupportedException on some platforms.
var key = new RSACryptoServiceProvider();

This is the practical weakness of the approach. The contract promises more than every implementation delivers, and you only discover the gap on the platform where it fails.

The mitigation is straightforward: test on every platform you claim to support. A library that says it targets netstandard2.0 and has only ever been run on .NET 10 has not really been verified.

docs.title: The deeper detail — multi-targeting is usually better
docs.text:
If you need both Framework consumers and modern APIs, multi-targeting beats .NET Standard:

<TargetFrameworks>net10.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks>

This builds twice. The net10.0 build gets the full modern API surface — Span<T>, IAsyncEnumerable<T>, everything. The netstandard2.0 build gets the smaller shared set for Framework consumers. NuGet gives each consumer the right one automatically.

Compare with targeting netstandard2.0 alone, where everybody — including your modern .NET consumers — is limited to the 2015-era API surface.

Where the two builds differ, use conditional compilation (3.7):

public static bool Contains(string text, char value)
{
#if NETSTANDARD2_0
    return text.IndexOf(value) >= 0;              // no char overload back then
#else
    return text.Contains(value);                   // modern, faster
#endif
}

netstandard2.0 also misses a lot that you can partly recover with packages:

Missing from netstandard2.0 Polyfill package Span<T>, Memory<T> System.Memory IAsyncEnumerable<T> Microsoft.Bcl.AsyncInterfaces System.Text.Json System.Text.Json Nullable annotations Nullable (build-time only)

Those close much of the gap, at the cost of extra dependencies your consumers inherit.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A library supporting both worlds properly:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFrameworks>net10.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <!-- Only the old target needs these polyfills -->
  <ItemGroup Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'netstandard2.0'">
    <PackageReference Include="System.Text.Json" Version="8.0.5" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Bcl.AsyncInterfaces" Version="8.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Nullable" Version="1.3.1" PrivateAssets="all" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Note LangVersion=latest. The C# language version is independent of the target framework, so you can use modern syntax like records and pattern matching even when targeting netstandard2.0 — as long as the feature does not need a runtime type that is missing. Records work; Span<T> does not without the polyfill.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is .NET Standard?

A specification listing APIs that several .NET platforms all agreed to implement. It is not a runtime — nothing runs on .NET Standard. It existed because around 2016 there were several separate .NET platforms, and a library author otherwise had to build separately for each. Targeting the standard meant one build that worked on .NET Framework, .NET Core, Xamarin and Mono alike.

Q: Is it still relevant?

Mostly not. It solved a fragmentation problem, and .NET 5 removed the fragmentation by unifying those platforms into one product. It is frozen at 2.1 and will never gain another version. The one remaining reason to target netstandard2.0 is if you publish a library that must still be consumable from .NET Framework, since that is the last version Framework supports. For anything else you target the current .NET directly and get the full API surface.

Q: Why would you target netstandard2.0 rather than netstandard2.1?

Because .NET Framework supports 2.0 and never supported 2.1. Supporting Framework consumers is essentially the only remaining reason to target Standard at all, so 2.1 removes the point of the exercise. If all your consumers are on modern .NET you should target net10.0 directly rather than 2.1, because you get the full API surface. That leaves 2.1 covering a niche that barely exists in practice.

Q: If you need to support both Framework and modern .NET, what would you do?

Multi-target rather than targeting .NET Standard alone. With <TargetFrameworks>net10.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks> the modern build gets the complete current API surface while the Standard build serves Framework consumers, and NuGet hands each consumer the right one. Targeting netstandard2.0 on its own would restrict everybody — including your modern consumers — to a 2015-era API surface. Where the two builds genuinely differ you bridge it with conditional compilation.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "It's a runtime." It is a specification. Nothing executes on .NET Standard.
  • Targeting netstandard2.1 gets you the worst of both — no Framework support, and a smaller API surface than targeting modern .NET.
  • Some APIs compile but throw PlatformNotSupportedException. The contract promises more than every implementation delivers.
  • Targeting Standard alone limits your modern consumers too, not just the old ones.
  • It is frozen. No version after 2.1 will ever ship.
  • The C# language version is independent of the target. You can use modern syntax on netstandard2.0, provided the feature does not need a missing runtime type.
  • Polyfill packages become your consumers' dependencies too. Adding System.Memory puts it in everyone's dependency tree.
