docs.title: 3.10 — Release Cadence: LTS vs STS
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 3. .NET Runtime and Platform Prev: 3.9 .NET Standard · Next: 4.1 What ASP.NET Core is

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
.NET ships a new major version every November, and each one is supported for a fixed period depending on whether it is LTS or STS.

  • Even numbers are LTS — Long-Term Support, 3 years. .NET 8, 10, 12.
  • Odd numbers are STS — Standard-Term Support, 18 months. .NET 7, 9, 11.
  • Both are equally stable. STS is not a preview or a beta — it is a full release with a shorter support window.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means LTS a support track Long-Term Support. 3 years of patches. Even-numbered releases. STS a support track Standard-Term Support. 18 months of patches. Odd-numbered releases. Cadence a release rhythm .NET ships one major version every November, without exception. End of support (EOL) a date After it, no more security patches. Running past it means known unpatched vulnerabilities. Patch release a version like 10.0.3 Bug and security fixes only. No new features. Safe to take immediately. Servicing the patch process Monthly patch releases, usually on the second Tuesday. global.json a file in your repo Pins which SDK version builds this repository. See 3.8. Roll-forward a runtime behaviour An app built for 10.0.0 will run on 10.0.5 automatically. Patch versions are compatible. Go-live a support status A preview Microsoft will support in production. Rare, and still a preview.

docs.title: Why there are two tracks
docs.text:
Different organisations want opposite things from a release schedule.

Some want stability. A bank or a hospital system does not want to upgrade its runtime every year. Every upgrade means regression testing, change approval and risk.

Some want the newest features. A startup shipping daily would rather have the latest performance improvements immediately.

Microsoft serves both with alternating tracks. Every November there is a release; every other one is supported for three years instead of eighteen months.

A picture: a bus route with two kinds of stop. Buses come at the same regular interval, but some are express services that stay in service much longer. You catch whichever suits how often you want to change buses.

docs.title: ⚠️ STS is not a beta
docs.text:
This is the most common misunderstanding, and it is worth being precise about in an interview.

.NET 9 is not "less finished" than .NET 8. It is a complete, production-ready, fully supported release. It receives exactly the same quality of patches. The only difference is that the support window is 18 months rather than 3 years.

In fact STS releases often contain features that appear in the next LTS after being proven — they are where new work lands first.

docs.title: The simple version — the schedule
docs.text:
Version Released Track Support ends .NET 6 Nov 2021 LTS Nov 2024 .NET 7 Nov 2022 STS May 2024 .NET 8 Nov 2023 LTS Nov 2026 .NET 9 Nov 2024 STS May 2026 .NET 10 Nov 2025 LTS Nov 2028

Notice something in that table: .NET 7 went out of support before .NET 6 did, even though it came out a year later. An 18-month window that starts later can still finish earlier. That catches people out when planning.

Always check the current dates against Microsoft's support policy page before an interview. This table is a memory aid, and the dates move as new versions ship.

docs.title: How it actually works — choosing a track
docs.text:
Choose LTS when:

  • Upgrading is expensive — heavy regression testing, formal change control
  • You are in a regulated industry
  • The application is stable and rarely touched
  • You have many services and cannot upgrade them all frequently

Choose STS when:

  • You deploy often anyway, so upgrading is routine
  • You want a specific new feature now
  • You have good automated test coverage, making upgrades cheap

The honest default for most teams is LTS. Not because STS is worse, but because a three-year window means you upgrade on your own schedule rather than to a deadline. Most organisations underestimate how much friction a forced upgrade creates.

But there is a trap in the middle. Staying on LTS and skipping every STS means jumping two major versions at a time — .NET 8 straight to .NET 10. That is a bigger change with more breaking changes at once than two smaller steps. If your team upgrades easily, taking every release is often less painful overall.

docs.title: Patch releases and roll-forward
docs.text:
Every month, usually the second Tuesday, Microsoft ships patch releases: 10.0.1, 10.0.2 and so on. These contain only bug and security fixes, never new features.

Take them promptly. They are where security vulnerabilities get fixed, and they are designed to be safe.

Roll-forward makes this easy. An app built against 10.0.0 automatically runs on 10.0.5 if that is what is installed — patch versions are binary compatible. You do not have to rebuild to pick up a security patch on the runtime.

You can control the behaviour in runtimeconfig.json:

{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "rollForward": "latestPatch"
  }
}
Setting Behaviour latestPatch Default. Use the newest patch of the same major.minor. minor Roll forward to a newer minor if the exact one is missing. major Roll forward across major versions. Risky. disable Exact version only. Fails if it is missing.

docs.title: The deeper detail — running past end of support
docs.text:
Once a version reaches end of support, no more security patches are issued. Ever.

That is not a minor operational detail. It means:

  • Any vulnerability found afterwards stays unpatched in your deployment, permanently.
  • Public CVEs tell attackers exactly what to try.
  • Compliance frameworks — PCI DSS, SOC 2, ISO 27001 — generally treat unsupported runtimes as an audit finding.
  • Container base images stop being updated, so vulnerability scanners flag every build.

Running on an unsupported .NET version is a security problem, not a technical debt item. Being able to frame it that way is genuinely useful, because it is the argument that actually gets upgrade work prioritised. "We should upgrade for the performance" loses to feature work. "We are running an unpatched runtime with published CVEs" does not.

docs.title: Pinning the SDK
docs.text:
The runtime and the SDK are versioned separately. A global.json pins which SDK builds your repository:

{
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.100",
    "rollForward": "latestFeature"
  }
}

Without it, whoever has the newest SDK installed builds with it, and subtle differences appear between developer machines and CI. See 3.8.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Checking what you are on and what is installed:

dotnet --list-runtimes      # every runtime present, side by side
dotnet --list-sdks          # every SDK present
dotnet --info               # everything, including the OS

Upgrading a project is usually one line:

<!-- Before -->
<TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>

<!-- After -->
<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>

Then rebuild and run the tests. In practice most upgrades are close to that simple — .NET has a strong compatibility record — but check the breaking changes list first, and expect some package updates to be needed alongside.

A sensible upgrade order:

  1. Read the breaking changes page for the target version.
  2. Change the TFM in one project and build.
  3. Update packages that complain.
  4. Run the full test suite.
  5. Deploy to a non-production environment and watch memory and latency for a day.

That last step matters because the differences that bite are usually runtime behaviour changes — a GC default, a thread-pool heuristic — rather than compile errors. .NET 9's DATAS change (3.4) is a good example: nothing fails to compile, but memory behaviour in containers changes.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between LTS and STS?

Both are full production releases shipped every November. LTS — Long-Term Support — gets three years of patches and lands on even-numbered versions like .NET 8 and .NET 10. STS — Standard-Term Support — gets eighteen months and lands on odd numbers. The common misunderstanding is that STS is somehow a preview or lower quality. It is not: same stability, same patch quality, only a shorter support window. STS releases are often where new features land first before appearing in the next LTS.

Q: Which would you choose for a new project?

Usually LTS, because a three-year window means you upgrade on your own schedule rather than against a deadline, and most organisations underestimate the friction of a forced upgrade. I would choose STS if the team deploys frequently anyway and has good automated test coverage, so upgrading is routine, or if there is a specific feature worth having now. There is a trap in between though — staying on LTS and skipping every STS means jumping two major versions at once, which bundles more breaking changes into a single step than taking them one at a time.

Q: What happens when a version reaches end of support?

No further security patches are issued, so any vulnerability discovered afterwards stays unpatched in your deployment permanently — and because CVEs are published, attackers know exactly what to try. Container base images also stop being updated, so scanners flag every build. Most compliance frameworks treat an unsupported runtime as an audit finding. I would frame it as a security issue rather than technical debt, because that is the argument that actually gets the upgrade prioritised against feature work.

Q: How do patch releases and roll-forward work?

Patch releases ship roughly monthly and contain only bug and security fixes, never new features, so they are safe to take promptly. Roll-forward means an application built against 10.0.0 will automatically run on 10.0.5 if that is what is installed, because patch versions are binary compatible — you do not need to rebuild to pick up a runtime security fix. The default policy is latestPatch, and you can change it in runtimeconfig.json if you need stricter or looser behaviour.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "STS is a beta." It is a full production release. Only the support window differs.
  • A newer version can go out of support first. .NET 7 ended before .NET 6 did.
  • Skipping every STS makes upgrades harder, because you jump two majors at once.
  • Running past end of support is a security problem, not just outdated tooling.
  • The SDK and runtime are versioned separately. A newer SDK can build for an older runtime.
  • Without a global.json, different machines build with different SDKs.
  • Upgrade problems are usually runtime behaviour, not compile errors. Watch memory and latency in a test environment before shipping.
  • Always verify the current dates. The schedule moves every November.

docs.title: 4.1 — What ASP.NET Core Is
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 3.10 Release cadence · Next: 4.2 Hosting model

Markers: 🔥 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's framework for building web applications and APIs. It is a complete rewrite of the old ASP.NET — cross-platform, much faster, and no longer tied to IIS or to Windows.

  • The old ASP.NET was built on System.Web, a library welded to IIS. ASP.NET Core threw that away entirely.
  • Everything is now opt-in. You add the pieces you want rather than starting with everything switched on.
  • Dependency injection and configuration are built into the framework, not bolted on afterwards.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means ASP.NET Core a web framework The library set for building web apps and APIs on .NET. Runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. ASP.NET (classic) the old web framework The 2002–2019 version, built on System.Web. Windows and IIS only. Now legacy. System.Web an old assembly The classic framework's core library. Contained HttpContext, session, the page lifecycle. Does not exist in ASP.NET Core. Kestrel a web server The cross-platform HTTP server built into ASP.NET Core. Your app hosts it directly. Middleware a pipeline component A piece of code that handles a request and can pass it along. See 5.1. Host the object that runs your app Owns the server, dependency injection, configuration and logging, and manages startup and shutdown. HttpContext a class Everything about the current request and response. Exists in both frameworks but is a different, lighter type in Core. Web API a project type An app that returns data (usually JSON) instead of HTML pages. Razor Pages a project type Page-focused server-rendered HTML. The modern replacement for Web Forms. Blazor a project type Building interactive UI in C# instead of JavaScript. Minimal API a style Defining endpoints as lambdas in Program.cs rather than in controller classes.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
A web application needs to do a lot of plumbing before it does anything useful. Accept TCP connections, parse HTTP, decide which code handles which URL, read configuration, write logs, handle authentication, serialise responses.

ASP.NET Core provides all of it, so you write the part that is actually your application.

docs.title: Why it was rewritten
docs.text:
The classic ASP.NET was built in 2002 on an assembly called System.Web. That assembly was fused to IIS — Microsoft's Windows web server. Not "designed for" it: fused to it. You could not separate them.

That created three problems that could not be fixed incrementally.

It could only run on Windows. IIS is a Windows product. As the industry moved to Linux servers and containers, ASP.NET could not follow.

It was heavy. Every application loaded the entire framework whether it used it or not — session state, the page lifecycle, view state, all of it. You paid for features you had never heard of.

It shipped inside Windows. New features arrived with Windows updates rather than with your application, so you waited on the operating system's release schedule.

So Microsoft rewrote it. ASP.NET Core has no System.Web at all. The whole framework is a set of NuGet packages your app references, and it hosts its own web server.

A picture: the old ASP.NET was a house built into a specific plot of land. You could not move it. ASP.NET Core is a caravan — it carries what it needs and can park anywhere.

docs.title: The simple version — what actually changed
docs.text: ASP.NET (classic) ASP.NET Core Runs on Windows only Windows, Linux, macOS Web server IIS only Kestrel, and optionally behind IIS or Nginx Ships with Windows Your application, as NuGet packages Features All loaded, always Opt-in — you add what you use Dependency injection Third-party, bolted on Built in Configuration web.config (XML) appsettings.json and many providers Request pipeline HttpModules and HttpHandlers Middleware Open source No Yes Speed Slower Roughly 10× faster on common benchmarks

docs.title: How it actually works — "everything is opt-in"
docs.text:
This is the change you feel most day to day.

In classic ASP.NET, a new project arrived with session state, authentication, view state and the full page lifecycle already running. Turning things off meant editing web.config and hoping.

In ASP.NET Core you start with almost nothing and add what you need:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Nothing is on by default. You add each capability deliberately.
builder.Services.AddControllers();          // want controllers? add them
builder.Services.AddAuthentication();       // want auth? add it

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();                  // want HTTPS redirect? add it
app.UseAuthentication();                    // order matters here — see 5.2
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Every line is a decision. Nothing you did not ask for is running.

The benefit is not only performance — it is that you can see the whole application's behaviour in one file. In classic ASP.NET, behaviour came from web.config, from Global.asax, from IIS settings and from machine-level config, and tracking down why something happened meant checking four places.

docs.title: The two halves of Program.cs
docs.text:
Notice the shape above. There are always two phases, separated by builder.Build():

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// PHASE 1 — REGISTER. What services exist?
builder.Services.AddSomething();

var app = builder.Build();      // ← the dividing line

// PHASE 2 — CONFIGURE. What happens to a request?
app.UseSomething();

app.Run();

builder.Services.Add... says what is available. app.Use... says what happens, and in what order. Confusing the two is the single most common beginner mistake, and after Build() is called you cannot add more services.

Covered properly in 4.3.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what is gone and what replaced it
docs.text:
If you have classic ASP.NET experience, these are the things that will not be there:

Gone Replaced by System.Web Nothing — the whole model changed Web Forms, .aspx, view state Razor Pages, Blazor HttpModules, HttpHandlers Middleware (5.1) Global.asax Program.cs web.config appsettings.json (7.1) HttpContext.Current (static) Injected IHttpContextAccessor (21.12) Session, on by default Opt-in, and usually avoided in APIs Server.MapPath IWebHostEnvironment.ContentRootPath

HttpContext.Current deserves a note. In classic ASP.NET it was a static property you could reach from anywhere. Convenient, and a design flaw — it made code untestable and tied every layer to the web. ASP.NET Core removed it. If you genuinely need the context outside a controller you inject IHttpContextAccessor, and needing it is usually a hint that something should have been passed as a parameter instead.

docs.title: The project types
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core is one framework covering several kinds of application:

  • Web API — returns JSON. The most common today.
  • MVC — server-rendered HTML with controllers and views.
  • Razor Pages — server-rendered HTML, organised per page rather than per controller.
  • Blazor — interactive UI written in C#.
  • gRPC — high-performance binary APIs between services.
  • Minimal APIs — endpoints as lambdas, no controllers.

They share the same host, the same dependency injection, the same middleware pipeline and the same configuration. Learning the fundamentals once covers all of them, which is why sections 4 to 8 of this roadmap matter more than any individual project type.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The smallest complete ASP.NET Core application:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();

app.MapGet("/", () => "Hello World!");

app.Run();

Four lines, and that is a real web server. Compare with classic ASP.NET, which needed a Global.asax, a web.config, a project structure and IIS configured to host it.

A realistic Web API startup, which is what you will actually see:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// ---- Phase 1: register services ----
builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

var app = builder.Build();

// ---- Phase 2: build the request pipeline ----
if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    app.MapOpenApi();                       // only expose the API schema in dev

app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAuthentication();                     // who are you?
app.UseAuthorization();                      // are you allowed?
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Everything the application does is visible in that one file. That readability is a deliberate design goal, and it is genuinely one of the strongest arguments for ASP.NET Core over what came before.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is ASP.NET Core and how does it differ from ASP.NET?

ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's web framework for building applications and APIs on .NET. It is a complete rewrite rather than an upgrade. The classic ASP.NET was built on System.Web, an assembly fused to IIS, which meant it only ran on Windows and always loaded the entire framework whether you used it or not. ASP.NET Core removed System.Web entirely, ships as NuGet packages with your application, hosts its own cross-platform server in Kestrel, and makes every feature opt-in. It also has dependency injection and configuration built into the framework rather than bolted on, and it is roughly ten times faster on typical benchmarks.

Q: Why was it rewritten rather than improved?

Because the problems were architectural. System.Web was fused to IIS, so cross-platform support was not something you could add — it would have meant replacing the foundation. The same applied to the always-on feature set and to shipping inside Windows, which tied the release schedule to the operating system. Fixing any of those meant a new foundation, so Microsoft built one and kept the good ideas.

Q: What happened to HttpContext.Current?

It is gone. In classic ASP.NET it was a static property reachable from anywhere, which was convenient and a genuine design flaw — it made code impossible to unit test and coupled every layer to the web. ASP.NET Core has no static context. If you truly need the request context outside a controller you inject IHttpContextAccessor, but needing it usually indicates that the value should have been passed as a parameter instead.

Q: What replaced HttpModules and HttpHandlers?

Middleware. In classic ASP.NET the pipeline was configured through modules and handlers registered in web.config, with an execution order that was hard to see. In ASP.NET Core the pipeline is built explicitly in Program.cs with a sequence of app.Use... calls, so the order is visible in the code, and each piece of middleware decides whether to pass the request on or short-circuit it.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• "ASP.NET Core is ASP.NET with a new version number." It is a rewrite. System.Web does not exist, and code depending on it will not port.
  • The name is confusing. The runtime dropped "Core" at .NET 5, but ASP.NET Core kept it. ASP.NET Core 10 runs on .NET 10.
  • Nothing is on by default. Forgetting app.UseAuthentication() means User is never populated and authorization silently fails.
  • Service registration must happen before builder.Build(). Adding after throws.
  • Web Forms did not port and never will. Migrating means rewriting the UI.
  • Session exists but is opt-in and rarely right for APIs. It makes your app stateful, which breaks horizontal scaling (24.12).

docs.title: 4.2 — Cross-Platform Hosting, Kestrel, and the Reverse-Proxy Model
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.1 What ASP.NET Core is · Next: 4.3 Program.cs

Markers: ⭐ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Kestrel is the web server built into every ASP.NET Core app. Your application is the web server — there is no separate IIS process required.

  • A reverse proxy (IIS, Nginx, a cloud load balancer) usually sits in front of Kestrel and forwards requests to it.
  • Kestrel is fast but deliberately minimal. The proxy handles TLS certificates, multiple sites on one machine, and slow-client protection.
  • The proxy hides the real client IP, so you need UseForwardedHeaders to get it back.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Web server a program Listens on a TCP port, speaks HTTP, hands requests to your code. Kestrel the built-in web server Cross-platform, fast, runs inside your application process. The default. Reverse proxy a server in front of yours Receives requests from the internet and forwards them to your app. IIS, Nginx, Apache, YARP. Edge server a role The server directly exposed to the internet. Either Kestrel alone, or the reverse proxy. IIS Microsoft's web server Windows only. In ASP.NET Core it acts as a reverse proxy, not as the host. HTTP.sys a Windows-only server An alternative to Kestrel. Supports Windows Authentication and port sharing. ANCM an IIS module ASP.NET Core Module. The piece of IIS that launches and forwards to your app. In-process hosting an IIS mode Your app runs inside the IIS worker process. The default on IIS, and faster. Out-of-process hosting an IIS mode IIS runs your app as a separate process and proxies to it over HTTP. TLS termination a responsibility Decrypting HTTPS. Usually done by the proxy, so traffic to Kestrel is plain HTTP. UseForwardedHeaders a middleware method Reads X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto so your app sees the real client IP and scheme. X-Forwarded-For an HTTP header Added by a proxy to record the original client IP.

docs.title: Your app is the web server
docs.text:
This is the biggest mental shift from classic ASP.NET.

In the old model, IIS was the web server and your application was a plugin inside it. IIS listened on port 80, decided your app should handle the request, and loaded your code into its worker process. You could not run the app without IIS.

In ASP.NET Core, your application contains a web server. Kestrel is a library your app references. Run the app and it opens a socket and starts listening itself. No IIS required, no Windows required.

That is why dotnet run just works, and why a container image can hold nothing but your app and the .NET runtime.

docs.title: So why is there usually still a proxy?
docs.text:
Kestrel is deliberately narrow: it handles HTTP well and fast, and does little else. A reverse proxy in front of it covers things Kestrel intentionally does not.

A picture: Kestrel is the kitchen; the reverse proxy is the front of house. The kitchen is excellent at cooking and nothing else. The front of house handles the door, the queue, difficult customers and directing people to the right table. You could serve straight from the kitchen — but you would not want to at a busy restaurant.

What the proxy gives you:

  • TLS certificates — issuing, renewing and terminating HTTPS in one place rather than per app.
  • Several apps on one machine — routing /api to one app and /admin to another, both on port 443.
  • Slow-client protection — an attacker sending a request one byte per second ties up the proxy, not your app.
  • Static files and caching, often faster than doing it in your app.
  • Load balancing across several instances of your app.
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"HTTPS :443"| P["Reverse proxy<br/>Nginx / IIS / ALB<br/>(handles TLS)"]
    P -->|"HTTP :5000"| K1["Kestrel<br/>your app, instance 1"]
    P -->|"HTTP :5000"| K2["Kestrel<br/>your app, instance 2"]

Note the traffic between proxy and app is usually plain HTTP. The proxy terminated TLS. That is fine when both sit inside a private network, and it is why your app can be configured without certificates.

docs.title: The simple version — the three servers
docs.text:
Server Platform Use it when Kestrel All Always. The default, and the only cross-platform option. IIS Windows Hosting on Windows Server. Acts as a reverse proxy in front of Kestrel. HTTP.sys Windows You need Windows Authentication or port sharing. Rare.

Kestrel is not optional in the way the others are — even behind IIS, Kestrel is what actually runs your code in the common in-process case.

docs.title: How it actually works — IIS in-process vs out-of-process
docs.text:
On Windows this distinction gets asked about, so it is worth being precise.

Out-of-process (the original model):

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] --> I["IIS<br/>w3wp.exe"]
    I -->|"HTTP over localhost"| K["Kestrel<br/>dotnet.exe<br/>(separate process)"]

IIS starts your app as a separate process and proxies each request to it over local HTTP. That is two HTTP hops per request.

In-process (the default since .NET Core 3.0):

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] --> I["IIS w3wp.exe<br/>── your app runs INSIDE ──"]

Your app runs inside the IIS worker process. No extra hop, no second process. Roughly 2–3× more throughput.

Set in the project file:

<AspNetCoreHostingModel>InProcess</AspNetCoreHostingModel>

In-process is the default and almost always what you want. The exceptions: you need a different .NET version per app in the same IIS app pool, or you are running something that must not share a process.

⚠️ One in-process gotcha. Because your app shares the IIS worker process, Server in the response says Microsoft-IIS, and some IIS-level settings apply that would not otherwise. More importantly, an unhandled crash can take down the app pool rather than just your process.

docs.title: Configuring Kestrel
docs.text:
Most apps never touch this, but it comes up:

builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel(options =>
{
    // Refuse request bodies over 10 MB
    options.Limits.MaxRequestBodySize = 10 * 1024 * 1024;

    // Slow-client protection: minimum 100 bytes/sec after a 10s grace period
    options.Limits.MinRequestBodyDataRate =
        new MinDataRate(bytesPerSecond: 100, gracePeriod: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));

    options.Limits.MaxConcurrentConnections = 1000;
    options.Limits.KeepAliveTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2);
});

Ports are usually set through configuration rather than code:

# Environment variable — the usual approach in containers
ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080

# Or on the command line
dotnet run --urls "http://localhost:5001;https://localhost:5002"

http://+:8080 means "listen on all network interfaces". Using localhost inside a container is a classic mistake — the app starts, appears healthy, and refuses every connection from outside the container because it is only listening on the loopback interface.

docs.title: The deeper detail — ⚠️ forwarded headers
docs.text:
When a proxy forwards a request, your app sees the proxy's IP address, not the client's. And if the proxy terminated TLS, your app sees http even though the client used https.

That breaks three things: IP-based rate limiting, audit logs, and any redirect your app generates (it will produce http:// links).

The proxy adds headers recording the originals:

X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.42        ← the real client IP
X-Forwarded-Proto: https             ← the original scheme
X-Forwarded-Host: api.example.com

Your app must be told to read them:

app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
{
    ForwardedHeaders = ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto
});

⚠️ This must be the first middleware in the pipeline, before anything that reads the IP or the scheme — including HTTPS redirection and authentication. Register it late and the earlier middleware still sees the proxy's values.

⚠️ And there is a security consideration. These headers are just headers — a client can send them. If your app trusts X-Forwarded-For blindly and it is reachable directly, an attacker can spoof any IP they like and bypass IP-based rules. In production, restrict which proxies are trusted:

var options = new ForwardedHeadersOptions
{
    ForwardedHeaders = ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto
};
options.KnownProxies.Add(IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1"));   // only trust our proxy

app.UseForwardedHeaders(options);

By default only loopback is trusted, which is why this "just works" in a local IIS setup and silently fails in Kubernetes — where the proxy is on a different pod IP. Clearing KnownProxies and KnownNetworks makes it accept anything, which is convenient and only safe if your app is genuinely unreachable except through the proxy.

See 24.13.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A typical container setup, where the pieces come together:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks();

var app = builder.Build();

// FIRST — so everything below sees the real client IP and scheme
app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
{
    ForwardedHeaders = ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto
});

// NOT UseHttpsRedirection here — the proxy already terminated TLS,
// and redirecting again would cause a loop.

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");

app.Run();

# The container listens on 8080, on ALL interfaces
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
EXPOSE 8080

The two comments in that code are both real production mistakes:

  • Forwarded headers registered late means your rate limiter blocks the proxy's IP and everyone shares one bucket.
  • UseHttpsRedirection behind a TLS-terminating proxy causes an infinite redirect loop: the app sees http, redirects to https, the proxy terminates TLS and forwards http again, forever.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is Kestrel and how does it differ from IIS?

Kestrel is the web server built into ASP.NET Core — it is a library your application references, so the app hosts its own server and can run anywhere. IIS is Microsoft's Windows web server, and in the classic ASP.NET model it was the host, loading your application as a plugin. In ASP.NET Core that relationship is inverted: IIS becomes a reverse proxy sitting in front of Kestrel, handling TLS and routing, while Kestrel actually runs your code. That inversion is what makes cross-platform hosting and containers possible.

Q: Why put a reverse proxy in front of Kestrel at all?

Kestrel is deliberately minimal — very fast at HTTP, and not much else. A proxy adds things Kestrel does not do: managing TLS certificates centrally, hosting several applications on one machine and port, protecting against slow-client attacks, serving static files efficiently, and load balancing across instances. Kestrel can be exposed directly and often is in Kubernetes, where the ingress controller plays the proxy role, but you rarely want it as the raw internet-facing server on a traditional host.

Q: What is the difference between in-process and out-of-process hosting?

Both apply to hosting on IIS. Out-of-process means IIS starts your application as a separate process and proxies each request to it over local HTTP, so there are two HTTP hops. In-process means your application runs inside the IIS worker process itself, removing that extra hop and giving roughly two to three times the throughput. In-process has been the default since .NET Core 3.0. You would choose out-of-process if you needed different .NET versions in the same app pool, or wanted isolation from the IIS process.

Q: Your app is behind a load balancer and every request looks like it comes from the same IP. Why?

Because the app sees the proxy's address rather than the client's. The proxy records the original in X-Forwarded-For, but ASP.NET Core does not read it unless you add UseForwardedHeaders, and that has to be the first middleware so everything downstream sees the corrected values. The subtlety is that by default only loopback proxies are trusted, which is why it works locally behind IIS and silently fails in Kubernetes where the proxy is on a different pod IP — you have to add the proxy to KnownProxies or KnownNetworks. And you should restrict it rather than trusting everything, because those headers are client-supplied and can be spoofed if the app is reachable directly.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• UseForwardedHeaders registered too late. Everything before it still sees the proxy's IP and scheme.
  • Only loopback proxies are trusted by default. Works locally, silently fails in Kubernetes.
  • Trusting forwarded headers from anywhere is a spoofing risk if the app is reachable directly.
  • UseHttpsRedirection behind a TLS-terminating proxy causes a redirect loop.
  • Binding to localhost in a container makes the app unreachable from outside. Use http://+:8080.
  • In-process hosting shares the IIS worker process, so a crash can take down the app pool.
  • Kestrel's default limits are not tuned for your app. Body size and data-rate limits exist for good reasons — raising them removes a protection.

docs.title: 4.3 — Program.cs: Generic Host vs Minimal Hosting
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.2 Hosting model · Next: 4.4 The legacy Startup.cs model

Markers: 🔥 💻 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Program.cs is where your application is assembled. It has exactly two phases, split by one line: builder.Build().

  • Before Build() you register services — what exists. After it you build the pipeline — what happens to a request.
  • Minimal hosting (WebApplication.CreateBuilder) is the modern default, since .NET 6. Everything in one file.
  • You cannot add services after Build(). That is the single most common error here.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Program.cs a file The entry point. Assembles and starts the application. Host an object Owns dependency injection, configuration, logging and the server. Manages startup and shutdown. Generic Host the older model Host.CreateDefaultBuilder() plus a separate Startup class. Still supported. Minimal hosting the current model WebApplication.CreateBuilder(). One file, no Startup class. Default since .NET 6. WebApplicationBuilder a class What CreateBuilder returns. Holds Services, Configuration, Environment, Logging. WebApplication a class What Build() returns. The running app. You call Use..., Map... and Run() on it. builder.Services a property The IServiceCollection. Where you register services. See 6.2. builder.Configuration a property The IConfiguration. Reads appsettings.json, environment variables and more. builder.Build() a method Creates the app and freezes the service collection. The dividing line. app.Run() a method Starts the server and blocks until shutdown. Always last. Top-level statements a C# feature Writing code without a Main method or class. Why Program.cs has no boilerplate. WebApplicationFactory a test class Boots your whole app in memory for integration tests. Needs Program to be reachable.

docs.title: The two phases
docs.text:
Every Program.cs has the same shape, and understanding it is most of this topic:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// ═══ PHASE 1: REGISTER ═══
// "What services can be injected? What is available?"
builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

var app = builder.Build();          // ◄── the dividing line

// ═══ PHASE 2: CONFIGURE ═══
// "What happens to an incoming request, and in what order?"
app.UseAuthentication();
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();                          // start listening, block until shutdown

A picture: phase 1 is stocking the kitchen; phase 2 is writing the recipe.

You cannot cook with an ingredient you did not buy, and you cannot buy ingredients once you have started cooking. builder.Build() is the moment the shop closes.

That is why builder.Services.Add... after Build() throws. The service collection is frozen so the container can be constructed. The error message — "Services cannot be added after the application is built" — is clear once you know the model and baffling before.

docs.title: Why it looks so short
docs.text:
Two C# features remove the boilerplate:

Top-level statements (C# 9) let you write code with no Main method and no class. The compiler generates them.

Implicit usings (3.7) add the common namespaces automatically, so there is no using block.

What you write:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapGet("/", () => "Hello");
app.Run();

What the compiler effectively produces:

internal class Program
{
    private static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
        // ...
    }
}

That generated Program class is internal, which matters for testing — see the trap later.

docs.title: The simple version — what CreateBuilder sets up for you
docs.text:
That one line does a surprising amount:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

It configures:

  • Configuration sources, in order of increasing priority: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, then User Secrets in development, then environment variables, then command-line arguments. See 7.1.
  • Logging — console and debug providers.
  • Dependency injection — the built-in container.
  • Kestrel as the web server, plus IIS integration if present.
  • The content root — the folder the app treats as its base.

You get a working, configurable, logging application from one line, and can override any part of it.

docs.title: The three objects you use
docs.text:
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services;          // register services (IServiceCollection)
builder.Configuration;     // read settings (IConfiguration)
builder.Environment;       // which environment am I in? (IWebHostEnvironment)
builder.Logging;           // configure logging providers
builder.Host;              // deeper host configuration
builder.WebHost;           // deeper server configuration (Kestrel, URLs)

var app = builder.Build();

app.Services;              // the BUILT container — resolve services from here
app.Configuration;         // same configuration
app.Environment;           // same environment

Note builder.Services (register into) versus app.Services (resolve from). Both exist and they are different things.

docs.title: How it actually works — Generic Host vs Minimal Hosting
docs.text:
Before .NET 6, Program.cs and Startup.cs were two separate files:

// Program.cs — the OLD Generic Host model
public class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args) =>
        CreateHostBuilder(args).Build().Run();

    public static IHostBuilder CreateHostBuilder(string[] args) =>
        Host.CreateDefaultBuilder(args)
            .ConfigureWebHostDefaults(webBuilder =>
            {
                webBuilder.UseStartup<Startup>();
            });
}

// Startup.cs — the two phases, as two methods
public class Startup
{
    public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)   // phase 1
    {
        services.AddControllers();
    }

    public void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IWebHostEnvironment env)   // phase 2
    {
        app.UseRouting();
        app.UseEndpoints(e => e.MapControllers());
    }
}

The two phases were always there — they were just two methods in a separate class. Minimal hosting flattened them into one file.

Generic Host + Startup Minimal hosting Files Program.cs + Startup.cs Program.cs only Phase 1 ConfigureServices Before builder.Build() Phase 2 Configure After builder.Build() Since .NET Core 3.0 .NET 6 Status Still supported The default

Both still work. A .NET 8 app can use the Startup pattern, and plenty of older codebases do. You should recognise both — see 4.4.

docs.title: The deeper detail — keeping it organised as it grows
docs.text:
Program.cs becomes unreadable at around forty registrations. The standard fix is extension methods on IServiceCollection (1.14):

// In Orders/OrderModuleExtensions.cs — next to the code it registers
public static class OrderModuleExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddOrderModule(
        this IServiceCollection services,
        IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
        services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
        services.Configure<OrderOptions>(config.GetSection("Orders"));
        return services;                 // return it so calls can chain
    }
}

// Program.cs stays readable
builder.Services
    .AddOrderModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddPaymentModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddNotificationModule(builder.Configuration);

Two benefits beyond tidiness: each module's registrations live next to that module's code, so deleting a feature does not leave orphaned lines in Program.cs, and it is how every built-in Add... method works, so it reads as idiomatic.

docs.title: ⚠️ Making Program visible to tests
docs.text:
Integration tests use WebApplicationFactory<Program> to boot the real app in memory (20.7). But the compiler-generated Program class is internal, so the test project cannot see it.

Two fixes. In the web project's .csproj:

<ItemGroup>
  <InternalsVisibleTo Include="MyApp.Tests" />
</ItemGroup>

Or at the bottom of Program.cs:

public partial class Program { }     // makes the generated class public

That one-line class at the end of Program.cs looks bizarre if you do not know why it is there. It exists purely so tests can reference the type.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic production Program.cs:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// ══════════ PHASE 1: services ══════════

builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();

builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(options =>
    options.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));

builder.Services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
        builder.Configuration.GetSection("Jwt").Bind(options));
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddDbContextCheck<AppDbContext>();

// Feature modules, each registering its own dependencies
builder.Services
    .AddOrderModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddPaymentModule(builder.Configuration);

var app = builder.Build();

// ══════════ PHASE 2: pipeline ══════════
// ORDER MATTERS HERE — see 5.2

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.MapOpenApi();                     // never expose the schema in production
}
else
{
    app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");    // friendly errors, no stack traces
    app.UseHsts();
}

app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAuthentication();                  // who are you?
app.UseAuthorization();                   // are you allowed?

app.MapControllers();
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");

app.Run();

Read it top to bottom and you can see the entire application: what it depends on, how it authenticates, what it exposes, and how it behaves differently in development. That readability is the point of the design.

docs.title: Running code once at startup
docs.text:
A common need — apply database migrations, seed data, warm a cache. Do it between Build() and Run(), and create a scope:

var app = builder.Build();

using (var scope = app.Services.CreateScope())
{
    var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
    await db.Database.MigrateAsync();
}

app.Run();

⚠️ The CreateScope() is not optional. AppDbContext is registered as scoped, and there is no ambient scope at startup — resolving it directly from app.Services throws. See 6.5.

⚠️ And auto-migrating on startup is contentious. With several instances starting at once, they all try to migrate simultaneously. It is convenient in development and a real risk in production, where migrations usually belong in the deployment pipeline — 14.9.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: Walk me through what Program.cs does.

It assembles and starts the application, in two phases separated by builder.Build(). Before that line you register services into the dependency injection container — what the application has available. After it you build the middleware pipeline — what happens to an incoming request and in what order. Then app.Run() starts the server and blocks until shutdown. The one-line WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args) at the top sets up configuration sources, logging, the DI container and Kestrel with sensible defaults, which is why the file can be so short.

Q: What is the difference between the Generic Host model and minimal hosting?

They are the same two phases arranged differently. The Generic Host model had Program.cs build a host that pointed at a separate Startup class, where ConfigureServices was phase one and Configure was phase two. Minimal hosting, the default since .NET 6, flattens that into a single Program.cs using top-level statements — registration before Build(), pipeline after. Both still work, and plenty of existing codebases use Startup, so it is worth recognising either.

Q: Why can't you register services after builder.Build()?

Because Build() constructs the dependency injection container from the service collection, and at that point the collection is frozen — the container needs a fixed set of registrations to resolve against. Adding afterwards throws with a message about services not being addable after the application is built. It is a common mistake when someone moves a registration line while reorganising the file.

Q: How would you run a one-off task at startup, like applying migrations?

Between builder.Build() and app.Run(), creating a scope first with app.Services.CreateScope(). The scope matters because things like DbContext are registered scoped and there is no ambient request scope during startup, so resolving directly from app.Services throws. I would also be careful about auto-migrating in production — with several instances starting simultaneously they all attempt it at once, so migrations usually belong in the deployment pipeline rather than in application startup.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Adding services after builder.Build() throws. The collection is frozen.
  • Resolving a scoped service directly from app.Services throws. Create a scope first.
  • Middleware order is not the same as registration order. Service registration order does not matter; pipeline order matters enormously — see 5.2.
  • app.Run() blocks. Anything written after it never executes.
  • WebApplicationFactory<Program> fails to compile because the generated Program is internal. Add public partial class Program { } or InternalsVisibleTo.
  • Auto-migrating on startup races when several instances start together.
  • app.Run(...) with a delegate is different from app.Run(). The overload with a parameter is terminal middleware, not "start the app" — 5.3.

docs.title: 4.4 — The Legacy Startup.cs Model
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.3 Program.cs · Next: 4.5 Host interfaces

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Startup.cs is the older way of arranging application setup, used from ASP.NET Core 1.0 until .NET 6. It splits the same two phases into two methods on a separate class.

  • ConfigureServices registers services. Configure builds the middleware pipeline. Exactly the same two phases as minimal hosting.
  • It still works today — it was never removed, only replaced as the default.
  • You need to recognise it because most existing production code still uses it.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Startup.cs a class, by convention Holds the two setup methods. Not an interface — the framework finds the methods by name. ConfigureServices a method Phase 1. Registers services into the DI container. Equivalent to code before builder.Build(). Configure a method Phase 2. Builds the middleware pipeline. Equivalent to code after builder.Build(). IApplicationBuilder an interface What Configure receives. You call Use... on it to add middleware. IHostBuilder an interface The Generic Host builder. Host.CreateDefaultBuilder(args) returns one. UseStartup<T> a method Tells the host which class holds the setup methods. IWebHostEnvironment an interface Tells you the environment name and content root. Injectable into Configure. Convention-based a discovery style The framework looks for methods by name, not by an interface. Misspell one and it is silently ignored. ConfigureContainer an optional method Used when swapping in a third-party DI container like Autofac. Environment-specific methods a convention ConfigureDevelopmentServices runs instead of ConfigureServices in Development.

docs.title: Why it existed
docs.text:
When ASP.NET Core launched in 2016, C# had no top-level statements. Every program needed a Main method inside a class, so the entry point was already boilerplate-heavy.

Rather than cram all setup into Main, the design put it in a dedicated class with two clearly named methods. That was a reasonable separation: Program.cs for "how do I start", Startup.cs for "what am I".

By .NET 6 the language had changed. Top-level statements and implicit usings removed the boilerplate, so the extra file was no longer buying anything — and having setup split across two files made it harder to follow. Minimal hosting merged them.

The important thing to understand: the two phases did not change. Only where you write them did.

docs.title: The simple version — the two files
docs.text:
// Program.cs — just wires up the host and points at Startup
public class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args) =>
        CreateHostBuilder(args).Build().Run();

    public static IHostBuilder CreateHostBuilder(string[] args) =>
        Host.CreateDefaultBuilder(args)
            .ConfigureWebHostDefaults(webBuilder =>
            {
                webBuilder.UseStartup<Startup>();     // ← the link
            });
}

// Startup.cs — the actual application setup
public class Startup
{
    public Startup(IConfiguration configuration)
    {
        Configuration = configuration;      // injected by the framework
    }

    public IConfiguration Configuration { get; }

    // ═══ PHASE 1 ═══ register services
    public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddControllers();
        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
            o.UseSqlServer(Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
        services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
    }

    // ═══ PHASE 2 ═══ build the pipeline
    public void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IWebHostEnvironment env)
    {
        if (env.IsDevelopment())
            app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();

        app.UseHttpsRedirection();
        app.UseRouting();
        app.UseAuthentication();
        app.UseAuthorization();

        app.UseEndpoints(endpoints =>
        {
            endpoints.MapControllers();
        });
    }
}

docs.title: Side by side with minimal hosting
docs.text:
Startup model Minimal hosting services.AddControllers(); in ConfigureServices builder.Services.AddControllers(); app.UseAuthentication(); in Configure app.UseAuthentication(); Configuration property builder.Configuration IWebHostEnvironment env parameter app.Environment app.UseEndpoints(e => e.MapControllers()) app.MapControllers()

The mapping is almost mechanical, which is why migrating is usually straightforward: move the body of ConfigureServices above builder.Build(), move the body of Configure below it, and rename services to builder.Services.

docs.title: ⚠️ Convention-based, not interface-based
docs.text:
This is the trap worth knowing. Startup implements no interface. The framework finds the methods by name, using reflection.

public class Startup
{
    // Typo — the framework never finds this.
    public void ConfigureService(IServiceCollection services)   // missing 's'
    {
        services.AddControllers();
    }
}

That compiles perfectly. It just never runs. Your app starts, and then every request fails with an unhelpful error about no controllers being found — because none were registered.

There is no compile-time protection at all. Minimal hosting removed this whole class of problem, since there are no magic method names to misspell.

docs.title: How it actually works — environment-specific methods
docs.text:
A lesser-known convention: you can define per-environment versions, and the framework prefers them:

public class Startup
{
    // Used in Development instead of ConfigureServices
    public void ConfigureDevelopmentServices(IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o => o.UseInMemoryDatabase("dev"));
        ConfigureCommonServices(services);
    }

    // Used everywhere else
    public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
            o.UseSqlServer(Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));
        ConfigureCommonServices(services);
    }

    // And the pipeline equivalent
    public void ConfigureDevelopment(IApplicationBuilder app, IWebHostEnvironment env) { }
}

The naming is Configure{Environment}Services and Configure{Environment}. It works, but it is obscure enough that most teams use env.IsDevelopment() checks instead — which is clearer and does not depend on a naming convention nobody remembers.

docs.title: The deeper detail — UseRouting and UseEndpoints
docs.text:
Old Startup code has a pattern that has since been simplified:

app.UseRouting();                          // "work out which endpoint matches"

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();                     // these sit BETWEEN the two

app.UseEndpoints(endpoints =>               // "now actually run it"
{
    endpoints.MapControllers();
});

The split exists because authorization needs to know which endpoint was selected before it can decide whether you are allowed to reach it. UseRouting selects; UseEndpoints executes; authorization sits in between with the answer available.

In minimal hosting that is implicit:

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();          // routing and endpoints are added automatically

WebApplication inserts UseRouting at the start and UseEndpoints at the end for you. You can still call them explicitly if you need something to sit at an exact position.

See 8.2.

docs.title: Should you migrate existing code?
docs.text:
Usually not, on its own. A working Startup.cs is not a bug. Migrating is a mechanical change with a small chance of subtly reordering middleware, and the benefit is stylistic.

Reasonable reasons to migrate: - You are already doing a major upgrade and want consistency. - New developers find the split confusing. - You are adopting minimal APIs and want everything in one place.

If you do, the migration is:

// BEFORE — Startup.cs
public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)
{
    services.AddControllers();
    services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
}

public void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IWebHostEnvironment env)
{
    if (env.IsDevelopment()) app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
    app.UseRouting();
    app.UseAuthorization();
    app.UseEndpoints(e => e.MapControllers());
}

// AFTER — Program.cs
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

var app = builder.Build();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Keep the middleware in exactly the same order. That is the one part where a mistake causes real behaviour changes rather than a compile error.

docs.title: Keeping Startup while using the new builder
docs.text:
A middle option that is genuinely useful during a gradual migration — you can keep the Startup class and call its methods from minimal hosting:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

var startup = new Startup(builder.Configuration);
startup.ConfigureServices(builder.Services);

var app = builder.Build();

startup.Configure(app, app.Environment);

app.Run();

This lets you move to the new host without rewriting a large Startup in one go.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is Startup.cs and is it still used?

It is the older way of organising ASP.NET Core setup, used from 1.0 until .NET 6. It holds two methods: ConfigureServices, which registers services into the DI container, and Configure, which builds the middleware pipeline. Those are exactly the same two phases as minimal hosting — before and after builder.Build() — just arranged as two methods on a separate class. It was never removed, so it still works, and most existing production codebases use it, which is why it is worth recognising.

Q: What is unusual about how the framework finds those methods?

They are discovered by convention rather than through an interface — the framework looks them up by name using reflection. So Startup implements nothing, and if you misspell ConfigureServices the code compiles fine and the method simply never runs. The app then starts with no services registered and fails at the first request with a confusing error. That whole class of problem disappeared with minimal hosting, because there are no magic method names any more.

Q: Why did old code have UseRouting and UseEndpoints as separate calls?

Because authorization needs to know which endpoint matched before it can decide whether the caller is allowed to reach it. UseRouting performs the match, UseEndpoints executes the selected endpoint, and authentication and authorization sit between them with the routing result available. In minimal hosting WebApplication adds both automatically — UseRouting at the start of the pipeline and UseEndpoints at the end — so you just call MapControllers. You can still add them explicitly if you need middleware at an exact position relative to routing.

Q: Would you migrate an existing Startup.cs to minimal hosting?

Not on its own. It works, and the change is stylistic rather than functional, so it is gratuitous risk on a working system. I would do it as part of a major upgrade or if the team was already moving towards minimal APIs. The mapping is nearly mechanical — the body of ConfigureServices goes above Build() and the body of Configure goes below — but the one thing to be careful about is preserving the exact middleware order, because getting that wrong changes behaviour without producing a compile error.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Method names are matched by convention, not an interface. A typo compiles and silently does nothing.
  • ConfigureServices and Configure have fixed signatures. Configure can take extra injected services; ConfigureServices cannot.
  • Only services can be injected into the Startup constructor — and only IConfiguration, IWebHostEnvironment and a few others, because the container is not built yet.
  • Migrating can silently reorder middleware. That changes behaviour with no compile error.
  • Environment-specific method names are obscure. ConfigureDevelopmentServices works, and almost nobody knows it exists, so prefer explicit environment checks.
  • UseEndpoints without UseRouting before it throws in the old model.

docs.title: 4.5 — IHost, IHostBuilder, IWebHostEnvironment and the Lifetime Interfaces
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.4 The legacy Startup.cs model · Next: 4.6 Application lifecycle

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The host is the object that owns everything your application needs to run: the dependency injection container, configuration, logging, and the web server. It also controls startup and shutdown.

  • IHost is the running application. IHostBuilder is what you use to construct it.
  • IWebHostEnvironment tells you which environment you are in and where the app's files are.
  • IHostApplicationLifetime lets you react to the app starting and stopping.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Host a concept The object owning DI, configuration, logging and the server, plus startup and shutdown. IHost an interface The built, runnable application. Has Services, StartAsync, StopAsync. IHostBuilder an interface Used to configure and then Build() an IHost. The older builder style. WebApplication a class Implements IHost. What builder.Build() returns in minimal hosting. WebApplicationBuilder a class The modern builder. Replaces IHostBuilder for web apps. IHostEnvironment an interface Environment name, application name, content root. Works for any .NET app. IWebHostEnvironment an interface IHostEnvironment plus WebRootPath — the wwwroot folder. Web apps only. Content root a folder path The app's base directory. Where appsettings.json and views are found. Web root a folder path The folder served publicly, normally wwwroot. A subfolder of the content root. IHostApplicationLifetime an interface Exposes ApplicationStarted, ApplicationStopping and ApplicationStopped tokens, plus StopApplication(). IHostedService an interface Something the host starts and stops with the app. Background work lives here. IServiceProvider an interface The built DI container. Reachable as app.Services.

docs.title: What a host actually is
docs.text:
Before ASP.NET Core, "starting a web app" meant IIS loading your DLL. There was no object representing your running application.

The host is that object. It owns four things:

  1. The dependency injection container — every registered service.
  2. Configuration — merged from JSON files, environment variables and more.
  3. Logging — the configured providers.
  4. The web server — Kestrel, listening on a port.

And it manages the lifecycle: start these things in the right order, run, then stop them cleanly in reverse order.

A picture: the host is the building manager. It does not do the work of any department, but it unlocks the building in the morning, makes sure everyone has what they need, and locks up properly at night.

docs.title: Why there are two families of interface
docs.text:
You will see both IHost/IHostBuilder and WebApplication/WebApplicationBuilder, and it is confusing until you know the history.

IHost is the general-purpose one. It works for any .NET application — a console app, a worker service, a scheduled job. It knows nothing about HTTP.

WebApplication is the web-specific one introduced with minimal hosting in .NET 6. It implements IHost and adds web-specific members like MapGet and UseRouting.

So WebApplication is an IHost with extra capabilities. Any code written against IHost works with either.

IHost                    ← general .NET host
  └── WebApplication     ← adds routing, middleware, MapGet, etc.

docs.title: The simple version — what you actually touch
docs.text:
In minimal hosting, most of this is reachable through the builder and the app:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services;         // IServiceCollection — register services
builder.Configuration;    // IConfiguration     — read settings
builder.Environment;      // IWebHostEnvironment — which environment?
builder.Logging;          // ILoggingBuilder     — configure logging
builder.Host;             // IHostBuilder        — deeper host config
builder.WebHost;          // IWebHostBuilder     — deeper server config

var app = builder.Build();          // app is a WebApplication, which IS an IHost

app.Services;             // IServiceProvider — the BUILT container
app.Configuration;
app.Environment;
app.Lifetime;             // IHostApplicationLifetime

Note the builder.Services versus app.Services distinction again. One is the collection you register into; the other is the built container you resolve from. Registering into the first after Build() throws; resolving from the second before Build() is impossible because it does not exist yet.

docs.title: IWebHostEnvironment — environment and paths
docs.text:
public class ReportService(IWebHostEnvironment env)
{
    public void Describe()
    {
        env.EnvironmentName;      // "Development", "Staging", "Production"
        env.ApplicationName;      // usually the assembly name
        env.ContentRootPath;      // where appsettings.json lives
        env.WebRootPath;          // the wwwroot folder

        if (env.IsDevelopment()) { }
        if (env.IsProduction()) { }
        if (env.IsEnvironment("QA")) { }    // for custom names
    }
}

⚠️ Content root and web root are different folders and people mix them up.

  • Content root — the application's base folder. appsettings.json, views, everything.
  • Web root — wwwroot, a subfolder. Publicly served. Anything here is downloadable by anyone.

That distinction is a security matter. Putting a file with connection strings in wwwroot publishes it to the internet. See 4.10.

Use these instead of hard-coded paths:

// ✗ breaks the moment you deploy, or run tests from a different directory
var path = @"C:\MyApp\templates\invoice.html";

// ✓ correct anywhere
var path = Path.Combine(env.ContentRootPath, "templates", "invoice.html");

This is what replaced classic ASP.NET's Server.MapPath.

docs.title: How it actually works — IHostApplicationLifetime
docs.text:
This gives you three CancellationTokens and one method:

public class StartupNotifier(
    IHostApplicationLifetime lifetime,
    ILogger<StartupNotifier> logger) : IHostedService
{
    public Task StartAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        lifetime.ApplicationStarted.Register(() =>
            logger.LogInformation("Application has started and is accepting requests"));

        lifetime.ApplicationStopping.Register(() =>
            logger.LogInformation("Shutdown beginning — finish in-flight work now"));

        lifetime.ApplicationStopped.Register(() =>
            logger.LogInformation("Shutdown complete"));

        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }

    public Task StopAsync(CancellationToken ct) => Task.CompletedTask;
}
Token Fires when ApplicationStarted The host has started and the server is accepting requests ApplicationStopping Shutdown has begun. In-flight requests are still finishing. ApplicationStopped Everything has stopped

ApplicationStopping is the useful one. It is your signal to stop accepting new work while existing work completes — the basis of graceful shutdown (4.6).

And you can stop the app yourself:

lifetime.StopApplication();     // triggers graceful shutdown

That is the right way to exit on a fatal startup condition — it runs shutdown properly, unlike Environment.Exit, which kills the process immediately and skips every cleanup handler.

docs.title: The deeper detail — IHostedService
docs.text:
The host starts and stops registered IHostedService implementations alongside the app. This is the foundation of all background work in ASP.NET Core:

builder.Services.AddHostedService<MyBackgroundWorker>();

The host calls StartAsync on each during startup and StopAsync on each during shutdown, in reverse registration order.

⚠️ StartAsync blocks startup. The host waits for it to complete before the server starts accepting requests. So doing slow work there delays your app becoming available — and in Kubernetes, a readiness probe that fails while you wait can get the pod killed before it starts.

For long-running work, inherit BackgroundService and use ExecuteAsync, which does not block startup. See 21.1.

docs.title: Configuring the host more deeply
docs.text:
Occasionally you need to reach past the convenience API:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Server-level configuration
builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel(o => o.Limits.MaxRequestBodySize = 10_000_000);
builder.WebHost.UseUrls("http://+:8080");

// Host-level configuration
builder.Host.UseSerilog();                    // replace the logging stack
builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(o =>
{
    o.ValidateScopes = true;                  // catch captive dependencies
    o.ValidateOnBuild = true;                 // fail fast on bad registrations
});

Those two validation options are worth knowing. ValidateScopes catches the captive dependency problem — a scoped service injected into a singleton (6.4). It is on by default in Development only, which is exactly why that bug reaches production. Turning both on everywhere costs a little startup time and catches a genuinely nasty class of error.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic hosted service using the lifetime for graceful shutdown:

public class QueueProcessor(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory,
    IHostApplicationLifetime lifetime,
    ILogger<QueueProcessor> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        // stoppingToken fires when ApplicationStopping fires
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            try
            {
                // A fresh scope per iteration — see 21.2
                using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
                var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

                await ProcessBatchAsync(db, stoppingToken);
                await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30), stoppingToken);
            }
            catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
            {
                logger.LogInformation("Shutting down cleanly");
                break;                       // normal — not an error
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Batch failed, will retry");
                await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), stoppingToken);
            }
        }
    }
}

Three deliberate decisions worth explaining in an interview:

  • The scope is created inside the loop, not outside. A scope held for the life of the service means a DbContext that never releases its change tracker (3.5).
  • OperationCanceledException is caught separately and logged as information, because cancellation during shutdown is normal traffic, not a failure (2.14).
  • Other exceptions do not kill the loop. An unhandled exception in a BackgroundService silently stops it, and by default the rest of the app keeps running — so you have a service that appears healthy while doing nothing.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the host in ASP.NET Core?

The object that owns everything the application needs to run — the dependency injection container, configuration, logging, and the web server — and manages the lifecycle, starting those things in order and stopping them cleanly in reverse. IHost is the general form that works for any .NET application, including console and worker services. WebApplication, which minimal hosting gives you, implements IHost and adds web-specific members like MapGet and the middleware pipeline.

Q: What is the difference between IHostEnvironment and IWebHostEnvironment?

IHostEnvironment gives you the environment name, application name and content root, and works in any .NET app. IWebHostEnvironment extends it with WebRootPath, which points at the wwwroot folder, so it only exists in web applications. The distinction that matters in practice is content root versus web root — content root is the app's base folder where appsettings.json lives, while web root is a subfolder that is publicly served. Putting a sensitive file in the web root publishes it to the internet.

Q: What is IHostApplicationLifetime for?

It exposes three cancellation tokens — ApplicationStarted, ApplicationStopping and ApplicationStopped — plus a StopApplication method. ApplicationStopping is the useful one: it fires when shutdown begins but while in-flight requests are still completing, so it is your signal to stop accepting new work and drain gracefully. StopApplication is also the correct way to shut down deliberately on a fatal condition, because unlike Environment.Exit it runs the normal shutdown sequence rather than killing the process outright.

Q: What are ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild?

Two options on the default service provider. ValidateScopes detects captive dependencies — a scoped service injected into a singleton, which pins a request-lifetime object for the life of the app. ValidateOnBuild checks at startup that every registration can actually be resolved, so a missing dependency fails immediately rather than on the first request that needs it. The important detail is that scope validation is enabled by default only in Development, which is precisely why that bug survives to production. Enabling both in all environments costs a little startup time and catches a genuinely painful class of error.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Content root and web root are different. Anything in the web root is publicly downloadable.
  • builder.Services versus app.Services. Register into the first, resolve from the second.
  • ValidateScopes is Development-only by default, so captive dependencies reach production undetected.
  • IHostedService.StartAsync blocks application startup. Slow work there delays readiness. Use BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync instead.
  • An unhandled exception in a BackgroundService stops it silently. The app keeps running and looks healthy.
  • Environment.Exit skips shutdown handlers. Use lifetime.StopApplication().
  • Hard-coded file paths break on deployment. Use env.ContentRootPath.
