docs.title: 4.6 — Application Lifecycle: Start, Run, Graceful Shutdown
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.5 Host interfaces · Next: 4.7 Environments

Markers: ⭐ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The application lifecycle is the sequence from process start, through serving requests, to a clean stop. The part that matters in production is the shutdown.

  • Graceful shutdown means: stop accepting new requests, let in-flight ones finish, then exit.
  • You get 5 seconds by default to do that. On a slow endpoint that is not enough, and requests get cut off.
  • Every deployment triggers a shutdown, so getting this wrong means dropped requests on every release.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Lifecycle a sequence Start → run → stop. Each phase has defined steps. app.Run() a method Starts the server and blocks the calling thread until shutdown is requested. app.RunAsync() a method The same, awaitable. Used when you need to do something after startup. app.StartAsync() a method Starts without blocking. You then control when to stop. Mostly used in tests. Graceful shutdown a behaviour Refuse new requests, finish in-flight ones, release resources, then exit. ShutdownTimeout a host setting How long the host waits for in-flight work. Default 5 seconds. SIGTERM an OS signal "Please stop." Sent by Docker, Kubernetes and systemd. Triggers graceful shutdown. SIGKILL an OS signal "Stop now." Cannot be caught or handled. The process dies immediately. ApplicationStopping a CancellationToken Fires when shutdown begins, while requests are still finishing. ApplicationStopped a CancellationToken Fires when everything has stopped. Drain a phase The period where existing requests complete but no new ones are accepted. Readiness probe a health check Tells the orchestrator whether to send traffic. Distinct from liveness. terminationGracePeriodSeconds a Kubernetes setting How long Kubernetes waits after SIGTERM before sending SIGKILL. Default 30s.

docs.title: The three phases
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Process starts"] --> B["Build the host<br/>DI, config, logging"]
    B --> C["Start IHostedServices<br/>in registration order"]
    C --> D["Kestrel binds the port"]
    D --> E["ApplicationStarted fires"]
    E --> F["RUNNING<br/>serving requests"]
    F -->|"SIGTERM / Ctrl+C"| G["ApplicationStopping fires"]
    G --> H["Stop accepting NEW requests"]
    H --> I["Wait for in-flight requests<br/>(up to ShutdownTimeout)"]
    I --> J["Stop IHostedServices<br/>in REVERSE order"]
    J --> K["Dispose the DI container"]
    K --> L["ApplicationStopped fires"]
    L --> M["Process exits"]

Two details in that diagram are worth noticing.

Hosted services stop in reverse order. If service A depends on service B, registering A after B means A stops first — so B is still available while A is shutting down. That is deliberate, and it mirrors how nested using blocks dispose.

There is a gap between "stop accepting new" and "process exits". That gap is the drain period, and it is where graceful shutdown either works or does not.

docs.title: Why shutdown matters more than startup
docs.text:
Startup problems are loud. The app fails to start, you see it immediately, you fix it.

Shutdown problems are silent and constant. Here is what happens on a badly-behaved deployment:

  1. Kubernetes decides to replace your pod and sends SIGTERM.
  2. Your app has 47 requests in flight, some of them long-running reports.
  3. The host waits 5 seconds — the default.
  4. Requests still running are cut off mid-response.
  5. Those users see a connection reset or a truncated response.
  6. Multiply by however many pods you replace, on every single deployment.

Nobody files a bug for this, because it looks like a transient network error. But it is a real, repeatable source of failed requests, and it is entirely avoidable.

A picture: closing a shop. Graceful shutdown is locking the door so nobody new comes in, then serving the customers already inside before switching the lights off. The default behaviour is announcing you are closing and pushing everyone out five seconds later, mid-purchase.

docs.title: The simple version — starting
docs.text:
var app = builder.Build();

app.Run();          // starts the server and BLOCKS here until shutdown
Console.WriteLine("this never runs until the app stops");

Run() blocks. Anything after it executes only during shutdown, which surprises people.

Three variants:

app.Run();                    // blocks until shutdown
await app.RunAsync();         // same, but awaitable
await app.StartAsync();       // starts WITHOUT blocking — you control the rest
// ... do something ...
await app.StopAsync();

StartAsync is mainly for tests and for tools that need to do work while the app runs.

docs.title: How it actually works — the shutdown timeout
docs.text:
The default is 5 seconds. That is almost always too short.

builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(options =>
{
    options.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
});

How to choose a value: it must be longer than your slowest normal request. If a report endpoint takes 20 seconds, a 5-second timeout guarantees those requests are killed on every deployment.

⚠️ And it must be shorter than your orchestrator's grace period. In Kubernetes:

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60     # Kubernetes waits this long

options.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(45);   // app finishes first

If the app's timeout is longer than Kubernetes', then Kubernetes sends SIGKILL while your app is still draining — and SIGKILL cannot be caught. Everything in flight dies instantly. So the ordering must be: app timeout < orchestrator grace period.

docs.title: Reacting to shutdown
docs.text:
Two ways, and they suit different situations.

In a hosted service, the stoppingToken is the signal:

public class Worker(ILogger<Worker> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await DoWorkAsync(stoppingToken);
            await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), stoppingToken);
        }

        logger.LogInformation("Worker stopped cleanly");
    }
}

⚠️ Ignoring stoppingToken is the classic mistake. A loop that never checks it keeps running until the timeout expires, then gets killed mid-work. See 2.14.

Anywhere else, use IHostApplicationLifetime:

public class ConnectionDrainer(IHostApplicationLifetime lifetime, IMessageBus bus)
{
    public void Setup()
    {
        lifetime.ApplicationStopping.Register(() =>
        {
            // Runs while in-flight requests are still finishing
            bus.StopConsuming();
        });
    }
}

docs.title: ⚠️ The Kubernetes race condition
docs.text:
This one catches almost everyone, and it is a genuinely good thing to be able to explain.

When Kubernetes terminates a pod, two things happen at the same time:

  1. SIGTERM is sent to your container.
  2. The pod is removed from the service endpoints, so the load balancer stops routing to it.

Those are not synchronised. Endpoint removal propagates through the cluster asynchronously and takes a second or two. So there is a window where:

  • Your app has received SIGTERM and stopped accepting new requests.
  • The load balancer has not yet learned that, and is still sending traffic.
  • Those requests are refused. Users see errors.

The fix is counter-intuitive: wait before you start shutting down.

lifetime.ApplicationStopping.Register(() =>
{
    // Keep serving for a few seconds while endpoint removal propagates
    logger.LogInformation("SIGTERM received, draining for 5s before shutdown");
    Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
});

Or better, fail the readiness probe first so traffic stops, then shut down:

app.MapHealthChecks("/ready", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = check => check.Tags.Contains("ready")
});

The sequence you want is: SIGTERM → readiness fails → load balancer stops sending → drain → exit. See 24.6 and 18.5.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what triggers shutdown
docs.text:
Trigger Signal Graceful? Ctrl+C in a terminal SIGINT ✅ Yes docker stop SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s ✅ Yes, if you finish in time Kubernetes pod termination SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period ✅ Yes, if you finish in time docker kill SIGKILL ❌ No — immediate death lifetime.StopApplication() — ✅ Yes Unhandled exception on a background thread — ❌ No — process crash Environment.Exit() — ❌ No — skips all handlers

Environment.Exit is worth calling out. It terminates immediately without running shutdown handlers, disposing services or finishing requests. If you need to exit deliberately, use lifetime.StopApplication(), which runs the proper sequence.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A complete, production-shaped shutdown configuration:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Longer than our slowest endpoint, shorter than Kubernetes' 60s grace period
builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(options =>
{
    options.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(45);
});

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck("ready", () => HealthCheckResult.Healthy(), tags: ["ready"]);

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");                          // liveness — am I alive?
app.MapHealthChecks("/ready", new HealthCheckOptions      // readiness — send me traffic?
{
    Predicate = c => c.Tags.Contains("ready")
});

var lifetime = app.Services.GetRequiredService<IHostApplicationLifetime>();
var logger   = app.Services.GetRequiredService<ILogger<Program>>();

lifetime.ApplicationStarted.Register(() =>
    logger.LogInformation("Started and accepting requests"));

lifetime.ApplicationStopping.Register(() =>
{
    logger.LogInformation("SIGTERM received — draining");
    // Give Kubernetes time to remove us from the load balancer
    Thread.Sleep(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
});

lifetime.ApplicationStopped.Register(() =>
    logger.LogInformation("Shutdown complete"));

app.Run();

# The matching Kubernetes side
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60      # must exceed the app's 45s
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["sleep", "5"]      # alternative to the Thread.Sleep above

The numbers must be consistent: app timeout (45s) < Kubernetes grace period (60s). Get that backwards and Kubernetes SIGKILLs an app that was shutting down correctly.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What happens when an ASP.NET Core application shuts down?

The host receives a shutdown signal, usually SIGTERM. It fires the ApplicationStopping token, stops accepting new requests, and waits for in-flight requests to complete — up to the shutdown timeout, which defaults to five seconds. Then it stops the registered hosted services in reverse registration order, disposes the dependency injection container, fires ApplicationStopped, and the process exits. The key point is that in-flight requests get a bounded window to finish, and anything still running when that window closes is cut off.

Q: Why is the default shutdown timeout a problem?

Five seconds is shorter than plenty of legitimate requests. If a report endpoint takes twenty seconds, every deployment cuts those requests off mid-response, and the user sees a connection reset rather than an error page. Since every deployment triggers a shutdown, it becomes a constant low-level source of failed requests that nobody reports because it looks like a transient network fault. The fix is to set ShutdownTimeout longer than your slowest normal request — but still shorter than the orchestrator's grace period, or the orchestrator will SIGKILL you mid-drain, which cannot be caught.

Q: There's a race condition when Kubernetes terminates a pod. What is it?

Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and removes the pod from the service endpoints at the same time, but those are not synchronised — endpoint removal propagates asynchronously across the cluster and takes a second or two. So there is a window where the app has stopped accepting new requests but the load balancer is still routing to it, and those requests fail. The counter-intuitive fix is to delay shutdown: on ApplicationStopping, keep serving for a few seconds while the endpoint removal propagates, either with a sleep or a preStop hook. Better still, fail the readiness probe first so traffic stops deliberately, then drain.

Q: What is the difference between app.Run() and app.StartAsync()?

Run() starts the server and blocks the calling thread until shutdown is requested, so anything written after it does not execute until the app is stopping. StartAsync() starts the server without blocking and returns, leaving you to decide when to call StopAsync(). That is mainly useful in tests and in tools that need to do work while the application runs. There is also RunAsync(), which is the awaitable equivalent of Run().

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• The default shutdown timeout is 5 seconds. Almost certainly too short.
  • The app's timeout must be shorter than the orchestrator's grace period, or you get SIGKILLed mid-drain.
  • Ignoring stoppingToken in a background service means it runs until killed, losing in-progress work.
  • The Kubernetes endpoint-removal race drops requests unless you delay shutdown or use a readiness probe.
  • Environment.Exit skips all shutdown handlers. Use lifetime.StopApplication().
  • app.Run() blocks, so code after it only runs during shutdown.
  • Hosted services stop in reverse registration order. Register dependencies before their dependents.
  • SIGKILL cannot be caught. Nothing you write helps if the orchestrator gives up waiting.

docs.title: 4.7 — Environments and ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.6 Application lifecycle · Next: 4.8 launchSettings.json

Markers: 🔥 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
An environment is a named context your app runs in — Development, Staging, Production — that changes its configuration and behaviour without changing its code.

  • Set by the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT environment variable. If it is missing, the app assumes Production.
  • It selects which appsettings.{Environment}.json file is layered on top of the base settings.
  • The names are just strings. Development is spelled exactly that way, and a typo silently gives you Production behaviour.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Environment a named context Which deployment this is. Changes config and behaviour, not code. ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT an environment variable Sets the environment name. The primary mechanism. DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT an environment variable The same, for non-web .NET apps. ASPNETCORE_ wins if both are set. Development a built-in name Local machine. Detailed errors, developer tools on. Staging a built-in name Production-like environment for final testing. Production a built-in name Live. The default when nothing is set. IWebHostEnvironment an interface Injectable. Tells you the environment name and paths. IsDevelopment() an extension method Case-insensitive check for the name "Development". IsEnvironment("x") an extension method Check for any custom name. appsettings.{Env}.json a config file Layered on top of appsettings.json for that environment. launchSettings.json a dev-only file Sets the variable when launching from an IDE or dotnet run. Never deployed — see 4.8. Developer exception page middleware Full stack traces in the browser. Development only, deliberately.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
The same compiled application needs to behave differently depending on where it is running:

  • On your machine you want full stack traces in the browser, a local database, and Swagger enabled.
  • In production you want a generic error page, the real database, no schema exposed, and logging going to a central system.

You could branch on a compile-time flag, but then dev and production are different builds — so what you tested is not what you shipped.

Environments solve it differently: one build, different configuration. The binary is identical everywhere. Only the settings it reads change.

A picture: the same car, driven in different countries. Same vehicle; you adjust the headlights and the speedometer units. You do not manufacture a different car.

docs.title: How the app knows which one it is in
docs.text:
One environment variable:

ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production

⚠️ If it is not set, ASP.NET Core assumes Production.

That default is deliberate and it is the safe choice — an app accidentally deployed without configuration behaves cautiously rather than exposing stack traces. But it catches people out locally: forget to set it and you get production behaviour on your own machine, wondering why your errors are unhelpful.

docs.title: The simple version — checking the environment
docs.text:
var app = builder.Build();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();     // full stack traces in the browser
    app.MapOpenApi();                    // expose the API schema
}
else
{
    app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");   // generic error page
    app.UseHsts();                       // force HTTPS for future visits
}

Available checks:

app.Environment.IsDevelopment();
app.Environment.IsStaging();
app.Environment.IsProduction();
app.Environment.IsEnvironment("QA");        // custom names
app.Environment.EnvironmentName;            // the raw string

These are case-insensitive, so development matches IsDevelopment(). That is one small mercy — but the file names are case-sensitive on Linux, which is not.

You can inject it into any service too:

public class EmailSender(IWebHostEnvironment env, ILogger<EmailSender> logger)
{
    public Task SendAsync(string to, string body)
    {
        if (!env.IsProduction())
        {
            logger.LogInformation("Would have emailed {To}", to);
            return Task.CompletedTask;      // never email real users from staging
        }

        return _client.SendAsync(to, body);
    }
}

docs.title: How it actually works — the configuration layering
docs.text:
This is the mechanism that does the real work.

At startup, WebApplication.CreateBuilder loads configuration in a specific order, and later sources override earlier ones:

1. appsettings.json                      ← base, always loaded
2. appsettings.{Environment}.json        ← layered on top
3. User Secrets                          ← Development only
4. Environment variables
5. Command-line arguments                ← highest priority

So with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Staging:

// appsettings.json — shared defaults
{
  "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information" } },
  "ConnectionStrings": { "Default": "Server=localhost;Database=App" },
  "Features": { "EnableNewCheckout": false }
}

// appsettings.Staging.json — only what differs
{
  "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Debug" } },
  "ConnectionStrings": { "Default": "Server=staging-sql;Database=App" }
}

The app sees Debug logging, the staging connection string, and EnableNewCheckout: false inherited from the base file.

Only put the differences in the environment file. Copying the whole base file into each environment file means every change has to be made in four places, and they drift.

See 7.1.

docs.title: ⚠️ The IsDevelopment() security trap
docs.text:
This is the one worth being careful about:

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
}

The developer exception page shows the full stack trace, source code snippets, the request headers, and all environment variables in the browser. That is exactly what you want locally and a serious information disclosure in production — connection strings and API keys are routinely visible in those environment variables.

So the danger is: anything that accidentally sets ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development in a deployed environment immediately exposes your secrets to anyone who can trigger an error.

That happens more often than you would expect — a copied Dockerfile, a Helm value that was never overridden, a base image with the variable baked in.

Defence in depth: do not rely solely on the environment check for anything genuinely sensitive. A production deployment can also verify the assumption at startup:

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment() && builder.Configuration["DeployRing"] == "prod")
    throw new InvalidOperationException(
        "Development environment on a production deployment — refusing to start.");

Failing to start is far better than running with debug tooling exposed.

docs.title: The deeper detail — custom environments
docs.text:
The three built-in names are just strings, and you can use your own:

ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=QA

if (app.Environment.IsEnvironment("QA"))
{
    app.UseMiddleware<TestDataSeedingMiddleware>();
}

appsettings.QA.json is then picked up automatically — the layering uses whatever name you set.

⚠️ But custom names are not "development-like". IsDevelopment() returns false for QA, so anything gated behind it is off. If you want QA to behave like development for tooling, you must say so explicitly:

var isDevLike = app.Environment.IsDevelopment() || app.Environment.IsEnvironment("QA");

Keep the list short. Every extra environment is another config file to maintain and another path that is rarely tested. Three or four is usually enough.

docs.title: Setting it in each place
docs.text:
# Locally — the shell
export ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development       # Linux/macOS
$env:ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT="Development"       # PowerShell

# Docker
ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production

# docker-compose
environment:
  - ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Staging

# Kubernetes
env:
  - name: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
    value: "Production"

# Azure App Service — an application setting of the same name

And in development, launchSettings.json sets it for you when you press F5 or run dotnet run:

{
  "profiles": {
    "MyApp": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
  }
}

⚠️ That file is development-only and never deployed. People assume it configures production and are surprised when nothing takes effect. See 4.8.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic environment-aware startup:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();

// Different database per environment, driven by configuration not code
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(options =>
    options.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));

// Detailed EF logging is expensive and leaks parameter values — dev only
if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(options =>
        options.EnableSensitiveDataLogging().EnableDetailedErrors());
}

var app = builder.Build();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();
    app.MapOpenApi();                          // never in production
}
else
{
    app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");         // generic, no internals leaked
    app.UseHsts();
}

app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Note EnableSensitiveDataLogging. It writes parameter values into your logs, so a query filtering by email address logs that email address. Genuinely useful when debugging locally, and a data-protection incident in production. The environment check is the only thing keeping those apart.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does ASP.NET Core know which environment it is running in?

From the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT environment variable. If it is not set, the framework defaults to Production, which is a deliberately safe choice — an app deployed without configuration behaves cautiously rather than exposing debug tooling. The name selects which appsettings.{Environment}.json file gets layered on top of the base appsettings.json, and you can check it in code through IWebHostEnvironment with IsDevelopment, IsProduction or IsEnvironment for custom names.

Q: What is the risk of the developer exception page?

It shows the full stack trace, source snippets, request headers and all environment variables in the browser. Environment variables routinely include connection strings and API keys, so if anything accidentally sets the environment to Development on a deployed system, triggering any error hands an attacker your secrets. That happens through copied Dockerfiles or Helm values that were never overridden more often than people expect. Beyond gating it on the environment check, I would have production refuse to start if it detects a Development environment name, because failing loudly beats running with debug tooling exposed.

Q: How do you configure different settings per environment?

Through configuration layering rather than code branching. appsettings.json holds shared defaults, and appsettings.{Environment}.json is layered on top with only the values that differ — so the staging file might override just the connection string and log level. Above those sit environment variables and command-line arguments, which take higher priority, and that is where secrets belong in a deployed environment. The point is that it is the same compiled binary everywhere, so what you tested is what you shipped.

Q: Can you have environments other than the three built-in ones?

Yes — the names are just strings, so setting ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=QA works and appsettings.QA.json is picked up automatically. The catch is that IsDevelopment() returns false for a custom name, so anything gated behind that check is off, and you have to opt into development-like behaviour explicitly. I would also keep the list short, because every extra environment is another config file to maintain and another code path that is rarely exercised.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Missing ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT means Production. Safe in deployment, confusing locally.
  • The developer exception page leaks environment variables, which usually contain secrets.
  • Environment names are case-insensitive in code but file names are case-sensitive on Linux. appsettings.production.json is silently ignored on Linux when the environment is Production.
  • launchSettings.json is development-only and never deployed.
  • Custom environments are not development-like. IsDevelopment() returns false for QA.
  • Copying the whole base file into each environment file causes drift. Override only the differences.
  • EnableSensitiveDataLogging writes parameter values to logs. Never outside development.
  • Do not put secrets in appsettings.{Environment}.json. Those files are in source control — see 17.7.

docs.title: 4.8 — launchSettings.json
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.7 Environments · Next: 4.9 Kestrel vs IIS vs HTTP.sys

Markers: ⚠️ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
launchSettings.json tells your IDE or dotnet run how to start the app on your own machine — which URL, which environment, which browser.

  • It lives in Properties/ and is development-only. It is never published and has no effect on a deployed application.
  • It is the usual place ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development gets set locally.
  • Do not put secrets in it. It is committed to source control.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means launchSettings.json a JSON file Lives in Properties/. Describes how to launch the app locally. Development only. Profile a named launch configuration One way of starting the app — the dropdown next to the run button in your IDE. commandName a profile setting Which launcher to use: Project (Kestrel), IISExpress, Executable, Docker. applicationUrl a profile setting The URLs to listen on locally. Semicolon-separated. environmentVariables a profile setting Variables set for that profile. This is where the environment name is set. launchBrowser a profile setting Whether to open a browser on start. dotnetRunMessages a profile setting Whether to print build/run progress messages. IIS Express a dev-only web server A lightweight IIS for local development on Windows. Not for production. ASPNETCORE_URLS an environment variable The deployed equivalent of applicationUrl. This one does apply in production.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
When you press F5, or run dotnet run, something has to decide:

  • Which port should the app listen on?
  • Which environment is this?
  • Should a browser open?

launchSettings.json answers those questions. It is a developer convenience file, and nothing more.

A picture: it is the preset on your car seat. It remembers how you like things when you get in. It has no effect on how the car behaves when someone else drives it, and it is certainly not part of the engine.

docs.title: ⚠️ The single most important fact
docs.text:
It is never deployed and has no effect in production.

dotnet publish does not copy it. The file sits in Properties/ next to your project, gets committed to git, and is used only by Visual Studio, Rider, VS Code and dotnet run.

This trips people up constantly:

"I set the environment to Staging in launchSettings.json but production is still running as Production."

Of course it is. The file was never deployed. Production takes its environment from a real environment variable set by the hosting platform — 4.7.

docs.title: The simple version — a typical file
docs.text:
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/launchsettings.json",
  "profiles": {
    // Profile 1 — run with Kestrel directly. The usual choice.
    "MyApp.Api": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "dotnetRunMessages": true,
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "swagger",
      "applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7183;http://localhost:5183",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },

    // Profile 2 — run behind IIS Express (Windows only)
    "IIS Express": {
      "commandName": "IISExpress",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },

    // Profile 3 — run in a container
    "Docker": {
      "commandName": "Docker",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "publishAllPorts": true
    }
  }
}

Each top-level key under profiles is a name you pick, and it appears in the run dropdown of your IDE.

Running a specific profile from the command line:

dotnet run --launch-profile "MyApp.Api"
dotnet run --no-launch-profile          # ignore the file entirely

docs.title: The commandName values
docs.text:
Value What it does Project Runs your app directly with Kestrel. The normal choice. IISExpress Runs behind IIS Express. Windows only, and increasingly rare. Executable Runs an arbitrary executable. Docker Builds and runs the container.

Project is what you want by default. It is closest to how the app runs in production — Kestrel, directly — so local behaviour matches deployed behaviour more closely. IIS Express introduces a proxy layer that can mask problems, or create ones that only exist locally.

docs.title: How it actually works — the precedence order
docs.text:
applicationUrl is one of several places a URL can come from, and the priority matters when they disagree:

1. app.Urls / UseUrls() in code        ← highest, wins over everything
2. --urls on the command line
3. ASPNETCORE_URLS environment variable
4. applicationUrl in launchSettings    ← development only
5. Default (http://localhost:5000)     ← lowest

Two practical consequences:

In production, only 1–3 exist. Setting ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080 in a container is the standard approach (4.2).

Calling UseUrls() in code overrides everything, which is why hard-coding a URL there makes the app impossible to configure at deployment time. Avoid it.

docs.title: Multiple profiles for different scenarios
docs.text:
The genuinely useful pattern:

{
  "profiles": {
    "Normal": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7183",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },

    // Point at a real staging database to reproduce a bug
    "Against Staging DB": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7183",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development",
        "ConnectionStrings__Default": "Server=staging-sql;Database=App;..."
      }
    },

    // Verify production-like error handling locally
    "Production mode": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7183",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Production"
      }
    }
  }
}

That third profile is worth having. Production behaviour differs — generic error pages, no Swagger, HSTS enabled — and being able to check it locally catches a class of bug that otherwise only appears after deployment.

Note the double underscore in ConnectionStrings__Default. That is how nested configuration keys are expressed as environment variables — __ becomes :. See 7.3.

docs.title: ⚠️ Do not put secrets here
docs.text:
// ✗ NEVER — this file is committed to git
"environmentVariables": {
  "ConnectionStrings__Default": "Server=prod;User=sa;Password=RealPassword123!",
  "ApiKeys__Stripe": "sk_live_abc123"
}

launchSettings.json is in source control by default. Anything in it is in your git history permanently, visible to everyone with repository access, and picked up by secret scanners.

Use User Secrets instead — they live outside the project folder and are never committed:

dotnet user-secrets init
dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:Default" "Server=localhost;..."
dotnet user-secrets set "ApiKeys:Stripe" "sk_test_..."

User Secrets are automatically loaded in Development only, which is exactly the right scope. See 7.3 and 17.7.

A pointer to a non-secret staging connection string in a launch profile is fine. Real credentials are not.

docs.title: The deeper detail — should it be in source control?
docs.text:
Yes, usually. It is genuinely useful for a team: everyone gets the same ports, the same profiles, and a new joiner can clone and press F5.

The friction is that it also carries personal preferences — one person wants the browser to open, another does not — so it generates small, noisy diffs.

Some teams gitignore it and provide a launchSettings.json.template instead. That works, at the cost of every new developer needing a setup step.

The pragmatic answer: commit it, keep it minimal, and never put a secret in it. The personal preferences are a small annoyance; a shared, working default is worth more.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A clean file for a typical API project:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/launchsettings.json",
  "profiles": {
    "API": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "dotnetRunMessages": true,
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "scalar/v1",
      "applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7183;http://localhost:5183",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
    "API (production mode)": {
      "commandName": "Project",
      "launchBrowser": false,
      "applicationUrl": "https://localhost:7183",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Production"
      }
    }
  }
}

And the deployed equivalent, which does not use this file at all:

ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
EXPOSE 8080

# Kubernetes
env:
  - name: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
    value: "Production"
  - name: ASPNETCORE_URLS
    value: "http://+:8080"

Those two blocks are the real configuration. launchSettings.json is only ever the local convenience.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is launchSettings.json and when does it apply?

It is a development-only file in the Properties folder that tells your IDE or dotnet run how to start the application locally — which URLs to listen on, which environment name to set, whether to open a browser. The critical point is that it is never published, so it has no effect whatsoever on a deployed application. Production takes its environment and URLs from real environment variables set by the hosting platform.

Q: Someone changed the environment in launchSettings.json but production is unchanged. Why?

Because the file is not deployed — dotnet publish does not copy it. It only affects local launches from an IDE or dotnet run. To change the environment in production you set the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT variable wherever the app is hosted: an ENV line in the Dockerfile, an env entry in a Kubernetes manifest, or an application setting in Azure App Service.

Q: Should secrets go in launchSettings.json?

No. It is committed to source control by default, so anything in it enters your git history permanently and is visible to everyone with repository access. For local development secrets the right tool is User Secrets, which store values outside the project folder in your user profile and are loaded automatically in Development only. A pointer to a non-sensitive local or staging resource is fine in a launch profile; real credentials are not.

Q: What is the difference between applicationUrl and ASPNETCORE_URLS?

They set the same thing but in different scopes. applicationUrl is a launch profile setting that only applies locally, while ASPNETCORE_URLS is a real environment variable that works everywhere, including in containers and on servers. The precedence runs from code — app.Urls or UseUrls — down through command-line arguments, then the environment variable, then launchSettings. Hard-coding URLs in code is worth avoiding because it overrides everything and makes the app impossible to configure at deployment time.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• It is never deployed. Changing it has zero effect on production.
  • Secrets in it end up in git history, permanently. Use User Secrets.
  • UseUrls() in code overrides everything, including the environment variable, making the app unconfigurable at deploy time.
  • IIS Express behaviour differs from Kestrel. Prefer the Project profile so local matches production more closely.
  • Nested config keys use double underscores in environment variables: ConnectionStrings__Default.
  • Deleting the file is harmless. The app falls back to http://localhost:5000 and Production.
  • dotnet run uses the first profile by default, which may not be the one you expect.

docs.title: 4.9 — Kestrel vs IIS vs HTTP.sys, In-Process vs Out-of-Process
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.8 launchSettings.json · Next: 4.10 Static files

Markers: ⭐ 🎯 · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core has three web servers, and you almost always use the first.

  • Kestrel — cross-platform, fast, the default. Runs inside your app process.
  • IIS — Windows only. In ASP.NET Core it acts as a reverse proxy in front of Kestrel, not as the host.
  • HTTP.sys — Windows only. The one case for it is Windows Authentication or port sharing.

In-process vs out-of-process is an IIS-only choice. In-process runs your app inside the IIS worker process and is roughly 2–3× faster. It is the default.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Kestrel a web server library Built into ASP.NET Core, cross-platform. Runs inside your application process. IIS Microsoft's Windows web server A separate Windows service. In ASP.NET Core it proxies to your app rather than hosting it. IIS Express a dev-only version of IIS Lightweight, for local development only. Never production. HTTP.sys a Windows kernel driver A server that uses the Windows kernel's HTTP stack directly. Alternative to Kestrel. ANCM an IIS module ASP.NET Core Module. The IIS component that launches your app or forwards requests to it. In-process an IIS hosting mode Your app runs inside the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). Default, faster. Out-of-process an IIS hosting mode IIS runs your app as a separate process and proxies over local HTTP. w3wp.exe a Windows process The IIS worker process. Hosts your app in in-process mode. App pool an IIS concept A worker process and its settings. Several sites can share one, or have their own. Windows Authentication an auth scheme Kerberos/NTLM domain authentication. Needs IIS or HTTP.sys. Port sharing an HTTP.sys feature Several processes listening on the same port. Kestrel cannot do this.

docs.title: Why there are three
docs.text:
They exist for different reasons, and only one of them is a real choice for most people.

Kestrel is the actual server. It is a library inside your application. Written for speed and cross-platform support. It is what runs your code in almost every deployment, including most IIS ones.

IIS is a Windows product that predates ASP.NET Core by fifteen years. Plenty of organisations run Windows Server with IIS already managing certificates, sites and app pools. Rather than force them to change, ASP.NET Core integrates with it.

HTTP.sys exists for two specific Windows features Kestrel cannot provide: Windows Authentication and port sharing. Outside those, there is no reason to pick it.

A picture: Kestrel is the engine. IIS is the garage it might be parked in. The engine still does the driving.

docs.title: The inversion from classic ASP.NET
docs.text:
This is the mental model shift worth being clear about.

Classic ASP.NET: IIS was the host. Your app was a plugin loaded into it. No IIS, no app.

ASP.NET Core: Your app is the host. Kestrel is inside it. IIS, if present, sits in front as a proxy.

That inversion is what makes dotnet run work with no web server installed, and what makes containers possible.

docs.title: The simple version — choosing
docs.text:
Situation Use Containers, Kubernetes, cloud Kestrel alone — the ingress or load balancer is the proxy Linux server Kestrel behind Nginx Windows Server, existing IIS estate Kestrel behind IIS, in-process Need Windows Authentication HTTP.sys, or IIS Need several processes on one port HTTP.sys Local development Kestrel — closest to production

The honest default for anything new is Kestrel behind whatever your platform already provides. In Kubernetes that is the ingress controller; in Azure App Service it is handled for you.

docs.title: How it actually works — in-process vs out-of-process
docs.text:
This is the part that gets asked about, so here it is precisely.

Out-of-process — the original model:

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"HTTPS :443"| I["IIS<br/>w3wp.exe"]
    I -->|"HTTP over localhost<br/>(a SECOND hop)"| K["Kestrel<br/>dotnet.exe<br/>separate process"]

IIS starts your application as a separate process and forwards each request to it over local HTTP. Two processes, two HTTP hops per request.

In-process — the default since .NET Core 3.0:

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"HTTPS :443"| I["IIS w3wp.exe<br/>─── your app runs INSIDE ───<br/>(IISHttpServer, not Kestrel)"]

Your application runs inside the IIS worker process. No second process, no extra hop. Roughly 2–3× the throughput.

⚠️ A detail worth knowing: in-process does not actually use Kestrel. It uses a different server implementation called IISHttpServer that talks to IIS directly. So "Kestrel behind IIS" is accurate for out-of-process and slightly wrong for in-process — which is a nice detail to have if an interviewer pushes.

Setting it:

<PropertyGroup>
  <AspNetCoreHostingModel>InProcess</AspNetCoreHostingModel>
</PropertyGroup>
In-process Out-of-process Extra HTTP hop No Yes Throughput 2–3× higher Lower Processes One Two Server used IISHttpServer Kestrel .NET version per app pool One shared Independent Crash isolation from IIS No Yes

Choose out-of-process when: several apps in one app pool need different .NET versions, or you want the app's crashes isolated from the IIS worker process.

Otherwise in-process, which is the default and almost always right.

docs.title: The deeper detail — what each server can and cannot do
Can Kestrel face the internet directly?
docs.text:
Yes, and it commonly does — every Kubernetes deployment does exactly this, with the ingress controller as the proxy.

Microsoft's guidance used to be "never expose Kestrel directly", and that has softened. Kestrel is a mature, security-reviewed server now.

What you still get from a proxy:

  • TLS certificate management in one place rather than per app
  • Several apps on one port, routed by path or hostname
  • Slow-client protection absorbed by the proxy
  • Request buffering, so slow clients do not occupy app threads
  • Static file serving, usually faster

On a single VM serving one app, Kestrel with a firewall is defensible. On a shared host, or anywhere you want centralised TLS, a proxy earns its place. See 4.2.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Configuring each, for reference:

// Kestrel — the default, so this is only needed to tune it
builder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel(options =>
{
    options.Limits.MaxRequestBodySize = 10 * 1024 * 1024;
    options.Limits.MaxConcurrentConnections = 1000;
    options.Limits.KeepAliveTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2);

    // Explicit endpoint with a certificate, if not terminating TLS at a proxy
    options.ListenAnyIP(5001, listen => listen.UseHttps("cert.pfx", "password"));
});

// HTTP.sys — replaces Kestrel entirely
builder.WebHost.UseHttpSys(options =>
{
    options.Authentication.Schemes = AuthenticationSchemes.Negotiate;
    options.Authentication.AllowAnonymous = false;
    options.MaxConnections = 100;
    options.UrlPrefixes.Add("http://+:8080");
});

<!-- IIS hosting model, in the .csproj -->
<PropertyGroup>
  <AspNetCoreHostingModel>InProcess</AspNetCoreHostingModel>
</PropertyGroup>

<!-- web.config — generated on publish for IIS. You rarely edit it by hand. -->
<configuration>
  <system.webServer>
    <handlers>
      <add name="aspNetCore" path="*" verb="*"
           modules="AspNetCoreModuleV2" resourceType="Unspecified" />
    </handlers>
    <aspNetCore processPath="dotnet"
                arguments=".\MyApp.dll"
                hostingModel="inprocess"
                stdoutLogEnabled="false" />
  </system.webServer>
</configuration>

⚠️ stdoutLogEnabled="true" is a common debugging step and a common production mistake. It writes every log line to disk with no rotation, and eventually fills the drive. Turn it on to diagnose a startup failure, then turn it off.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: What is the relationship between Kestrel and IIS in ASP.NET Core?

The relationship is inverted from classic ASP.NET. There, IIS was the host and your application was a plugin loaded into it. In ASP.NET Core, Kestrel is a library inside your application, so the app is self-hosting, and IIS — when present — acts as a reverse proxy in front of it, handling TLS, site routing and process management. That inversion is what makes cross-platform hosting and containers possible, because the app no longer needs IIS to exist at all.

Q: What is the difference between in-process and out-of-process hosting?

Both apply only when hosting on IIS. Out-of-process means IIS launches your application as a separate process and proxies each request to it over local HTTP, which costs a second HTTP hop per request. In-process means the application runs inside the IIS worker process itself, removing that hop and roughly doubling to tripling throughput. In-process has been the default since .NET Core 3.0. One detail worth knowing is that in-process does not use Kestrel at all — it uses a separate IISHttpServer implementation that talks to IIS directly.

Q: When would you choose HTTP.sys over Kestrel?

Two cases, both Windows-only. Windows Authentication — Kerberos or NTLM — which Kestrel cannot do on its own, so on Windows without IIS, HTTP.sys is the option. And port sharing, where several processes need to listen on the same port for different URL paths; HTTP.sys can do that because it is a kernel driver, whereas Kestrel opens a normal socket and owns the port exclusively. Outside those two, there is no reason to prefer it.

Q: Can you expose Kestrel directly to the internet?

Yes, and it is common — every Kubernetes deployment does it, with the ingress controller acting as the proxy. Microsoft's older guidance against it has softened as Kestrel matured. What a proxy still gives you is centralised TLS certificate management, hosting several apps on one port routed by hostname or path, absorbing slow-client attacks, and buffering requests so slow clients do not tie up application threads. On a single VM serving one application behind a firewall, Kestrel alone is defensible.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• In-process does not use Kestrel. It uses IISHttpServer, which is a different implementation.
  • In-process shares the IIS worker process, so an unhandled crash can take down the app pool.
  • stdoutLogEnabled="true" has no log rotation and will eventually fill the disk.
  • Kestrel cannot do Windows Authentication alone. It needs IIS or HTTP.sys in front.
  • HTTP.sys is Windows-only, so choosing it rules out Linux and containers permanently.
  • IIS Express is not IIS. Local behaviour can differ from the deployed server.
  • The web.config for IIS is generated on publish. Hand-edits to the one in your project can be overwritten.
  • Kestrel's default limits exist for protection. Raising MaxRequestBodySize without thinking removes a denial-of-service guard.

docs.title: 4.10 — wwwroot and Static Files
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.9 Kestrel vs IIS vs HTTP.sys · Next: 4.11 Project structure

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Static files are files served exactly as they are on disk — images, CSS, JavaScript, PDFs. No code runs to produce them.

  • Only the wwwroot folder is served, and only if you call app.UseStaticFiles(). Nothing else in your project is reachable.
  • Anything you put in wwwroot is public. There is no authentication on it by default.
  • Register the middleware early in the pipeline, so image requests do not run authentication and routing for nothing.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Static file a file served as-is Returned byte-for-byte from disk. No processing, no code execution. Web root a folder wwwroot by default. The only folder publicly served. Content root a folder The app's base directory, where appsettings.json and DLLs live. Not served. UseStaticFiles() a middleware method Enables serving files from the web root. Without it, nothing is served. UseFileServer() a middleware method Static files + default files + optional directory browsing, in one call. UseDefaultFiles() a middleware method Serves index.html when a directory is requested. Must come before UseStaticFiles. UseDirectoryBrowser() a middleware method Lists folder contents in the browser. A security risk — see traps. StaticFileOptions a class Configures caching headers, extra folders, content types. MIME type a content-type string image/png, text/css. Unknown extensions are not served by default. FileExtensionContentTypeProvider a class Lets you register MIME types for unusual extensions. PhysicalFileProvider a class Serves from a specific disk folder. Used to add folders beyond wwwroot. MapStaticAssets() a method (.NET 9+) Newer alternative with build-time compression and fingerprinting.

docs.title: Two folders, one of them public
docs.text:
Every ASP.NET Core app has two important directories, and confusing them is a security problem.

MyApp/                          ← CONTENT ROOT (not served)
├── appsettings.json            ← contains connection strings. NOT reachable.
├── Program.cs
├── MyApp.dll
└── wwwroot/                    ← WEB ROOT (publicly served)
    ├── css/site.css            ← anyone can download
    ├── js/app.js               ← anyone can download
    └── images/logo.png         ← anyone can download

Only wwwroot is served. A request for /appsettings.json returns 404, because that file is in the content root, not the web root.

That is a deliberate safety design. In classic ASP.NET the whole application folder was inside the site, so protecting files meant configuring IIS correctly. ASP.NET Core inverts the default: nothing is public unless you put it in wwwroot.

A picture: wwwroot is the shop window. Everything else is the stockroom. Anything you put in the window, anyone walking past can see. There is no lock on it.

docs.title: Nothing is served unless you ask
docs.text:
Consistent with everything else in ASP.NET Core, static file serving is opt-in:

app.UseStaticFiles();     // without this line, wwwroot is not served at all

A brand-new Web API project does not include this, because an API has no CSS or images to serve. Add it only if you actually need it.

docs.title: The simple version — enabling it
docs.text:
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseStaticFiles();     // serve everything in wwwroot

app.Run();

A file at wwwroot/css/site.css is now reachable at /css/site.css. The wwwroot part is not in the URL — it is the root.

Referencing it in HTML:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="~/css/site.css" />
<img src="~/images/logo.png" alt="Logo" />

The ~/ is a Razor convention meaning "from the web root", and it resolves correctly even when the app is hosted in a subfolder.

docs.title: ⚠️ Where to put it in the pipeline
docs.text:
Early — before authentication and routing.

app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseStaticFiles();          // ← HERE
app.UseRouting();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

Why it matters: middleware runs in order, and static files short-circuit the pipeline. When a request for /images/logo.png matches a file, that middleware returns it immediately and nothing below runs.

Put UseStaticFiles after authentication and every image request goes through JWT validation, a database lookup for claims, and routing — before serving a file that needed none of it. On a page with forty assets, that is forty pointless authentication cycles.

See 5.2.

docs.title: ⚠️ Static files are not protected
docs.text:
This is the security point of the note.

UseStaticFiles runs before authentication in the recommended order, which means files in wwwroot are served to anyone, with no authentication check at all.

wwwroot/
└── documents/
    └── salaries-2026.pdf     ← anyone who guesses the URL can download this

No login. No authorization policy. Just the URL.

If a file needs protection, it must not be in wwwroot. Serve it through a controller instead:

[Authorize(Policy = "HR")]
[HttpGet("documents/{id:guid}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Download(Guid id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var doc = await _docs.GetAsync(id, ct);
    if (doc is null) return NotFound();

    // Stored OUTSIDE wwwroot, so it is not directly reachable
    var path = Path.Combine(_env.ContentRootPath, "protected-docs", doc.FileName);

    return PhysicalFile(path, "application/pdf", doc.OriginalName);
}

Now the file lives outside the web root, and every download passes through authorization.

⚠️ And never build that path from user input — Path.Combine(root, userSuppliedName) with ../../appsettings.json is a path traversal attack. Look the filename up from your database using an ID, as above. See 17.11.

docs.title: How it actually works — caching
docs.text:
By default static files are served with no caching headers, so browsers re-request them every time. For anything real you want caching:

app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    OnPrepareResponse = ctx =>
    {
        // Cache for 7 days
        ctx.Context.Response.Headers.CacheControl = "public,max-age=604800";
    }
});

That creates the classic problem: how do users get a new version of site.css? They will keep the cached copy for a week.

The standard answer is cache busting — change the URL when the content changes:

<!-- Razor's asp-append-version adds a hash of the file contents -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="~/css/site.css" asp-append-version="true" />
<!-- renders as: /css/site.css?v=Kl_dqr9NVtnMdsM2MUg4qthUnWZm5T1fCEimBPWDNgM -->

The hash changes only when the file changes, so browsers cache aggressively and still pick up updates immediately.

In .NET 9+, MapStaticAssets() does this automatically, plus build-time compression:

app.MapStaticAssets();     // fingerprinting + gzip/brotli precompression

It is the better default for new apps.

docs.title: The deeper detail — serving other folders and unknown types
docs.text:
A folder outside wwwroot:

app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
{
    FileProvider = new PhysicalFileProvider(
        Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "uploads")),
    RequestPath = "/files"        // reachable at /files/...
});

⚠️ Everything in that folder is now public too. The same rule applies — do not put anything sensitive there.

Unknown file extensions are not served. If the MIME type is unrecognised, the file is skipped and you get a 404 — which is confusing, because the file is clearly there:

var provider = new FileExtensionContentTypeProvider();
provider.Mappings[".glb"] = "model/gltf-binary";
provider.Mappings[".webmanifest"] = "application/manifest+json";

app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions { ContentTypeProvider = provider });

This is a deliberate safety default. Serving files of unknown type with a guessed content-type invites browsers to interpret them in unexpected ways. Register the types you genuinely need rather than enabling ServeUnknownFileTypes, which turns the protection off wholesale.

docs.title: Should your app serve static files at all?
docs.text:
In production, often not. A CDN or reverse proxy does it better:

  • Served from an edge location near the user
  • Compression and caching handled for you
  • Your application threads stay free for actual requests

So the common production setup is: static assets on a CDN, API served by your app. Serving them from ASP.NET Core is fine for small apps and for development, and it is one of the first things to move when traffic grows.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A complete configuration for an app that does serve its own assets:

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    // No caching locally, so changes appear immediately on refresh
    app.UseStaticFiles();
}
else
{
    app.UseStaticFiles(new StaticFileOptions
    {
        OnPrepareResponse = ctx =>
        {
            ctx.Context.Response.Headers.CacheControl = "public,max-age=604800";
        }
    });
}

app.UseRouting();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

And the folder layout that keeps sensitive files out of reach:

MyApp/
├── appsettings.json              ← not served
├── protected-docs/               ← not served — reached only via controller
│   └── salaries-2026.pdf
└── wwwroot/                      ← PUBLIC
    ├── css/
    ├── js/
    └── images/

The rule to remember: if it should not be on the public internet, it does not go in wwwroot.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How does ASP.NET Core serve static files?

Through the static files middleware, enabled with app.UseStaticFiles(). It serves the web root folder, which is wwwroot by default, and nothing else — so a request for appsettings.json returns 404 because that lives in the content root rather than the web root. Nothing is served unless you add the middleware, which is why a new Web API project has no static file support at all. The wwwroot segment does not appear in URLs; it is the root.

Q: Where should UseStaticFiles go in the pipeline, and why?

Early — before routing and authentication. Static file middleware short-circuits the pipeline when it matches a file, returning it immediately without running anything below. If you put it after authentication, every image and stylesheet request runs JWT validation and any claims lookup before serving a file that needed none of it. On a page with forty assets that is forty wasted authentication cycles per page load.

Q: Are static files protected by authorization?

No, and that is the important security point. Because the middleware runs before authentication, anything in wwwroot is downloadable by anyone who knows the URL, with no login and no policy check. So a file that needs protection must not live in wwwroot at all — you store it outside the web root and serve it through a controller action with an [Authorize] attribute, returning it with PhysicalFile. And you look the filename up by ID rather than building a path from user input, or you have created a path traversal vulnerability.

Q: How do you handle caching for static files?

By default they are served with no caching headers, so you set Cache-Control through OnPrepareResponse in StaticFileOptions. That creates the cache-invalidation problem, which you solve by changing the URL when the content changes — Razor's asp-append-version appends a content hash so browsers cache aggressively but pick up new versions immediately. In .NET 9 and later MapStaticAssets does the fingerprinting and build-time compression automatically. In production, though, static assets are often better served from a CDN entirely, which keeps your application threads free for real requests.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Anything in wwwroot is public. No authentication, no authorization, ever.
  • UseStaticFiles placed after authentication wastes work on every asset request.
  • Nothing is served without UseStaticFiles(). New API projects do not include it.
  • Unknown file extensions return 404, which looks like the file is missing. Register the MIME type.
  • ServeUnknownFileTypes = true disables a safety check wholesale. Register specific types instead.
  • UseDirectoryBrowser lists your folder contents to anyone. Never enable it in production.
  • UseDefaultFiles must come before UseStaticFiles, or it has no effect.
  • Building a file path from user input is path traversal. Look it up by ID.
  • Content root and web root are different folders. Only one of them is public.

docs.title: 4.11 — Project Structure Conventions for a Web API
docs.text:
← Roadmap · Section: 4. Fundamentals and Application Startup Prev: 4.10 Static files · Next: 5.1 What middleware is

Markers: ⭐ · Confidence: 🔴 · Last reviewed: —

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
There is no official ASP.NET Core project structure. The framework does not care where your files live — but the choice shapes how the codebase ages.

  • Start with one project and folders. Split into separate projects only when you have a real reason.
  • Two common approaches: layer-based (Controllers, Services, Models) and feature-based (Orders, Payments, Customers).
  • Feature-based scales better, because a change to one feature touches one folder instead of five.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term What it is What it means Project one .csproj Compiles to one assembly. See 3.6. Solution one .sln file A container grouping several projects. Layer-based structure a folder convention Folders named after technical roles: Controllers/, Services/, Models/. Feature-based structure a folder convention Folders named after business capabilities: Orders/, Payments/. Vertical slice an architectural style Each feature holds everything it needs, top to bottom. See 22.11. Clean Architecture an architectural style Layers as separate projects, with dependencies pointing inward. See 22.7. Modular monolith an architectural style One deployable app, internally split into independent modules. DTO a class Data Transfer Object. The shape you expose over HTTP, distinct from your database entity. Registration extension a static method An AddSomething(this IServiceCollection) method grouping a module's DI registrations.

docs.title: The framework has no opinion
docs.text:
This surprises people coming from frameworks with enforced conventions. ASP.NET Core does not require Controllers/ to be called that, does not care where your services live, and will happily find a controller anywhere in the assembly.

So structure is entirely a maintainability decision, and the honest answer to "what is the right structure?" is it depends on size.

The failure mode worth avoiding is starting with the structure you think a large system needs. A four-project Clean Architecture solution for a service with six endpoints is a lot of ceremony buying nothing — and it is a very common mistake, because it looks professional.

A picture: you do not build a warehouse with loading bays and a forklift to store six boxes. You use a cupboard, and you build the warehouse when you have enough boxes to justify it.

docs.title: The simple version — layer-based
docs.text:
The default from the templates, and fine for small projects:

MyApp.Api/
├── Program.cs
├── appsettings.json
├── Controllers/
│   ├── OrdersController.cs
│   ├── CustomersController.cs
│   └── PaymentsController.cs
├── Services/
│   ├── OrderService.cs
│   ├── CustomerService.cs
│   └── PaymentService.cs
├── Models/
│   ├── Order.cs
│   ├── Customer.cs
│   └── Payment.cs
├── Data/
│   └── AppDbContext.cs
└── wwwroot/

Folders are named after what a thing is technically.

It works well up to maybe 10–15 endpoints. Past that, a problem appears: adding one field to an order means editing Controllers/OrdersController.cs, Services/OrderService.cs, Models/Order.cs and Data/AppDbContext.cs — four folders, and the related code is scattered.

docs.title: Feature-based — the one that scales
docs.text:
Folders named after what the code does for the business:

MyApp.Api/
├── Program.cs
├── Features/
│   ├── Orders/
│   │   ├── OrdersController.cs
│   │   ├── OrderService.cs
│   │   ├── OrderRepository.cs
│   │   ├── CreateOrderRequest.cs
│   │   ├── OrderDto.cs
│   │   └── OrderModuleExtensions.cs      ← its own DI registration
│   ├── Payments/
│   │   ├── PaymentsController.cs
│   │   └── ...
│   └── Customers/
│       └── ...
├── Common/
│   ├── Middleware/
│   └── Extensions/
└── Data/
    └── AppDbContext.cs

Now everything about orders is in one folder. Three practical consequences:

  • A change to orders touches one folder. Easier to review, easier to reason about.
  • Deleting a feature is deleting a folder. With layers, orphaned pieces get left behind.
  • Ownership is obvious. One team owns Features/Payments/.

The trade-off is that shared code needs a home, which is what Common/ is for. Watch that it does not become a dumping ground.

For a new API of any size, feature-based is the better default.

docs.title: How it actually works — the registration extension pattern
docs.text:
Feature folders pair naturally with keeping each module's DI registrations next to its code:

// Features/Orders/OrderModuleExtensions.cs
public static class OrderModuleExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddOrderModule(
        this IServiceCollection services,
        IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
        services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
        services.Configure<OrderOptions>(config.GetSection("Orders"));
        return services;                   // return it so calls chain
    }
}

// Program.cs stays readable no matter how many features exist
builder.Services
    .AddOrderModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddPaymentModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddCustomerModule(builder.Configuration);

Two benefits: Program.cs does not grow linearly with the codebase, and deleting a feature folder does not leave orphaned registrations behind — because they were inside it.

See 1.14 and 4.3.

docs.title: The deeper detail — when to split into separate projects
docs.text:
The real question is not folders but projects. Each project is a separate assembly with its own build.

Reasons that justify a split:

  • You genuinely share code between two deployables — an API and a worker service both needing the same domain types.
  • You want to enforce a dependency direction. If Domain is a separate project that references nothing, the compiler stops anyone importing EF Core into it. Folders cannot enforce that.
  • Separate test projects, which is standard and not really a debate.

Reasons that do not:

  • "It looks more professional."
  • "The tutorial did it."
  • "We might need it later."

Every extra project adds build time, another .csproj to maintain, and more navigation friction. Start with one, split when the pain is real.

A reasonable progression:

# Stage 1 — a small API
MyApp.Api/
MyApp.Api.Tests/

# Stage 2 — logic worth isolating and testing separately
MyApp.Api/
MyApp.Core/            ← domain + business logic, no framework dependencies
MyApp.Core.Tests/
MyApp.Api.Tests/

# Stage 3 — full Clean Architecture, if it earns its place
MyApp.Api/             ← controllers, middleware, DI wiring
MyApp.Application/     ← use cases, interfaces, DTOs
MyApp.Domain/          ← entities, value objects. References NOTHING.
MyApp.Infrastructure/  ← EF Core, HTTP clients, file system

Most services never need stage 3, and reaching it too early costs more than it saves. See 22.7.

docs.title: Things that are not negotiable
docs.text:
A few conventions genuinely matter:

Keep DTOs separate from entities. Returning your EF entity from a controller leaks your database schema, invites over-posting, and causes serialization cycles through navigation properties. See 10.11 and 11.10.

Nothing sensitive in wwwroot. It is public — 4.10.

Controllers stay thin. A controller reads the request, calls one service, and returns a result. Business logic in a controller cannot be unit tested without the whole web stack.

// ✓ Thin — delegates and translates
[HttpPost]
public async Task<IActionResult> Create(CreateOrderRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var result = await _orders.CreateAsync(request, ct);
    return result.IsSuccess
        ? CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = result.Value.Id }, result.Value)
        : BadRequest(result.Error);
}

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
A realistic feature-based API structure:

MyApp.Api/
├── Program.cs
├── appsettings.json
├── appsettings.Development.json
│
├── Features/
│   ├── Orders/
│   │   ├── OrdersController.cs
│   │   ├── OrderService.cs
│   │   ├── IOrderService.cs
│   │   ├── Contracts/
│   │   │   ├── CreateOrderRequest.cs
│   │   │   └── OrderResponse.cs
│   │   ├── Validators/
│   │   │   └── CreateOrderValidator.cs
│   │   └── OrderModuleExtensions.cs
│   │
│   └── Payments/
│       └── ... (same shape)
│
├── Common/
│   ├── Middleware/
│   │   └── GlobalExceptionHandler.cs
│   ├── Extensions/
│   │   └── ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
│   └── Results/
│       └── Result.cs
│
├── Data/
│   ├── AppDbContext.cs
│   ├── Configurations/          ← IEntityTypeConfiguration classes
│   └── Migrations/
│
└── wwwroot/                     ← public. Nothing sensitive.

// Program.cs — short regardless of how many features exist
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")));

builder.Services
    .AddOrderModule(builder.Configuration)
    .AddPaymentModule(builder.Configuration);

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Notice that Program.cs looks the same whether there are three features or thirty. That is the point of the pattern.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Q: How would you structure an ASP.NET Core Web API project?

The framework has no required structure, so it is purely a maintainability decision. For anything beyond a handful of endpoints I would organise by feature rather than by technical layer — a folder per business capability holding its controller, service, DTOs and validators together, rather than separate Controllers, Services and Models folders. The reason is that changes arrive by feature, so a feature folder means one place to look, and deleting a capability is deleting a folder rather than hunting for orphaned pieces across five directories.

Q: When would you split into multiple projects?

When there is a concrete reason, not by default. Genuine reasons are sharing code between two deployables, such as an API and a worker service needing the same domain types, or enforcing a dependency direction — if the domain is its own project referencing nothing, the compiler prevents anyone importing EF Core into it, which folders cannot do. Test projects are separate as a matter of course. What I would avoid is starting with a four-project Clean Architecture solution for a small service, because every project adds build time and navigation friction and you get nothing back until the codebase is large enough to need the separation.

Q: What is the difference between layer-based and feature-based organisation?

Layer-based names folders after technical roles — Controllers, Services, Models — which is what the templates give you and works fine for small projects. Feature-based names them after business capabilities — Orders, Payments, Customers — with each folder holding everything that feature needs. The practical difference shows up as the codebase grows: with layers, adding a field to an order means editing four folders, and the related code is scattered. With features it is one folder. Feature-based also makes ownership obvious when several teams work in the same repository.

Q: What conventions genuinely matter regardless of structure?

Three. DTOs stay separate from entities, because returning an EF entity leaks your schema, enables over-posting, and causes serialization problems through navigation properties. Nothing sensitive goes in wwwroot, since it is served publicly with no authorization. And controllers stay thin — read the request, call one service, translate the result — because business logic in a controller cannot be unit tested without standing up the whole web stack.

docs.title: Traps ⚠️
docs.text:
• Adopting Clean Architecture before the codebase needs it. Four projects for six endpoints is cost with no benefit.
  • Common/ becoming a dumping ground. If everything depends on it, you have recreated a single layer.
  • Returning EF entities from controllers. Leaks the schema and invites over-posting.
  • Business logic in controllers. Untestable without the full web stack.
  • DI registrations all in Program.cs. It grows without limit and deleting a feature leaves orphaned lines.
  • Anything sensitive in wwwroot. It is public.
  • Splitting projects to "enforce" a rule that a folder would have expressed. Only a project boundary is compiler-enforced — use one when that enforcement is the point.
